sens: what is given or received in return for something else
compensation or reward for an action or service
H2500.detail:
1. The word evokes a transaction where something is received in return for something else: it is the idea of a fair exchange. In Numbers 18:21, the Levites receive the tithe "in exchange for" the service they render at the tabernacle — it is their remuneration for their dedicated work.
2. More broadly, it is a compensation or reward: what is given or received to fulfill a function or obligation. In Numbers 18:31, the Levites may eat this tithe "in return for" their ministry — it is the price of their consecration to the service of God.
H2500.origine: The Hebrew word חֵלֶף comes from a root that fundamentally means "to change" or "to substitute for": the idea is that one thing replaces another, that there is an exchange. The constructed form (as in our verses) introduces the term of this exchange: that for which something is given or received. It is a classic Hebrew word, without a common Greek equivalent, that appears infrequently in the Old Testament.
H2500.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, and always in the context of the priestly law of Leviticus and Numbers. In Numbers 18:21 and 18:31, God prescribes that the Levites receive the tithe from the Israelites "in exchange for" or "in return for" their ministry at the tabernacle. This is not an ordinary salary: it is a divine reward for dedicated service, a share that rightfully belongs to them according to the covenant. The word emphasizes the fairness of the sharing: those who serve God in worship receive their food directly from the people, without owning land like the other tribes.
H2500.portee: This notion of just and divine exchange reminds the Christian that service rendered to God has value and bears fruit: God never leaves without reward those who dedicate themselves to His worship and work. It also affirms that God's ministers have the right to live from their ministry — a principle that the Apostle Paul will reiterate in the New Testament by teaching that the worker deserves his wages.

sens: border town of the territory of Naphtali
H2501.detail: Heleph is a locality in the northern region of Canaan, marking the starting point of the border of the territory allocated to the tribe of Naphtali during the land distribution (Joshua 19:33). The name evokes the idea of "exchange" in Hebrew, perhaps because this place constituted a crossing point or a commercial crossroads.
H2501.origine: The Hebrew name Heleph (חֵלֶף) derives from a root meaning "to change" or "to barter." This etymology suggests that the place was a point of exchange or a border where territories met and changed. The biblical geography of tribal borders often uses names that reflect characteristics of the landscape or the function of the site.
H2501.emploi: Heleph appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:33, during the detailed description of the borders of the territory of Naphtali. This passage is part of the account where Joshua divides the land of Canaan among the twelve tribes of Israel after the conquest. Heleph is mentioned as the starting point ("from Heleph") of the northwestern boundary of the Naphtalite territory, followed by other localities such as Allon, Tsaanannim, and Jabneel before reaching the Jordan.

sens: To take away, physically remove
To take off, strip of clothing or armor
To rescue from danger, save
To free from oppression or the power of someone
H2502A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is material: to take away or remove something. In Leviticus 14:40, it is commanded to remove the diseased stones from a house and throw them outside: it is a concrete act of separation and withdrawal.

2. The verb can also mean to remove clothing or armor. In Deuteronomy 25:10, the woman removes the sandal from the husband who refuses his duty: a symbolic and legal gesture that marks dishonor.

3. Figuratively, to deliver means to pull someone from immediate danger or threat. In Psalms 34:8, the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them from danger: an image of active protection that pulls a person out of peril.

4. The word expands further to express a deeper liberation: saving someone from the power of an oppressor, suffering, or even death itself. In Psalms 116:8, God has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling: a total deliverance that touches the whole being.
H2502A.origine: The root חלץ evokes the idea of pulling out, extracting, freeing. It paints the image of something coming out of a situation of confinement or danger. The verb has three main forms depending on the context: the simple form expresses withdrawal or removal; the passive form (Niphal) describes the act of being delivered; the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the idea of pulling out or rescuing with force and urgency.
H2502A.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms (nearly 10 occurrences) and the legal books. It primarily designates a concrete act: removing stones (Leviticus), taking off a sandal (Deuteronomy). But its use grows: it is God who delivers Israel in times of crisis. The psalmist constantly implores: "Deliver me from evil, save me from my enemies," and he praises God for past deliverances. This word expresses God's saving action toward His threatened people. In Proverbs 11:8-9, we see justice delivering the righteous from danger while the wicked sink into it: to deliver is also the effect of divine justice.
H2502A.portee: This verb reminds the believer that God is not a distant God: He acts, intervenes, and pulls His people from distress. When we pray "Deliver me," we acknowledge that our salvation depends solely on God, not on our strength. It is a word of hope in the Psalms, showing that God hears the cry of those who fear Him and actively protects them. For a child of God, knowing this verb is to learn to rely on God's liberating power in the face of all that threatens us.

sens: To equip warriors with their weapons for battle
To prepare for combat by putting on one's weapons
To be equipped with strength or ability to carry out an action
H2502B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to equip soldiers with their weapons in preparation for battle: Moses asks the people to equip men for the army that will march against Midian (Numbers 31:3). It is the act of providing warriors with the necessary martial equipment.
2. The word also applies to the state of the warrior who has armed himself and is preparing to fight: the Gadites and Reubenites arm themselves and cross the Jordan, ready for battle before the Lord (Numbers 32:20). It is the act of putting on one's own weapons.
3. By extension, the term can mean to be equipped with an inner strength or vigor: in Isaiah 58:11, the Lord strengthens and invigorates the one who fasts sincerely, as if giving him the spiritual means to advance.
H2502B.origine: The Hebrew verb חָלַץ comes from a root that evokes the idea of detaching, extracting, or making available. Its basic image is that of girding or putting on — as one adjusts their weapons before battle. The same family of words can express the idea of strength and vigor, hence its metaphorical use to reinforce or invigorate.
H2502B.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Chronicles) and occasionally in the prophets. It regularly describes Israel's military deployment: the equipping of warriors for a campaign (Numbers 31:3, 32:20-29), the armed march before the Ark during the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 4:13), or the siege of Jericho (Joshua 6:9). The uses show that the term is less attached to the weapon itself than to the state or action of equipping and preparing. Its meaning nuances between the material equipment of the warrior and, in prophetic context, the strength or spiritual vigor conferred by God.
H2502B.portee: This word reminds us that the fight of faith requires conscious preparation: to arm oneself is to equip oneself with everything necessary to stand firm. For the believer, this evokes the call to put on the armor of God and to be strengthened in His power — not by our own strength, but by the strength that God gives us. It is also a call not to remain passive, but to be ready and equipped in the face of the challenges that arise.

sens: Warrior of Ephraim in the service of King David
Military chief responsible for the seventh month
Man of Judah, son of Azariah
H2503G.detail:
1. Helets is an Ephraimite, meaning a man from the tribe of Ephraim, who is listed among David's thirty elite warriors. He is mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:26 as coming from Peleth, and was a renowned fighter in the service of the king.
2. Helets holds a military administrative position under David's reign: he leads the seventh monthly division of the royal army, commanding a unit of twenty-four thousand men (1 Chronicles 27:10). This responsibility highlights the importance of his role in the military organization of the kingdom.
3. Another man bearing the same name is mentioned in the genealogical record of Judah, identified as the son of Azariah (1 Chronicles 2).
H2503G.origine: The name Helets literally means "he has saved" or "he has delivered," derived from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of rescue or liberation. This type of theophoric name (containing a reference to God) was common in Israel and reflected values of divine protection and deliverance.
H2503G.emploi: Helets appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in lists of officers or warriors of King David. In 2 Samuel 23:26 and 1 Chronicles 11:27, he is counted among David's thirty mightiest warriors, with mention of his place of origin (Peleth or Palon). In 1 Chronicles 27:10, he is presented as commander of the seventh month in David's rotating system, indicating an administrative rise after his time as a fighter. These three mentions place him in the time of the united Church, under David's reign.
H2503G.portee: Helets illustrates the role of loyal warriors to the king and the administrative organization that David established to ensure the stability of his kingdom. His ascent from fighter to commanding officer shows how loyal service and military capabilities could lead to governmental responsibilities. For the Christian reader, his story reminds us of the importance of faithfulness and service, even within human structures of authority.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Azariah and father of Elasa
H2503H.detail:
1. Halets is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of this tribe during the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 2:39). He is a secondary character in the biblical narrative, primarily known for his place in the family lineage.
2. Halets is the son of Azariah and the father of Elasa, as indicated in his entry in the genealogical tree of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:39). He represents a link in the chain of generations that connects the families of Judah to one another.
H2503H.origine: The name Halets means "he has saved" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing salvation or deliverance. This theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel and reflected the parents' trust in divine protection.
H2503H.emploi: Halets appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:39, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as part of the lineage of Judah during the divided monarchy. This genealogical mention served to establish the identity and land rights of the families of Judah after the return from exile. Although not detailed, this verse confirms his role in the continuity of God's people.

sens: Part of the body located below the ribs, on either side of the spine
Seat of strength, virility, and fertility
Seat of pain and suffering, especially during childbirth
Center of intimate emotions and moral conscience
H2504.detail:
1. The loins are primarily a part of the human body, the organ located beneath the ribs. Job speaks of his "loins" that have not blessed him, referring to himself in his living body (Job 31:20).

2. The loins represent the source of life and creative power: this is why a descendant comes from the loins of his father (Genesis 35:11; 1 Kings 8:19). This image expresses how life is transmitted from generation to generation through man.

3. The loins are also where strength and courage are tied. When God tells Job, "Gird up your loins like a man," He invites him to brace himself, to prepare with determination to face what is coming (Job 38:3).

4. Finally, the loins can be the seat of deep pain, particularly the suffering of a woman in childbirth. The prophet Jeremiah says that Zion cries "like a woman in labor" (Jeremiah 30:6), thus expressing an agony that permeates the whole being.
H2504.origine: The Hebrew word חָלָץ (chalats) comes from a root that means primarily "to gird" or "to surround." The loins are what is girded, what one surrounds with a belt to prepare for action — hence the expression "gird up your loins." In biblical Hebrew, the loins are also associated with the seat of moral conscience and deep emotions, like the heart or soul.
H2504.emploi: The word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mostly in the poetic and prophetic books. It first denotes the human body concretely, but soon becomes a spiritual symbol. In Genesis and Kings, "to come out of someone's loins" means to be his direct descendant. In Job, girding the loins is a call to preparation and courage in the face of existential questions. In the prophets, the pain of the loins expresses the spiritual agony of the people or of Zion in distress. The image always nuances between the physical and the inner: it is never just the body, it is always what is rooted within — strength, life, conscience, suffering.
H2504.portee: For the Christian reader, the loins remind us that God knows not only what we do, but who we are at our core. When we speak of girding the loins, we learn to be ready, to strengthen ourselves in the face of trials, knowing that this is where our capacity to obey and persevere is born. And when we read that suffering passes through the loins, we recognize that God does not deny our pain — He sees it and participates in it.

sens: Dividing something into parts, portions
Distributing to each their share
Appropriating through plunder
Assigning a function, a role
Enjoying something together
H2505A.detail:
1. Dividing something into parts, portions: this means separating a whole to make several pieces. When Abraham "divided his forces" (Genesis 14:15), he separated them into groups to attack at night. When God says, "I will divide Shechem" (Psalms 60:8), He refers to a division of the conquered territory.

2. Distributing to each their share: giving each person what is due to them. David "distributed to all the people... to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins" (2 Samuel 6:19). This is a fair and generous sharing.

3. Appropriating through plunder: taking a share of the spoils from a defeated enemy. In biblical wars, soldiers "share" the spoils (Psalms 22:19, Isaiah 53:12).

4. Assigning a function, a role: distributing responsibilities among people. The priests and Levites were "distributed in the house of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 23:18) to carry out their specific duties.

5. Enjoying something together: the meaning can become social or moral sharing, sharing a common reality (Proverbs 29:24: "Whoever is enticed by a thief hates his own soul; he hears the oaths, but does not declare it").
H2505A.origine: The root חלק (cha-laq) evokes the fundamental idea of being smooth, polished, of something divided or separated. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words expressing division, sharing, and contribution. The verb appears in several forms that nuance the meaning: the simple form (Qal) mainly expresses neutral sharing, while the intensive form (Piel) reinforces the idea of active division, and the reflexive form (Hithpael) emphasizes mutual sharing among several. This vocabulary is rooted in the daily reality of the people: the sharing of conquered lands, the spoils of war, and cultic responsibilities.
H2505A.emploi: This verb appears 55 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Joshua, Samuel, Chronicles), the Psalms, and the prophets. Its usage varies according to the context: with lands, it describes the division of the Promised Land among the tribes (Joshua 13:7, 18:2, 19:51), realized by divine lot. With goods and spoils, it signifies generous distribution (2 Samuel 6:19) or taking plunder in war (Isaiah 53:12). With functions, it designates the assignment of sacred roles (1 Chronicles 24:3-5). In poetry and among the prophets, the word takes on a theological dimension: God "divides" the world and its goods according to His sovereign will (Deuteronomy 4:19, Psalms 60:8).
H2505A.portee: This word reminds us that everything we possess can be divided and redistributed: our goods do not belong to us absolutely. It invites generosity: David shares food and joy with all the people. It also shows that responsibilities in the service of God are distributed among all believers, not concentrated in a few. Finally, in speaking of the sharing of the spoils of the Messiah (Isaiah 53:12), it affirms the final victory of Christ and the invitation to partake in His fruits.

sens: Being smooth, slippery, sweet-talking
Speaking with deceptive sweetness to seduce or deceive
Caressing someone with false words in order to manipulate them
Having an attractive appearance that hides malicious intentions
H2505B.detail: 1. The word first evokes a smooth and slippery surface, which offers no grip — it is an image of lies that slide without leaving a hold on the truth. 2. To flatter is to address someone with sweet words, pleasant to the ear, but false or self-serving. In Proverbs 55:22, the mouth of the treacherous is "smoother than cream," his words "sweeter than oil," but it is a weapon: they hide war in his heart. 3. The flatterer seeks to seduce his victim by praising them insincerely, often to lead them away from good or to gain profit. Proverbs 2:16 and 7:5 show the foreign woman using sweet words to seduce the young man. 4. What is flattering can also refer to what is pleasant in appearance but hollow or deceitful — a surface sweetness without true substance.
H2505B.origine: The Hebrew word חָלַק (cha.laq) comes from a root meaning "to be smooth, slippery." The basic image is that of a surface without roughness, where nothing can hold firmly — hence the figurative meaning of words that slide without anchoring in truth. The same root can also mean "to share" or "to divide," as what is smooth separates easily. The verb in the causative form (Hiphil) develops the meaning of "making smooth" or "polishing," then "flattering" in the sense of making sweet through words.
H2505B.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs, books of wisdom that warn against lies and seduction. In Psalms 5:10, the psalmist denounces those whose "tongue is flattering" — these are deceptive words that conceal the malice of the heart. In Proverbs 28:23, he who rebukes his neighbor finds more favor than he "whose tongue is flattering," showing that honest correction is better than false sweetness. Proverbs often return to this danger: the foreign woman, the corrupt person, the unbeliever seduce with flattering words. It is a weapon of deception and manipulation.
H2505B.portee: This word calls us to vigilance: promises without anchoring, excessive praise, sweet words that hide troubled intentions are spiritual traps. It also invites us to prefer frank truth, even if harsh, over false sweetness. It teaches us to discern, in others and in ourselves, the difference between true kindness and the intention to seduce or deceive.

sens: fils de Galaad et chef de famille dans la tribu de Manassé
H2507.detail: Hélek is a man from the tribe of Manasseh, the second son of Gilead. He is first presented in the census of the Israelite people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:30), where his descendants form a distinct family called the Helekites. During the sharing of the promised land, his descendants receive a portion of inheritance in Canaan, mentioned alongside the other Manassite clans (Joshua 17:2). His name means "portion," which evokes the inheritance that God grants to his clan.
H2507.origine: The name Hélek (חֵלֶק) literally means "portion" or "part of inheritance." It is formed from the root that designates sharing and the allocation of lands. This name symbolizes the covenant that God makes with Israel: each clan receives its "portion" of the promised land according to its genealogical heritage.
H2507.emploi: Hélek appears twice in the Bible, only in texts related to the census and the sharing of lands after the exodus from Egypt. In Numbers 26:30, he is counted among the Manassite family heads in the wilderness, confirming his status as a founding patriarch of a lineage. In Joshua 17:2, his descendants are listed among the beneficiaries of the drawing of lots for the distribution of Canaan. These two mentions structure the land inheritance of Israel and remind us that each clan possesses a promised part.
H2507.portee: The mention of Hélek and his descendants illustrates God's faithfulness to keep His promises to Israel. Each name, each family listed represents a maintained covenant. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that God knows each of His children by name and that the spiritual inheritance He offers is real and personalized.

sens: Ce qui appartient à quelqu'un en propre, sa part ou sa portion
La condition ou le sort assigné à quelqu'un
H2508.detail:
1. What belongs to someone in their own right, their part or portion. The word designates wealth, a possession: in Ezra 4:16, the king will no longer retain his "possession" beyond the river, meaning his right of dominion and ownership over that territory.
2. The condition or lot assigned to someone. The word can also mean the lot, the share of life one receives: in Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, the uprooted tree will have for its "share" with the beasts to feed on grass — this is its new condition, its assigned lot.
H2508.origine: The Hebrew word חֲלָק (cha.laq) comes from a root that means "to divide" or "to share." It originally designates a part obtained by division, then any good, any portion that one possesses. It is an Aramaic word that corresponds to the Hebrew חֵלֶק (che.leq), very common in the Hebrew Old Testament to express the idea of lot or share.
H2508.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Bible, and only in Aramaic in the books of Daniel and Ezra, which are the Aramaic portions of the Old Testament. In Ezra 4:16, it designates the king's territorial possession, his political domain. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, it appears twice in the same context: the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, where the fallen tree will have a "share" with the wild beasts, meaning a common condition with them. The word emphasizes the idea of an assigned, received part, rather than one that is conquered.
H2508.portee: This word invites us to meditate on what God entrusts to us and on the acceptance of our lot. In Daniel's dream, it reminds us that even a powerful king can only accept the share that God reserves for him, without controlling his future. For the Christian, it is a lesson in trust: our life, our circumstances, our "share" come from God, and it is by accepting them in faith that we find peace.

sens: That is smooth and slippery to the touch, without roughness
That pleases the ear and heart with its deceptive sweetness
That lulls with flattering or deceitful words
H2509.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the word designates what is smooth and slippery: Jacob tells his mother that Esau is hairy while he himself has smooth skin (Genesis 27:11). It is the absence of roughness, a soft surface to the touch.
2. Applied to speech and feelings, "smooth" describes what is sweet, pleasant to hear, and seductive: the lips of the foreign woman are smoother (sweeter) than oil (Proverbs 5:3), evoking a deceptive sweetness that attracts.
3. In a figurative and moral sense, the word qualifies flattering or deceitful speech: flattering tongue (Proverbs 26:28) and deceptive oracles (Ezekiel 12:24) are smooth because they slide easily, manipulating while hiding the truth under a pleasant appearance.
H2509.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of what glides, what is smooth and fluid. The word is first used to describe a physical texture — hairless skin — and then extends to the moral and rhetorical domain to designate speech that does not clash, that insidiously glides into the mind, seducing without convincing through truth.
H2509.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. One occurrence describes the physical (Jacob's skin). The other three apply the image of smoothness to deceitful speech: seductive words (Proverbs 5), the crushing flattering tongue (Proverbs 26), and false oracles (Ezekiel 12). This is why translations vary: "hair" for the concrete sense, "sweet" for sensual seduction, "flattering" and "deceptive" for the moral dimension of disguised lies.
H2509.portee: This word warns us against the deceptive power of pleasant speech. A flattering tongue or a sweet promise are not signs of truth: they can, on the contrary, conceal lies and lead to ruin. The Bible invites us to discern behind the sweetness of words whether they serve the truth or mislead us.

sens: mountain in the south of Judah
H2510.detail: Halak is a mountain in the southern part of the land of Judah. It marks the southern boundary of Joshua's conquests: it is to this mountain that the territories Joshua took from the Canaanite kings extend (Joshua 11:17 and 12:7).
H2510.origine: The name Halak means "smooth" or "bald" in Hebrew, probably because the mountain was bare or had a smooth and rounded summit, unlike the more jagged mountains of other regions.
H2510.emploi: Halak appears twice in the book of Joshua, in chapters 11 and 12, always to delineate the southern area of Joshua's conquests. These two verses mark the conclusion of the military campaign: Joshua conquered all the kings and all the territories "from Kadesh-Barnea to Gaza, and all the land of Gosen to Gibeon" (Joshua 10:41), and these boundaries are specified by saying that his conquests extend "from Mount Halak that rises toward Seir" in the north to other borders in the south.

sens: smooth and shiny to the touch
slippery, without roughness
H2511.detail: 1. The word describes a smooth and shiny surface, which can be polished through friction or the wear of time. In Isaiah 57:6, the prophet speaks of the "polished stones of the torrents": these are pebbles that water has smoothed by rolling them for years, making them smooth and shiny. 2. This smooth surface also evokes something slippery, without roughness, offering little grip — an image of what is unstable or futile.
H2511.origine: The Hebrew root חלק (halaq) literally means "to glide, to be slippery." It evokes the image of a surface on which one glides. The word first describes a physical, tactile quality: what has become smooth through friction or wear.
H2511.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 57:6. The prophet reproaches Israel for worshiping idols and pouring offerings before polished stones — objects that have been worked to beautify them, symbolizing the artifice and futility of false gods. It is a contrast: beautiful stones to the touch, but empty of meaning, incapable of saving.
H2511.portee: This word invites the reader to discern between outward beauty and inner truth. The polished stones of Isaiah remind us of the danger of being seduced by the smooth and shiny appearance of false gods. The text urges us to seek not superficial allure, but the solidity and truth of our relationship with the living God.

sens: smooth and shiny, without roughness
easy to handle
H2512.detail:
1. The word describes a smooth and shiny surface, like that of stones worn and rounded by water or friction. When David chooses his stones for his sling against Goliath, he takes five "polished" stones, that is, smooth and soft to the touch (1 Samuel 17:40) — rounded pebbles from the stream, ideal for throwing without snagging.
2. By extension, the word also suggests something easy to handle, well-fitted to the hand, without defects that would hinder. A polished stone glides better between the fingers and is thrown farther with precision.
H2512.origine: The Hebrew word חַלֻּק comes from a root that evokes the idea of smoothing, wearing down, making smooth through friction or the flow of water. It is a very concrete image: stones that roll in a stream lose their sharp angles and become polished and rounded. The word belongs to the family of verbs designating the action of rubbing or polishing.
H2512.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in the account of David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40). In this context, it characterizes the stones chosen by David for his battle against the giant — smooth and polished stones, proof that David does not act on impulse but with practical intelligence. The specific mention of this detail emphasizes that David, a simple shepherd, knows well the weapons and chooses the best equipment for battle.
H2512.portee: This small detail reveals the hidden wisdom behind David's courage. Even before praying or fighting, he checks his equipment and chooses the best tools — a silent lesson that faith does not exclude prudence and thoughtful preparation. In this way, David becomes the model of the wise warrior.

sens: Small plot of arable land, individual or family property
Land owned by someone, considered as their personal property
Area of land designated or delimited for a specific use or event
H2513A.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a plot, a portion of land intended to be cultivated or exploited. In Genesis 33:19, Jacob buys a "parcel" of field where he had pitched his tent: it refers to a specific small piece of land that can be acquired and owned.
2. By extension, it is land that one possesses and on which one exercises a right of ownership. When Joab asks Absalom, "Why have your servants set fire to the field that belongs to me?" (2 Samuel 14:31), he speaks of land that is his own, which he can defend and dispose of. Similarly, Naboth's field (2 Kings 9:25) is a specific asset, an identified possession.
3. The word can also refer to any stretch of land—cultivated or not—that one identifies, traverses, or fights over. Ruth goes to glean "in a field" (Ruth 2:3) where she walks and works; David's soldiers "position themselves in the midst of the field" to fight (1 Chronicles 11:14).
H2513A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to divide, to share": a "chelqa" is literally a part, a portion obtained by division. This is why it is also translated as "portion" or "piece" of land. The image is that of land received as a share, which can be delineated and becomes personal property.
H2513A.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books. It regularly designates land ownership: that which is purchased (Genesis 33:19), inherited, defended against an enemy, or on which significant events unfold. In Deuteronomy 33:21, it is a "portion" of territory promised as a share. In 2 Kings 3:19, the "fields" (the good lands) are ruined to devastate the enemy's country. The word always emphasizes the personal and limited nature of the land: it is property that one identifies, recognizes, protects, or covets.
H2513A.portee: For the biblical reader, this word recalls the importance of land in the life of the Hebrew people: land was not an abstract asset, but a concrete possession, often received by inheritance or purchased at the cost of negotiations. It was the means of livelihood and the expression of belonging to a family, to a people. Understanding what a "chelqa" is helps grasp the real stakes of biblical conflicts—such as the one surrounding Naboth's field—and the spiritual value that the Bible attaches to the possession of a promised land.

sens: Smooth and slippery aspect of a surface, skin, or path
Sweet and pleasant speech that seeks to please rather than tell the truth
Deceptive words presented in a seductive manner
Paths that cause one to stumble, an image of moral fragility
H2513B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: it refers to the smooth surface of skin, fabric, or a path, without roughness. In Genesis 27:16, Rebekah covers Jacob's neck with goat skins to make him smooth like Esau. It is also a slippery surface on which one cannot maintain footing, as in Psalms 73:18 where God places the wicked "on slippery paths."
2. From a smooth surface, the word naturally transitions to what easily slips from the mouth: sweet, flattering words that do not tell the truth but seek to seduce and please. The psalmist denounces "flattering lips" (Psalms 12:3-4), and Proverbs 6:24 warns against "the smooth tongue of the foreign woman."
3. These flattering words are a form of deceit: instead of speaking uncomfortable truths, one prophesies "smooth things" and "illusions" (Isaiah 30:10), which mislead the people.
4. Morally, slippery paths are those where instability and downfall prevail—they represent the spiritual path of the wicked that appears easy but leads to destruction.
H2513B.origine: The Hebrew word חֶלְקָה (chelqah) comes from the root חלק (heleq), which expresses the idea of what is smooth, slippery, polished. From this root arises the adjective "smooth" and the noun "flattery." The image is very vivid: just as a smooth surface does not hold one who walks on it, flattering words slip away, do not cling to the truth but seduce and deceive the listener. This is why the word comes to designate flattery and seductive lies.
H2513B.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in the figurative sense of flattery or seductive words. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew terms related to deceit and illusion. Genesis 27:16 uses it alone in its concrete sense of smoothness. But the Psalms and Proverbs use it extensively to describe a major spiritual danger: the flattering words of the wicked who speak with "a double heart" (Psalms 12:3), those of the corrupt woman (Proverbs 6:24), or those of false prophets who prophesy to please the people rather than to proclaim the truth of God (Isaiah 30:10). The word thus encompasses the cunning of seductive speech that misleads.
H2513B.portee: The Bible uses this word to warn the believer: sweet and pleasant words are not always true, and sometimes they hide lies and danger. The word invites spiritual vigilance, to discern between what flatters the ear and what truly edifies faith. It is a call to prefer the austere truth of the Lord over the seduction of false promises.

sens: flattering and deceptive words
seduction by pleasant promises
betrayal through sweet speech
H2514.detail:
1. Flattery is the art of saying sweet and pleasant words to seduce someone and lead them astray. It is a seductive tactic that uses the sweetness of promises to deceive. In Daniel 11:32, the tyrant "will seduce by flattery the traitors of the covenant": he uses sweet words to convince the unfaithful to betray their commitment to God.
2. Flattery is also the promise of pleasant goods that do not correspond to reality. It speaks to what pleases the ear and heart to bypass good judgment. It is a formidable weapon because it makes one believe in something that is not true.
3. Flattery leads to betrayal and sin: one who is seduced by flattering words abandons their commitments and faithfulness. It transforms a deceptive promise into an act of rebellion.
H2514.origine: The Hebrew word חֲלַקָּה (cha.laq.qah) comes from the root חלק (cha.laq) which means "to smooth, to polish, to make sweet." This connection with sweetness is very telling: just as a smoothed surface slips under the finger, flattering words easily slide into the ear and seduce effortlessly. Flattery is thus literally the quality of what is smooth, polished, pleasant—hence its meaning of "sweet words that deceive."
H2514.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 11:32, in a context of religious crisis. The prophet describes how an impious king will seduce those who have betrayed the covenant with God by using flattery—tempting but false promises. This passage shows that flattery is a powerful weapon to divert people from their faithfulness, particularly effective among those who are already tempted to betray.
H2514.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the danger of sweet and deceptive words. In a time when seduction can take the form of comfortable promises that contradict the Word of God, it invites us to remain vigilant and cultivate a firm knowledge of God, as the passage itself exhorts: "the people who know their God shall be strong and carry out great exploits." Flattery can only seduce those who do not hold firmly to the truth.

sens: Distribution into distinct groups according to a rule or criterion
Division of people according to their function or origin
Established order among shares or portions
H2515.detail:
1. The word designates an organized distribution into distinct groups. In 2 Chronicles 35:5, it refers to the arrangement of the Levites in the sanctuary "according to the classification of the ancestral houses": each group of Levites, defined by their family, occupies a specific place in the worship. This is not a random division, but an order that recognizes different origins and responsibilities.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of sharing according to portions or lots assigned to each. Each division receives what is due to it, and this order allows everyone to fulfill their role in the whole.
H2515.origine: The word comes from the root חלק ("to share, divide"), which primarily expresses the physical act of dividing a property or space. The root also appears in other biblical words meaning "part," "portion," or "inheritance." The basic idea is simple: one divides so that everyone has their own, and this division creates an order, a classification.
H2515.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 35:5, where King Josiah organizes the celebration of Passover. He instructs the Levites to position themselves in the sanctuary "according to the classification of the ancestral houses." The context shows that this classification is not arbitrary: it reflects the Levitical genealogies and liturgical roles. It is an administrative and cultic term, used to organize the order of divine service.
H2515.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that God loves order and clarity in the worship rendered to Him. Organization is not a matter of whim, but of respecting the responsibilities and gifts of each person. It is an invitation to see in the structure and regularity of divine service, not a constraint, but a wisdom: each in their place, all in harmony towards a common goal.

sens: Descendant of Hélek, son of Gilead from the tribe of Manasseh
H2516.detail: 1. The Hélekites are the descendants of Hélek, son of Gilead and grandson of Manasseh. They constitute a family or clan within the tribe of Manasseh, listed among the family groups of the people of Israel at the time of the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:30).
H2516.origine: The name Hélekite comes from Hélek (חֵלֶק in Hebrew), whose primary meaning is "portion" or "part." Hélek is the son of Gilead mentioned in the genealogy of Manasseh. The term "Hélekites" simply designates the members of this family, formed according to the usual pattern of Israelite clan names.
H2516.emploi: The term appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:30, during the census of the tribes of Israel in the wilderness of Moab. At that time, the Hélekites are listed among the six families of the clan of Gilead, alongside the Jezerites, Asrielites, Shechemites, Shemidaites, and Perizzites. This census served to count the available warriors and to allocate territories in Canaan. Hélek had several brothers — Abiezer, Asriel, Shechem, and Pherer — each founding their own clan family.

sens: Priest in charge of a priestly family at the time of the return from exile
H2517.detail: Helkaï is a chief of a priestly family during the time of the high priest Joiakim, mentioned in the list of priests who returned from exile in Babylon. He was responsible for the house of Meremoth and oversaw the organization of worship in the restored temple of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:15).
H2517.origine: The Hebrew name חֶלְקָי (Helkaï) literally means "my portion is Jehovah": it is composed of "helq" (part, portion) and the abbreviated divine name "-aï" (my, to me). This name expresses the conviction that a priest has — his share, his inheritance, is God Himself and the service of the temple.
H2517.emploi: Helkaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:15, in an official list of the heads of priestly families during the time of the high priest Joiakim. This list enumerates the leaders of each Levitical house: Helkaï represents the family of Meremoth. His appearance underscores the importance of maintaining order and continuity of worship after the return from exile.

sens: Chief of the house of King Hezekiah, father of Eliakim
H2518G.detail: Hilkija is a figure from the kingdom of Judah during the reign of King Hezekiah (8th century B.C.). He is known as the father of Eliakim, who holds the important position of chief of the royal house — that is, administrator of palace affairs and representative of the king. Hilkija appears in the accounts of the crisis caused by Rabshakeh, the envoy of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:18, Isaiah 36:3), where Eliakim, as the son of Hilkija, represents Judah against Assyrian claims. The name means "my portion is the Lord" — a beautiful expression of trust in God.
H2518G.origine: The name Hilkija is formed from two Hebrew elements: "hilqah" (part, portion) and the divine name "Yah" (Lord). It expresses the idea that a person's true wealth and true inheritance are found in God alone. It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, where personal names proclaimed their faith.
H2518G.emploi: Hilkija is mentioned six times in the provided usages, all concentrated in three parallel passages: 2 Kings 18 and Isaiah 36, which recount the same crisis event with Rabshakeh, and a solitary mention in Isaiah 22:20. In each occurrence, Hilkija is designated solely as the father of Eliakim; it is through his son that his memory is preserved. The passages highlight Eliakim's political and diplomatic role as the king's representative, reflecting Hilkija's importance as the father of a statesman.
H2518G.portee: The name Hilkija reminds us that even the political and administrative leaders of Israel recognized that their true possession was not power or earthly riches, but God Himself. The example of Eliakim, son of Hilkija, shows how an official charge can be exercised in service to the earthly king while confessing allegiance to the King of heaven.

sens: High priest during the reign of King Josiah
Key figure in the religious reform of Judah in the 7th century B.C.
A figure of faithfulness in the service of the Temple and the divine Law
H2518H.detail: Hilkiah is the name of a major historical figure in the Kingdom of Judah. He is best known as the high priest during the reign of King Josiah (circa 640-609 B.C.), during the period of the divided monarchy. His role in the rediscovery of the Book of the Law in the Temple is fundamental: he discovers this scroll during restoration work on the Temple, an event that triggers a vast religious reform. The text of 2 Kings 22:8 and 2 Chronicles 34:14-15 reports this pivotal discovery. Hilkiah also works closely with the king and royal officials to implement changes: he is a consultant to King Josiah (2 Kings 22:12) and participates in the great celebration of Passover (2 Chronicles 35:8). His father is Shallum, and he is the ancestor of several generations of priests and Temple servants. Hilkiah's priestly lineage extends to Ezra (Ezra 7:1) and includes the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 29:3 mentions him in connection with the prophet's family).
H2518H.origine: The name Hilkiah literally means "my portion is the Lord" (or "the Lord is my part"), expressing a trust in God as the true inheritance. It is a typical theophoric name in biblical Hebrew, where the personal name proclaims a relationship of faith. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but Hilkiah the high priest remains the most famous. His historical importance makes him an emblematic figure of the faithful Levitical priesthood during the late monarchy period.
H2518H.emploi: Hilkiah appears 19 times in the Old Testament, primarily in 2 Kings 22-23 and 2 Chronicles 34-35, which recount the reign of Josiah. It is under his high priesthood that the Book of the Law is found in the Temple (2 Kings 22:8), an event that transforms the kingdom by bringing it back to faithfulness to the divine covenant. He represents the religious and priestly authority of the moment: the king consults him directly, the leaders respect him, and the Temple collections go through him (2 Chronicles 34:9). His actions are part of the continuity of the priestly function: his descendants perpetuate the priesthood (Ezra 7:1, Nehemiah 11:11). He is a figure of moral and religious stability during a troubled period.
H2518H.portee: Hilkiah illustrates the role of the faithful priest who does not merely maintain appearances but actively works for a true spiritual renewal of the people. The discovery of the Book of the Law under his ministry reminds us that the Word of God, even when forgotten or hidden, remains the living foundation upon which the people must rely. His example shows how religious leaders can be agents of authentic reform when they bring the people into direct contact with the divine Law. For the contemporary reader, Hilkiah becomes a figure of institutional repentance: a man who helps his king and his people return to the forgotten covenant.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Amzi
H2518I.detail: 1. Hilkiah is a proper name designating a man from the tribe of Levi. In the passage of 1 Chronicles 6:45, he appears in a genealogy as the son of Amzi and father of Amatziah, listed among the singers and servants of the temple assigned to their duties by King David. This Hilkiah represents a lineage of Merarite Levites dedicated to divine service.
H2518I.origine: The name Hilkiah literally means "my part is the Lord." It expresses a statement of faith: the one who bears it acknowledges that God Himself is his inheritance and wealth. It is a typical name of the Levites, for whom the Lord had said that He would indeed be their portion, without land to cultivate but with a sacred role in worship. Several historical figures bore this name: priests, royal officials, the father of the prophet Jeremiah.
H2518I.emploi: Hilkiah appears in the genealogies of the Levites listed in the book of Chronicles. The text of 1 Chronicles 6:45 places him in the succession of temple servants assigned by David, among the Merarite Levites responsible for singing and liturgical service. He is a distant ancestor in a long lineage of faithful temple ministry.

sens: Son of Hosha, temple porter during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H2518J.detail: Hilkiah is a proper name designating a man from the tribe of Levi, son of Hosha. He is mentioned in the context of the porters of the temple in Jerusalem. According to 1 Chronicles 26:11, he was the second son of Hosha, after whom his brothers Thebalia and Zechariah followed. These brothers formed a significant part of the temple porters, as all the sons and brothers of Hosha numbered thirteen.
H2518J.origine: The name Hilkiah means "my portion is Jehovah," composed of the Hebrew חִלְקָה (portions, part) and the divine name יָהוּ (Jehovah). This type of theophoric name expresses the faith of the parents in God and proclaims that God is the heritage and wealth of the child. Several characters bear this name in the Hebrew Bible, including the high priest during the time of King Josiah and the father of the prophet Jeremiah.
H2518J.emploi: Hilkiah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:11, where he is listed among the sons of Hosha, a Levitical porter. He is presented as the second in a significant sibling group responsible for guarding the temple gates. This mention is part of the list of porters and overseers of the temple established during the organization of worship in the kingdom of Judah, likely under the reign of King David or one of his successors.

sens: Man who stood beside Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H2518K.detail: 1. Hilkiah is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4, where he stands at the right hand of Ezra the scribe while he reads the Law to the people of Israel after the Babylonian exile. His presence beside Ezra and several other important men suggests that he was himself a person of rank, likely a priest or a Levite, tasked with assisting in this solemn celebration of the Word of God.
H2518K.origine: The name Hilkiah means "my portion is the Lord" or "the Lord is my part" in Hebrew, formed from two elements: "hilqa" (portion, part) and the name of God "Yah." This name expresses the conviction that God is the true wealth and ultimate inheritance of the one who bears it. Several people bore this name in the Old Testament, including the high priest during the reign of Josiah, but the one mentioned in Nehemiah 8:4 is a distinct figure from the time of the return from exile.
H2518K.emploi: Hilkiah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. This passage recounts the moment when, after the return from exile in Babylon, Ezra the scribe summons the people to read the Law of Moses. Hilkiah is among the men who stand near Ezra during this solemn public reading — at his right, alongside Matthithiah, Shema, Aniah, Uriah, and Maaseiah. This privileged position indicates that he was a respected religious authority in the restored community.
H2518K.portee: Hilkiah's presence at this key moment in Israel's history, during the rediscovery and public proclamation of the Law, reminds us that the restoration of the people after exile was not merely a political or territorial restoration: it was primarily a return to obedience to the Word of God. Men like Hilkiah, whose very name means that God is his portion, illustrate the spiritual leadership that guided this community reconstruction around the Law.

sens: High priest or chief priest during the time of the Exile and the Return
H2518L.detail: 1. Hilkiah is an important figure among the Jewish people at the time when the Hebrews return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of the leaders of the priests and their brothers during the time of Joshua (Nehemiah 12:7), and again in Nehemiah 12:21 where his name is listed among the leaders of the restored worship.
H2518L.origine: The name Hilkiah means "my portion is the Lord" (hil = portion, kiyah = the Lord): it is a theophoric name, that is, a name that proclaims the relationship of the bearer with God. Names of this type were common among the Hebrews and expressed the trust that the parent placed in God when giving birth to the child.
H2518L.emploi: Hilkiah appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both times in chapter 12 which lists the leaders of the priests who returned from Babylon with Joshua (the high priest of the return). These lists testify to the restoration of temple worship after the exile. Hilkiah is mentioned among the official figures who directed the religious service of the restored Jerusalem.

sens: priest from Anathoth, father of the prophet Jeremiah
H2518M.detail: Hilkiah is a priest (a high priest) who lives in the city of Anathoth, in Benjamin. He is the father of the prophet Jeremiah, one of the greatest prophets of Israel. His name literally means "my portion is the Lord", suggesting a family aware of its belonging to God. Although Hilkiah is mentioned only briefly in the Bible — he appears solely as the father of Jeremiah — he plays a fundamental role: it is from him that the prophetic ministry arises that will mark the last decades of the kingdom of Judah before the Babylonian exile (Jeremiah 1:1).
H2518M.origine: The name Hilkiah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "portion" or "part" (hlq), associated with the word Lord (Yah). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common in pious families of Israel. Several individuals bore this name in the history of Israel (high priests, Levites, royal officials), but this one is defined solely as the father of the prophet Jeremiah.
H2518M.emploi: Hilkiah is named only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 1:1, where he is presented as a priest (high priest) from Anathoth and the father of Jeremiah. This single mention is sufficient to identify him: it is through it that we learn about the origin of the prophet Jeremiah and the religious context of his family. The fact that he is a priest shows that Jeremiah is born into a family dedicated to the service of the true God's worship.
H2518M.portee: Hilkiah reminds us that the service of God is passed down through families and that men of faith often beget sons called to great spiritual responsibilities. The mention of his name, although brief, honors the father before the son, recognizing that every prophet is born from a human lineage and the ministry of his parents. It is an invitation to take seriously the spiritual education we give to our children.

sens: That slips, that is slippery; without firm grip
That leads astray, that deceives; way without foundation
Unfair maneuver, underground scheme
Feigning adherence, surface hypocrisy
H2519.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word evokes a slippery path where the foot finds no grip: it is the image of instability and the danger of falling. In Psalms 35:6 and Jeremiah 23:12, the paths of the wicked are described as "slippery", suggesting that they will perish in the chaos they have sown.
2. By extension, what is slippery is also what deceives: the smooth words of the false prophet slip towards the one who listens, without nourishing him, like a smooth surface where nothing sticks. It is the image of treacherous seduction.
3. In Daniel 11:21, this word designates intrigue, hidden scheming: Antiochus uses cunning to seize the throne, slipping into the cracks of power through deceitful promises.
4. In Daniel 11:34, it describes hypocrisy, apparent adherence without sincerity: those who join the revolt by "hypocrisy" do so only for self-serving reasons, their support slips superficially without true commitment.
H2519.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to slip" or "to be smooth". In Hebrew, this image of smoothness is often used to describe what is false, deceptive, or unstable: a smooth surface cannot hold onto virtue. It is a poetic word that paints through imagery rather than abstract concepts.
H2519.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe ruses, deceptive ways, or lies. In Psalms and Jeremiah, it qualifies the path of the wicked who will be judged. In Daniel, it specifically designates the political maneuvers of Antiochus and the hypocrisy of those who support him for selfish reasons. The context is always that of divine judgment: the slippery, the deceptive will not stand.
H2519.portee: This word reminds the believer that the smooth and seductive promises of lies, compromise, or hypocrisy build nothing: they lead to a fall. It is an invitation to seek the solid, the true, the faithful word of God, rather than the beautiful appearances that deceive. For those who suffer in the face of injustice, it affirms that the cunning of the wicked is never stable: they slip towards their own condemnation.

sens: city in the territory of Asher
Levitical city assigned to the Gershonites
H2520.detail:
1. Helkath is a city located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of the promised land. It marks a landmark on the boundary of this territory (Joshua 19:25).
2. This city was given along with its surrounding lands to the Levites of the family of the Gershonites, who did not have a land inheritance like the other tribes (Joshua 21:31). It served as a city of refuge and a Levitical center in northern Canaan.
H2520.origine: The name Helkath means "smooth" or "united" in Hebrew, probably referring to the nature of the terrain in this place. The Bible also mentions Hukok as an alternative name for this same locality (Joshua 21:32), indicating that the two names refer to the same place or nearby locations.
H2520.emploi: Helkath appears twice in the book of Joshua. The first mention, in Joshua 19:25, situates it as a landmark on the border of the territory of Asher during the division of Canaan among the tribes. The second mention, in Joshua 21:31, includes it in the list of cities assigned to the Levites of the Gershon lineage. This double mention shows its administrative and religious importance in the territorial organization of Israel.

sens: Field located near the pool of Gibeon where the warriors of Ishbosheth and those of David clashed under the command of Joab
H2521.detail: Helkath-Hazzurim is a geographical location whose name means "field of swords" or "field of knives". It is near the pool of Gibeon that this bloody event took place: the men of King Ishbosheth, son of Saul, were killed by the warriors of David under the command of Joab. This battle marks a decisive moment in the struggle for the throne of Israel after the death of Saul, when David extends his power over the kingdom.
H2521.origine: The Hebrew name חֶלְקַת הַצֻּרִים combines two words: chel-qah means "portion of land, field" and tsa-rim means "swords" or "knives". This name literally evokes the field where swords crossed, a memory of the battle that took place there. The name conveys both a geographical marker and a historical reminder of the violence that occurred there.
H2521.emploi: This location appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 2:16. The context is that of the rivalry between the house of Saul and that of David for the crown of Israel. After the death of Saul, Ishbosheth reigns over the north while David reigns over Judah. Joab, commander of David, encounters the men of Ishbosheth near the pool of Gibeon. What begins as a confrontation between two groups leads to a brutal fight where Ishbosheth's soldiers are defeated and killed. This location thus embodies a pivotal moment in the establishment of David's kingship over all Israel.

sens: lose strength, become weak
be brought down, knocked down
defeat, put out of action
H2522.detail:
1. The verb first describes the state of one who loses strength or becomes powerless: the body weakens, energy disappears. It is physical and vital weakening. Job expresses this when he says that man "loses his strength" in dying (Job 14:10): the word evokes the gradual decline of the living.
2. The word can also describe a more dramatic collapse: one is thrown to the ground, brought low, prostrated. The fall is not gradual but brutal and definitive. Isaiah uses it for the king of Babylon, this "shining star" who "is brought down to the ground" (Isaiah 14:12): from the height of glory, a total fall.
3. In military action, the verb means to defeat, to overcome an enemy: when one weakens the opponent to the point of knocking him down, one defeats him. Joshua "defeated" Amalek and his people "with the edge of the sword" (Exodus 17:13) — that is, he weakened, disarmed, subdued them.
H2522.origine: The root חלש fundamentally evokes physical weakening, loss of vigor. It also produces a noun (חלש) meaning "weak." The starting image is that of a body that can no longer hold up, that collapses. The Hebrew word conveys the idea that strength abandons, that solidity yields.
H2522.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Segond, always in the past tense (simple form of the Qal). It is used in very different contexts: first in military narration (Exodus 17:13), then in philosophical reflection on death and human impotence (Job 14:10), and finally in the prophetic poetry of Isaiah (14:12). Each time, the meaning remains consistent: moving from a state of strength to a state of impotence, whether through defeat in battle, through the approach of death, or through the fall of the powerful.
H2522.portee: This verb reminds us that human strength, whether that of a king or a people, is fragile and subject to God. It invites the reader not to rely on their own power and to recognize that every victory, every survival depends on divine grace, not on our own strength.

sens: lacking physical strength or power
devoid of courage or resolution
powerless in the face of difficulty
symbolically: one who recognizes their insufficiency
H2523.detail: 1. The word first evokes an absence of physical strength, of bodily vigor — one who cannot perform intense effort. 2. It also designates one who lacks courage or determination in the face of a trial, who does not have the moral firmness to resist. 3. It applies to one who finds themselves unable to act in the face of an obstacle or threat: impotence, fragility before circumstances. 4. In the passage from Joel, "let the weak say: I am strong" reverses the natural order — it is a promise that God will give supernatural strength to one who recognizes their powerlessness (Joel 3:10), and not to one who relies on their own strength.
H2523.origine: The Hebrew חַלָּשׁ (challash) comes from a root that evokes the idea of relaxation, loosening, weakening. Words from the same family express the loosening of hands, the sinking of the heart. The word characterizes one whose strength has been drained, like a string that has lost its tension.
H2523.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Joel 3:10, in the context of God's judgment on the enemies of Israel. There it designates one who recognizes themselves as lacking their own strength to fight. It is a cry that changes everything: instead of counting themselves as defeated or ignoring their weakness, the one who is truly weak accepts to cry "I am strong" — not out of bravado, but because they now rely on God. It is a call to let God manifest His power in us.
H2523.portee: This word teaches that there is no shame in recognizing our weakness: on the contrary, it is the way to experience the power of God. The Bible encourages the believer not to rely on themselves, but to cry from the heart "I am strong" — in other words, to confess their trust in God's victory that acts through our insufficiencies. It is an invitation to faith rather than self-sufficiency.

sens: The father of a woman's husband
The father of a man's wife
H2524.detail:
1. The word designates the father of the husband, from the woman's perspective. Tamar calls Judah her "father-in-law" (Genesis 38:13, 25), as he is the father of her husband Er. It is a kinship bond through marriage, not by blood.
2. The word is also used for the father of a man's wife. The daughter-in-law of Phinehas — his wife — learns of the death of her "father-in-law" Eli (1 Samuel 4:19, 21), that is, the father of her husband Phinehas.
H2524.origine: The Hebrew word חָם (cham) likely comes from a root meaning "to be warm" or "to be bound by marriage." It is a familial term that designates the bonds created by marriage, not by birth.
H2524.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in familial and painful contexts. It is found in the story of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38), where Tamar addresses her father-in-law Judah to seek justice. It also appears in the account of the death of Eli and his sons (1 Samuel 4), where Phinehas's pregnant wife learns of the simultaneous deaths of her father-in-law, her husband, and the capture of the ark. In all cases, the father-in-law is an important figure in the kinship created by marriage.
H2524.portee: This word reminds us that family is not limited to blood: marriage creates sacred bonds and mutual responsibilities. Judah, Tamar's father-in-law, becomes responsible for her justice; Eli, Phinehas's father-in-law, is involved in the fate of his daughter-in-law. These bonds require honor and fidelity.

sens: Having a high temperature, burning or warming
Providing warmth, warming the body
H2525.detail:
1. The word describes what has a high temperature, that burns or warms. The bread still hot comes out of the oven or from a source of heat (Joshua 9:12: the Gibeonites bring their "hot" bread as proof that they come from afar, as it has had time to cool during the journey).
2. It also qualifies what provides warmth to the body, what warms. Clothes become "hot" when they absorb the heat of the sun or the midday wind, a natural protection against the cold (Job 37:17).
H2525.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing heat and high temperature. It is a simple, direct adjective that describes an immediate physical sensation. The root evokes the idea of what burns or warms, without moral or figurative connotation.
H2525.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It is used very concretely: to describe fresh bread coming from a supply (Joshua 9:12), and to qualify clothes soaked with warmth from the midday wind (Job 37:17). In both cases, it designates an observable and immediate physical property, without metaphorical development.

sens: Second son of Noah
Father of the peoples of the south and Egypt
Collective name for the Egyptians
H2526G.detail:
1. Cham is the second of Noah's three sons, along with Shem and Japheth. He appears in the genealogy before the Flood (Genesis 5:32) and enters the ark with his family (Genesis 7:13). After the Flood, Scripture reports an incident where Cham sees his father Noah's nakedness and tells his brothers, which brings a curse upon his descendants (Genesis 9:22-25).
2. Cham is the father of Canaan, Cush, Egypt, and Put, meaning the peoples who inhabited North Africa and East Africa (Genesis 10:6). His name means "hot," and his descendants are associated with the warm regions of the south.
3. In later uses of Scripture, "Cham" collectively refers to the Egyptians, as a way to summarize the peoples of the known world prior to the eyes of Israel.
H2526G.origine: The name Cham literally means "hot" in Hebrew, which may reflect the warm regions where his descendants settled, or symbolize his temperament. His name associates him with both a physical and geographical characteristic. He appears in the main genealogies of the Old Testament as the ancestor of significant peoples.
H2526G.emploi: Cham is mentioned 10 times in Scripture, primarily in chapters 5 to 10 of Genesis, where he appears in the genealogical lists of Noah and in the account of the Flood. He is named with his brothers Shem and Japheth at his birth (Genesis 5:32, 6:10), during the entry into the ark (Genesis 7:13), and upon exiting (Genesis 9:18). The incident in Genesis 9:22, where he sees Noah's nakedness, is a key moment that engages his moral responsibility. Finally, Genesis 10:1-20 and 1 Chronicles 1:4-8 list his descendants: Canaan, Cush, Egypt, and Put, founders of the ancient peoples of the south and Africa.

sens: son of Noah, ancestor of the peoples of the south and the Middle East
collective term for the lands and peoples descended from Cham, particularly Egypt
H2526H.detail:
1. Cham is one of the three sons of Noah mentioned in the Old Testament. The name literally means "hot" in Hebrew, likely evoking the warm lands of the south and the East that became the territory of his descendants (1 Chronicles 4:40 refers to him as the ancestor of peoples established in fertile regions).
2. By extension, "the land of Cham" or "the tents of Cham" refer to Egypt and the warm lands of the Middle East populated by his descendants. The Psalms often use this expression to speak of Egypt where Israel dwelled and where God performed wonders (Psalms 105:23; 105:27; 106:22: God acts "in the midst of" the land of Cham).
H2526H.origine: The name Cham comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be hot." It is a personal name that also becomes the collective name for his descendants and their lands, according to the common practice in ancient Asia where the names of peoples derived from their eponymous ancestors.
H2526H.emploi: Cham appears five times in the Old Testament, exclusively in poetry and chronicles. He is mentioned as the father or ancestor of peoples established in prosperous regions (1 Chronicles 4:40). The Psalms regularly use his name to refer to Egypt, particularly in passages recalling the Exodus: God struck "the firstborn of strength under the tents of Cham" (Psalms 78:51), performed "miracles in the land of Cham" (Psalms 105:27; 106:22). This poetic terminology emphasizes God's sovereignty over the Egyptian territory and His power over the nations.
H2526H.portee: Cham reminds us that all peoples and their lands descend from a common history: that of creation and the flood. By placing Egypt under the name of Cham, the Bible inscribes the story of the Exodus within a universal framework where God governs all nations. For the Christian, this affirms that God's sovereignty extends over all peoples, without exception.

sens: High temperature from the sun or climate
Time of day when the sun is strongest
Physical sensation of heat
Intensity, fervor of an action
H2527.detail:
1. The word refers to the physical heat produced by the sun or fire. In Genesis 8:22, it is listed as one of the great regularities of creation, alongside cold and seasons.
2. Very often, the "heat of the day" characterizes the time when the sun is the hottest, usually between noon and afternoon. In 1 Samuel 11:9 and 2 Samuel 4:5, it is mentioned to situate the time of an action: it is when people seek shade and rest.
3. The word can also describe the sensation of heat felt by the body. In 1 Samuel 21:6, the "hot" bread has just been taken from the sanctuary to be replaced by fresh bread.
4. Sometimes the word takes on a more figurative sense, designating the intensity or fervor of an action (such as the vigor of a battle fought "in the heat of the day").
H2527.origine: The Hebrew word חֹם (chom) comes from the root חם (chm), which expresses the idea of heat and burning. This root also produces the verb "to be hot." It is a simple and direct word, without nuance: it describes the tangible sensation that every inhabitant of the Levant knows well — that of the heat of the sun in summer.
H2527.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Old Testament. It is first used to describe the natural and unavoidable heat of creation (Genesis 8:22). It is then frequently used to situate a moment of the day: "the heat of the day" is a fixed expression, designating the hours when the sun is at its zenith, when many stop to rest in the shade (1 Samuel 11:9 and 11:11; 2 Samuel 4:5). It can also qualify bread or other food that is still hot. In poetic or more general passages (Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah), the word retains its sense of physical heat, often related to the sun or climatic conditions.
H2527.portee: For the Christian reader, the heat of the day reminds us of the immutable order of creation established by God: it is good and regular. The expression "heat of the day" also becomes a practical reference in the daily life of biblical times — a key to understanding the rhythms of work and rest of the ancients. It invites the modern believer to meditate on the natural cycle that God has ordained and to recognize His wisdom in the regularities of creation.

sens: Violent outburst of anger
State of extreme rage that transforms a person
H2528.detail:
1. Fury is a sudden and violent anger, a passionate outburst. In Daniel 3:13, King Nebuchadnezzar becomes "furious" upon learning of the disobedience of the three young men: his rage is immediate, prompting him to give orders without thinking.
2. Fury is also a prolonged state of rage that engulfs the entire person and changes their behavior. In Daniel 3:19, Nebuchadnezzar is "filled with fury" to the point that his face changes: rage completely seizes him and dominates him, triggering extreme actions such as ordering the furnace to be heated far beyond normal.
H2528.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken in Babylon) comes from the Hebrew word chemah (חֵמָה), which also means "rage" or "fury." This root evokes the idea of a feeling that boils and escapes, like heat intensifying. The same word appears in Hebrew in the Old Testament to describe the anger of God and that of men.
H2528.emploi: The word appears only twice in biblical Aramaic, both in Daniel 3, describing King Nebuchadnezzar's anger towards the three young men who refuse to worship the golden statue. First, he is "furious" (Daniel 3:13), then this fury intensifies to the point that it "fills" him (Daniel 3:19) and changes his expression. These two occurrences show a progression: from initial irritation to a rage that possesses him and drives him to commit an act of extreme cruelty.
H2528.portee: This word reminds the reader of the destructive power of uncontrolled anger. When fury dominates a person, it can lead them to commit injustice and violence, like the king who wants to burn innocent young men. It is a call to recognize how rage blinds and to ask God for mastery over the heart.

sens: Fatty substance obtained by churning milk
Dairy product served at the table or offered in honor
Rich food that symbolizes abundance and prosperity
H2529A.detail:
1. Cream is the product obtained by churning or pressing milk: the verse in Proverbs 30:33 states explicitly, "the pressing of milk produces cream." It is a fatty substance, richer than milk alone.
2. In daily life, it is a food served at the table, especially during important meals. Abraham offers it to his three heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:8); the prophetess Deborah receives it as a mark of honor (Judges 5:25); it is brought to David to nourish him during his trials (2 Samuel 17:29). It is a sign of hospitality and respect.
3. Cream also evokes the abundance and riches of God's people: in Moses' blessing, the cream of the cows is among the treasures of the promised land (Deuteronomy 32:14). It embodies the fertility of the land and the goodness of God.
H2529A.origine: The Hebrew word חֶמְאָה (chemah) specifically refers to the product of churning milk. Its original image is that of movement, of agitation that separates the fatty part from the rest. It is a concrete word, very ancient in Hebrew, that designates a culinary richness well known to the pastoral people of Israel.
H2529A.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Old Testament, mainly in narrative and poetic passages. It first describes an ordinary but appreciated food, offered as a sign of hospitality and honor (Genesis 18:8; Judges 5:25; 2 Samuel 17:29). It is also an agricultural product that testifies to the richness of the land and divine blessing (Deuteronomy 32:14; Isaiah 7:15 and 7:22). There is no negative nuance: cream is always presented as a desirable good and a sign of prosperity.
H2529A.portee: Cream reminds Christians that simple material goods — food, home, family — are gifts from God and opportunities to show hospitality and generosity. It also invites us to see in the foods we share a symbol of the abundance that God reserves for His people and of His faithfulness to us.

sens: fatty and creamy substance that separates from milk
material wealth and abundance
H2529B.detail:
1. Cream is the fatty and rich part of milk that rises to the surface and can be collected. In Job 29:6, the image of "feet bathing in cream" evokes extreme abundance and luxury — a prosperity so great that one is surrounded by it everywhere, even in the most sensual details of daily life.
2. By extension, cream designates material abundance itself, the best and richest there is. Job speaks of the blessed time in his life when divine blessing covered everything — his feet, the ground, the rock itself — as if to say: "Wealth was all around me."
H2529B.origine: The Hebrew word חֵמָה (chemah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of heat and thickness, since cream is one of the densest and richest substances in milk. The word can also refer to fever (body heat) or even snake venom — all images of something intense and concentrated. In biblical language, words related to liquids and bodily substances often intertwine in their etymology.
H2529B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Job 29:6. Job paints a picture of his past happiness: before the trials that struck him, he was surrounded by riches. His feet "bathed in cream," and the rock gave him streams of oil — two twin images of a profusion of goods. It is a poetic and orientalized language to express exceptional material prosperity.
H2529B.portee: For today's reader, this biblical image of cream reminds us that God's blessing can also encompass concrete life and physical well-being — but it does not always last. The story of Job teaches that we should neither idolize these riches nor rebel when God takes them away. It is an invitation to see beyond the visible.

sens: To ardently desire something or someone
To find beautiful, precious, pleasant to look at or to possess
To take pleasure in, to delight in
H2530A.detail:
1. To covet is to intensely desire what belongs to another or what one does not possess — a desire that can lead to theft or deceit. Achan "coveted" the beautiful cloak and gold from the spoils and took them (Joshua 7:21), and the tenth commandment forbids coveting "your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:17).
2. The word also describes what is beautiful, alluring, worthy of desire — what pleases the eyes or the heart. The trees of the garden of Eden are "pleasant to look at" (Genesis 2:9), and a beautiful woman can seduce if one "covets" her in his heart (Proverbs 6:25).
3. To covet can simply mean to take pleasure, to delight: the beloved in the Song of Songs says, "I desired to sit in his shade" (Song of Songs 2:3), expressing a joyful attraction rather than guilt.
H2530A.origine: The Hebrew verb חָמַד comes from a root that expresses sensory desire, the attraction to what is beautiful or pleasant. The same root is found in Hebrew words denoting desire or covetousness. In biblical Hebrew, this verb encompasses both innocent admiration (finding beautiful) and guilty desire (coveting what does not belong to oneself).
H2530A.emploi: The verb appears 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom and law books. God "covets" the good — His laws aim to protect against the coveting of evil (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21). But the text often warns: Achan covets and transgresses (Joshua 7:21); the wicked covets relentlessly (Proverbs 12:12); Micah denounces those who "covet fields" (Micah 2:2). Sometimes the word remains neutral, simply describing what is beautiful or desirable (Genesis 2:9; Song of Songs 2:3). The context shows whether the desire is just (admiring created beauty) or unjust (wanting to appropriate what belongs to another).
H2530A.portee: This word reveals a major spiritual truth: our desires shape our actions. The Bible does not condemn the desire for beauty — God created a world pleasant to see — but it warns against coveting, which arises when we look at what is not ours and want it.
