The tenth commandment exposes the heart: one cannot possess justly without first desiring justly. Recognizing our covetousness and offering it to God is a path to freedom.

sens: Having great material or market value
Rare, difficult to obtain
Worthy of esteem and respect due to its excellence
Dear to the heart, valued
H2530B.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: an object that is worth a lot of money or possesses great intrinsic wealth. Jehoshaphat and his soldiers find among the spoils of war precious items, material riches that are contested to take away (2 Chronicles 20:25), and the gold cups of Ezra are described as precious because they are of great value (Ezra 8:27).
2. What is rare and difficult to acquire, thus valued highly. The precious stones and valuable items mentioned in Daniel 11:38 are not common; their rarity makes them desirable.
3. What deserves respect and consideration due to its superior quality. The riches that the king covets in Egypt (Daniel 11:43) include not only gold and silver but everything that is precious — everything that testifies to excellence and prestige.
4. By extension, what is esteemed, dear, worthy of affection — the word expresses not only an objective value but also the attachment one has to it.
H2530B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to desire," "to covet." This is why "precious" not only describes the objective quality of an object but also the desire it provokes, its "preciousness" in the sense that it attracts, seduces, and becomes desired. The name expresses the idea of something that pleases, that deserves to be coveted — something desirable.
H2530B.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in the context of material wealth or treasures. It qualifies the spoils of war in Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles), the sacred cups of Ezra returning from exile, and the treasures that the conquering king desires to appropriate in Egypt (Daniel). The context of Daniel 11 shows the king accumulating gold, silver, and everything that is precious — revealing the covetousness that characterizes this power. The word is used indiscriminately for treasures worthy of worship, military spoils, or national wealth: wherever the Bible mentions what has value.
H2530B.portee: The Christian sees in this word how the Bible does not underestimate material wealth — it recognizes that there are precious, beautiful things worthy of esteem. But the biblical uses, especially in Daniel, also reveal that the covetousness for precious things can become idolatry, a driving force for conquest and injustice. The believer learns to discern between appreciating beauty and value, and allowing covetousness to reign in their heart.

sens: What pleases the eye or heart, what seduces
Beauty, physical attractiveness
Desirability, the desirable nature of a thing
Excellence, remarkable quality
H2531.detail:
1. Charm is primarily what attracts and pleases, what provokes desire in those who see or contemplate it. It is the pleasant impression that a person or thing produces on us. Ezekiel describes young men of beautiful appearance as "charming" creatures (Ezekiel 23:6), full of natural seduction.
2. In particular, charm refers to physical beauty, elegance, the grace of the body. The Assyrian and Babylonian warriors are presented as handsome, young, and attractive (Ezekiel 23:12, 23), embodying a beauty that seduces and fascinates.
3. The word also expresses the desirable, wishful character of a material thing: what deserves to be desired, coveted. Thus, Amos speaks of "excellent vines" (Amos 5:11), worthy of desire and covetousness, which the unjust have planted for themselves.
4. By extension, it denotes excellence, superior quality, perfection that makes a thing remarkable and worthy of admiration. A "charming" or "excellent" vine is one that produces the best wine, one that is in every way worthy of attention.
H2531.origine: The Hebrew word חֶמֶד (chemad) comes from a root meaning "to desire" or "to covet." It expresses the idea of what evokes desire, what attracts the heart. The root also appears in the verb "to covet" (חָמַד, chamad), showing that charm and desire are closely linked in Hebrew: what has charm is what is desired. The word thus refers to an objective quality — beauty — but also to the effect it produces — temptation, attraction.
H2531.emploi: The word appears six times in biblical Hebrew, always in the prophets. Isaiah uses it to denote the productive beauty of a vine, a source of joy (Isaiah 27:2, 32:12); Ezekiel, in his account of Oholiba's infidelities, uses it three times (Ezekiel 23:6, 12, 23) to describe the seductive allure of the Assyrian and Babylonian warriors, showing how physical charm can become a moral trap. Amos uses it to qualify the vines planted by the oppressors (Amos 5:11), ironically commenting on the beauty of ill-gotten goods: excellent in the eyes of the thief, but doomed to the sterility of divine judgment. In all cases, charm is what seduces, attracts, pleases — but sometimes also what deceives and leads to evil.
H2531.portee: This word reminds us that beauty and charm are visible and powerful realities, capable of seducing the heart. The Bible does not condemn charm in itself, but it warns us: what is charming and desirable in the eyes of the flesh can lead us away from God. Ezekiel shows how the attraction to physical beauty led Jerusalem to infidelity; Amos shows how the "excellent" goods stolen from the poor will serve no purpose. The Christian must learn to discern: to admire beauty without submitting to it, to enjoy good things without becoming enslaved to them.

sens: Something one desires to possess or keep
Object of great value, rich or rare
What is beautiful and appreciated, a source of pleasure or pride
Treasure, accumulated wealth
What has a high price
H2532A.detail: 1. The word first designates what the heart desires, what attracts and tempts. In 2 Chronicles 32:27, King Hezekiah accumulates "all the objects that can be desired": these are the things one seeks to possess. 2. It refers to objects that have great value, of rare beauty: Ezekiel speaks of "precious objects" of silver and gold (Daniel 11:8). 3. In Psalms 106:24, Israel despises the "land of delights" — the promised land, beautiful and rich, to which God invited them. It is the idea of a good that brings joy, that is envied. 4. Jeremiah 25:34 calls the people a "vessel of price," as if their preciousness depended on their value in the eyes of God. 5. The word can also express price, market value: what costs a lot, what cannot be easily replaced.
H2532A.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to desire," "to lean towards." The same idea is found in words of the same family: that of attraction, the desire that pushes towards an object. The basic image is that of the heart turning towards something because it finds it beautiful or useful. This is why "what one desires" eventually comes to mean "what has value" — because one naturally desires what is good and precious.
H2532A.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in prophetic texts and in the Psalms. It has several shades depending on the context. In 1 Samuel 9:20, David is a precious person, desirable for Israel — a man of value. In 2 Chronicles 32:27, it refers to concrete treasures: gold, stones, rare objects. But Jeremiah also uses it in a more poetic and theological way: the "land of delights" (Jeremiah 3:19) is the land that God offers to his people, a symbol of his favor. In Ezekiel and Daniel, the word regularly returns for the coveted riches of the temple or the treasures of a king. It is thus a rich word that ranges from concrete desire ("I would like to have that") to higher value ("it is a treasure") and even to spiritual beauty ("it is a gift from God").
H2532A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that there is a difference between what the heart naturally desires and what has true value. Israel despises God's "land of delights" out of unbelief: it prefers what it sees to what God promises. The word invites us to question our own desires: do we pursue true riches, those that come from God, or are our eyes blind to his gifts? It is also an invitation to see the preciousness of what God gives us — the earth, grace, his word — rather than to despise them.

sens: That which is precious, desirable, worthy of being chosen
That which pleases by its beauty or elegance
That which is delicate, refined, luxurious
One who is cherished, esteemed above others
H2532B.detail:
1. The word designates that which has value and deserves to be desired or sought after: it is the opposite of what is ordinary or uninteresting. When Rebecca chooses "the finest garments of Esau" (Genesis 27:15), she selects those that have prestige and brilliance.
2. The "brilliance" here speaks of visible beauty, graceful or imposing appearance: it is a garment that stands out and pleases the eye. The adjective evokes elegance and finesse.
3. The "delicacies" that Daniel refuses (Daniel 10:3) are refined, tasty foods reserved for wealthy tables. It is culinary luxury, that which flatters the palate.
4. When the angel calls Daniel "beloved man" (Daniel 9:23; 10:11, 19), he expresses that he is precious in God's eyes, cherished, worthy of esteem and special attention. It is an honor, a mark of divine favor.
H2532B.origine: This word comes from an ancient Hebrew root meaning "to desire" or "to take pleasure in." The same root produces other words in the biblical family that speak of desire, preference, attraction. The image is that of what draws one to itself, captivating the gaze or the heart: first the object that one desires (a beautiful garment, an exquisite dish), then the person one cherishes.
H2532B.emploi: This word appears five times in the Bible, all in the contexts of the Greek or late Old Testament: three times in Daniel (as a title of honor for Daniel himself) and once in Genesis. In Genesis, it describes Esau's garments as precious and sought after. In Daniel, the word shifts registers: it is no longer about material things, but about a moral or spiritual quality. Daniel is "beloved" because he prayed sincerely and fasted piously (Daniel 10:3, 12); the angel designates him three times by this title, marking his tenderness and respect for the prophet.
H2532B.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not look only at outward appearance, but honors those who seek Him sincerely. Being called "beloved" by a messenger of God is an assurance of divine favor and protection. It is also an invitation to abandon superfluous refinements to devote oneself to prayer and communion with God, as Daniel did.

sens: A man from the time of the Patriarchs, son of Dishon
H2533.detail: Hemdan is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the Horites. He is the son of Dishon, himself the son of Anah, and he has three brothers: Eshban, Jithran, and Karen (Genesis 36:26). His name means "desire" in Hebrew. He lived during the time of the patriarchs, in the early days of biblical history.
H2533.origine: The name Hemdan comes from the Hebrew word חמד (hemad), which means "to desire" or "to covet." The name thus evokes an object of desire or something pleasant. A variant of the name, Chamran, is also attested in ancient manuscripts.
H2533.emploi: Hemdan appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 36:26, where he is listed among the descendants of Esau and the peoples who lived in Canaan before the conquest. This genealogy places Hemdan among the Horites, inhabitants of Edom. His unique mention shows that Moses recorded the names of the peoples and families that populated the promised land before Israel's arrival.

sens: Intense heat, fever
Venom or poison of an animal
Fierce anger, intense rage
Indignation, wrath
Unreasoned outburst
Visible manifestation of anger
H2534.detail:
1. Fury primarily designates an extreme physical heat, that of fever or poison that burns the body — a sensation of internal fire that consumes.
2. In animals, it is the venom, the poison that flows under their lips: the Psalms speak of the "venom of asps" (Psalms 140:4) to describe the deadly words of the enemy.
3. Literally, fury is an intense and overflowing anger: Haman "was filled with fury" (Esther 3:5) upon seeing that Mordecai did not kneel before him.
4. It also expresses holy or righteous indignation, often that of God in the face of sin: God "pours out His fury like fire on the tent of the daughter of Zion" (Lamentations 2:4).
5. Fury is an outburst that seizes the one who feels it, an unreasoned movement of the heart: Proverbs advises to "abandon fury" (Proverbs 22:24).
6. It manifests concretely in actions: the arm that rises, the judgment that strikes — "My fury has served as support for me" (Isaiah 63:5), where anger becomes active force.
H2534.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be hot, to burn." The basic image is thermal: fury is a heat that devours from within, like a fever or like poison that burns. This root appears in other words related to fire or destruction. In Aramaic, the equivalent form retains the same meaning of "rage." The Old Testament uses this word over a hundred times, showing that fury — whether human or divine — is a major reality in the biblical experience.
H2534.emploi: The word fury appears 118 times in the Old Testament. It primarily describes human anger: that of Esau against Jacob (Genesis 27:44), that of Haman (Esther), or the warnings of Proverbs against angry men. But the majority of uses concern God's fury in response to the sin of Israel or the nations: it burns against unfaithfulness (Leviticus 26:28), it pours out like a devastating fire (Lamentations 2:4; Ezekiel 20:34), it strikes with judgment. Among the psalmists, divine fury is terrible and feared (Psalms 90:7), but it can also be restrained by intercession (Numbers 25:11). Proverbs teaches wisdom: "A soft answer turns away fury" (Proverbs 15:1).
H2534.portee: Understanding biblical fury helps the Christian grasp two truths. First, anger is not always a sin: it can be just and holy when it responds to sin and injustice. But it is dangerous in humans: carried away by rage, a person destroys without wisdom. Second, in the face of God's fury, the believer learns that judgment is real and that sin has serious consequences — but also that grace can turn away this anger. It is a word that calls for reverential fear and repentance.

sens: The celestial body that shines in the sky and warms the earth
The heat radiated by this celestial body
The brilliant light of the sun
The power and majesty of the sun in the created order
H2535.detail:
1. The sun is the luminous body that rises in the east and sets in the west, traversing the sky each day. It is the most concrete image of the word: in Psalms 19:7, the psalmist describes the sun that "rises at one end of the heavens and makes its circuit to the other end."
2. The heat of the sun is its intense and penetrating warmth: it can darken the skin and burn (Job 30:28: "I go about darkened, but not by the sun").
3. The sun symbolizes radiant beauty and purity. In Song of Solomon 6:10, the beloved is described as "beautiful as the sun."
4. The sun also represents the power and glory of God in creation. In Isaiah 24:23 and 30:26, the sun is mentioned in contexts of judgment and future restoration, where its light and strength testify to the power of the Lord.
H2535.origine: The Hebrew word cham.mah designates primarily the visible and warm celestial body. It comes from a common Semitic root that evokes burning heat. In Hebrew, the two meanings—sun and heat—are closely linked, as the sun is primarily perceived through the heat it produces on the earth and living beings.
H2535.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the provided texts, mainly in wisdom and prophetic poems. In Psalms 19, it describes the regular movement of the sun as an image of the reliability of God's Word. In Job 30:28 and Song of Solomon 6:10, it refers to the visible effects of the sun: darkening of the skin on one side, radiant beauty on the other. In the passages from Isaiah (24:23 and 30:26), the sun appears in eschatological visions: sometimes covered with shame during judgment, sometimes multiplied in splendor during restoration. Thus, the sun transitions from a regular testimony of divine faithfulness to a symbol of judgment and future glory.
H2535.portee: The sun in the Bible is never a rival deity, but a creature of God that manifests His power. Recognizing the sun as a gift from God, a source of warmth and light necessary for life, invites the reader to see in creation a testimony of the wisdom and goodness of the Creator. The eschatological passages remind us that even the celestial bodies will be renewed and subjected to the glory of God.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H2536.detail: Hammuel is a man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in a genealogy where he is presented as the son of Mischma and the father of Zaccur (1 Chronicles 4:26). His name means "heat of God" in Hebrew, expressing divine protection or power.
H2536.origine: The name Hammuel is formed from two Hebrew elements: "ham" (חַם) meaning "heat" or "ardor," and "el" (אֵל) which designates God. It is a common construction in Hebrew proper names, combining a quality or action with the divine name to express a relationship with God.
H2536.emploi: Hammuel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:26, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Simeon. He is part of the family of Shaul, an important branch of this tribe. His mention, although brief, situates him in the time of the divided monarchy in Israel.

sens: Wife of King Josiah, mother of two kings of Israel
H2537.detail: Hamuthal is a woman from the time of the divided monarchy. She is the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah and married King Josiah. She gave birth to two sons who both reigned over Judah: Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. She is mentioned in the accounts of the reigns of her two sons, as the mother of the king.
H2537.origine: The name Hamuthal means "the father-in-law is protection." It comes from two Hebrew roots: the word for "father-in-law" and the one for "protection" or "shelter." This name reflects a trust or dependence on the protection of a father-in-law or a protective male figure, which was important in royal families of antiquity.
H2537.emploi: Hamuthal appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always identified as the mother of a reigning king. She is first mentioned in 2 Kings 23:31 as the mother of Jehoahaz, who reigns for three months in Jerusalem. She is then found in 2 Kings 24:18 and Jeremiah 52:1 as the mother of Zedekiah, who reigns for eleven years. These three verses repeat the same information: she is the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. Her repeated mention emphasizes her role as the mother of kings and her connection to a respectable provincial family.

sens: son of Perez and grandson of Judah
ancestor of a family from the tribe of Judah
H2538.detail:
1. Hamul is the youngest son of Perez, who is himself the son of Judah and Tamar. He appears in the family genealogies of Judah during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:12): he is a direct ancestor of the people of Israel.
2. His descendants form a distinct family within the tribe of Judah, the Hamulites, mentioned in the census of the wilderness (Numbers 26:21). This family is listed among the genealogical branches of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:5).
H2538.origine: The name Hamul means "spared" or "compassionate" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking the idea of grace and clemency. The patronymic "Hamulite" designates the descendants of Hamul, formed according to the Hebrew custom for naming a clan family.
H2538.emploi: Hamul is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in genealogical contexts. He first appears in Genesis 46:12 among the sons of Perez who descend with Jacob into Egypt. His name reappears in Numbers 26:21 during the census of the sons of Israel in the wilderness, where his descendants are organized into an official clan family. Finally, he is listed in the Davidic genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:5, confirming the genealogical significance of his lineage within the tribe of Judah.

sens: Descendant of Hamul, man of the tribe of Judah
H2539.detail: 1. The term designates a member of the clan of the Hamulites, that is, a descendant of Hamul. Hamul was the son of Perez and grandson of Judah, born from the union of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 46:12). At the time of the census in the wilderness, the Hamulite clan formed a distinct family within the tribe of Judah, alongside the clan of the Hezronites descended from his brother Hezron (Numbers 26:21).
H2539.origine: The term comes from the proper name Hamul (H2538), which means "spared" or "to have pity." Hamul was the son of Perez and the grandson of the patriarch Judah. The Hebrew suffix forms names of family groups: thus "Hamulite" designates all those who descend from this ancestor. Like many clan names in the Old Testament, it carries within it the genealogical history of the people of Israel.
H2539.emploi: The Hamulites appear only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:21, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness, forty years after the exodus from Egypt. This passage enumerates the families of the tribe of Judah descended from Perez and his descendants. The Hamulites are listed alongside the Hezronites as two major branches of this Judean clan. This census served to establish the order of the tribes for the journey in the wilderness and the future distribution of the promised land.
H2539.portee: This small verse reveals how God keeps a detailed account of His people and preserves the memory of each family, even the most modest. The Hamulites remind us that every believer belongs to a genealogy of faith that traces back to Judah and his promises, and that we are all counted and precious in the eyes of our Father.

sens: City of Naphtali in Northern Israel
Dwelling place of the Levites
H2540.detail:
1. Hammon is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, in Northern Israel, not far from the Phoenician coast. Its name means "hot springs," which likely refers to thermal springs near the site. It appears in the list of cities in the Naphtali territory in Joshua 19:28, listed between Ebron and Kana, toward Sidon the Great.
2. Hammon is assigned to the Levites as a city of refuge and place of residence. According to 1 Chronicles 6:76, it is among the Levitical cities of the tribe of Naphtali, alongside Kedesh in Galilee and Kirjathaim. It is one of the forty-eight cities granted to the sons of Levi for them to have dwellings and pastures, according to God's order.
H2540.origine: The name Hammon comes from the Hebrew root חַמַּ (hamma), which means "heat" or "hot." This word is related to חַמָּה (hamma, "heat of the sun") and evokes the idea of a hot spring or thermal source. The name also appears in the forms "Hammath" and "Hammoth-dor," which are variants of the same place or related names designating the same geographical region.
H2540.emploi: Hammon appears only twice in the Bible. It first appears in Joshua 19:28 as a city in the territory of Naphtali during the division of the land among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. It is then mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:76 in the list of the forty-eight cities assigned to the Levites. These two references indicate that Hammon was a locality in northern Canaan, integrated into the system of Levitical cities where priests and worship assistants could reside with their families and flocks.

sens: one who suffers oppression, violence, or injustice from others
one who is crushed by the power, wealth, or strength of another
H2541.detail: 1. The oppressed is a person who is a victim of violence or injustice: they suffer the abuse of power from someone stronger or wealthier who mistreats them. In Isaiah 1:17, God commands His people to "defend the oppressed" alongside the orphan and the widow — three figures of weakness and vulnerability that justice must protect. 2. The word evokes one who is crushed, devoid of recourse, reduced to powerlessness. That is why it often appears in a context where God takes the side of the weak against the powerful who exploit them.
H2541.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pressing, crushing, or squeezing. It is constructed to describe not the act of oppressing, but the one who is the victim of it — the crushed, the tortured. The Bible often uses this word to refer to the weak and the needy whom God takes under His protection.
H2541.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 1:17, where God exhorts Judah to seek justice. In this passage, the oppressed is mentioned alongside the orphan and the widow as a category of person that the law must protect. It is a call to defend the most vulnerable against those who mistreat them.
H2541.portee: This word reminds Christians that God cares for the weak and victims of injustice, and that He invites His disciples to do the same. Biblical faith is not limited to personal piety: it demands social justice, the protection of those who cannot defend themselves. It is a word that challenges consciences and calls for action.

sens: The gentle curve of a shape, the line that delineates a surface
The silhouette or rounded shapes of the human body
H2542.detail:
1. The word designates a curve, a line that rounds and delineates a shape. It is the image of something that bends gradually, like the contours of a basin or a molded object.
2. In the text of the Song of Songs (7:2), it describes the graceful forms of the beloved: "The contours of your hips are like jewels." Here, the word evokes the soft and rounded lines of the body, creating an image of natural beauty and harmony.
H2542.origine: The Hebrew word חַמּוּק (chammuq) comes from a root that expresses the idea of bending or curving. It describes the curve itself, this line that bends gradually. The word belongs to the family of verbs of movement and transformation of form, common in Hebrew to paint images of physical beauty and grace.
H2542.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in the Song of Songs 7:2. It is used in this love poem to describe the shapes of the female body. Its poetic and celebratory context shows that "contour" is here an aesthetic term of admiration, used to express the harmonious beauty of the beloved. The comparison with "jewels" emphasizes the brilliance and grace of these rounded forms.
H2542.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the beauty of the human body as a creation of God. In the Song of Songs, it reminds us that respectful and loving appreciation of the physical beauty of another has its place in the life of a faithful couple. It is an invitation to see in the shapes of the human body, not an occasion for unbridled sensuality, but a testimony of the harmony and order that God has established.

sens: Beast of burden and riding, robust and enduring, used for transport and work
Economic asset and sign of wealth
Creature subject to the law of God like the rest of the livestock
H2543.detail:
1. The donkey is a domesticated animal commonly used in Israel for carrying loads, riding, or pulling vehicles. Abraham receives donkeys among his herds (Genesis 12:16), and a woman rides one to travel (1 Samuel 25:20). It is a reliable and rustic work animal.

2. Owning donkeys in number indicates wealth and social importance: Jacob has thirty (Genesis 32:5), and Joseph claims the Egyptians' donkeys to raise taxes during a famine (Genesis 47:17). Having donkeys marks a family's economic status.

3. The donkey appears in the Law as an object of protection and moral obligation: one must not let an enemy's donkey succumb under its burden (Exodus 23:5), and the donkey has the right to rest on the Sabbath like any creature (Exodus 23:12). The animal falls under divine will for social and moral order.
H2543.origine: The Hebrew word חֲמוֹר (chamor) has its root in the idea of red or brown — the natural color of the animal. It is distinct from the word for horse (סוּס, sus): the donkey is slower but more resilient. The word appears 93 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the narratives of the Pentateuch and the Judges, reflecting its economic and daily importance in Israel.
H2543.emploi: The donkey appears 93 times, predominantly in Genesis, Exodus, and Judges. It is the companion of the patriarchs — Abraham, Jacob, and their descendants own them in herds (Genesis 12:16, Genesis 30:43, Genesis 32:5). During famines or commercial exchanges, donkeys are used as currency and tribute: Joseph receives them as tax (Genesis 47:17, Numbers 31:28). In the Mosaic Law, the donkey is protected: one respects that of one's neighbor (Exodus 23:4-5), one does not yoke it with the plow (Deuteronomy 22:10), and it rests on the Sabbath (Exodus 23:12). Finally, during a siege, its flesh becomes so precious that a donkey's head sells for a high price (2 Kings 6:25). The donkey embodies ordinary wealth, subsistence economy, and moral responsibility towards creatures.
H2543.portee: The donkey reminds the reader that biblical wealth is not abstract, but concrete — livestock, land, servants. For the modern believer, this detail makes the narratives of the Pentateuch more vivid and rooted in a peasant reality. The Law that protects the donkey from the enemy (Exodus 23:5) also teaches that mercy towards creatures is a form of obedience to God — a moral lesson that is still valid today.

sens: Hivite prince of Shechem during the patriarchal period
Father of Shechem
Landowner from whom Jacob bought a field
H2544.detail:
1. Hamor is a Hivite prince who rules over the city of Shechem when Jacob arrives in Palestine after his stay with Laban. He appears in the dramatic story of Shechem and Dinah (Genesis 34), where he plays a role as a political and family leader.
2. He is the father of Shechem, the young man who falls in love with Dinah, Jacob's daughter. It is in this capacity that Hamor intervenes in the negotiations between his family and Jacob's.
3. Jacob buys a portion of land near Shechem from Hamor and his sons to pitch his tent and establish his dwelling (Genesis 33:19). This acquisition of land in Canaan marks an important step in Israel's settlement in the promised land.
H2544.origine: The name Hamor (חֲמוֹר) literally means "donkey" in Hebrew — a term that referred both to the pack animal and, by extension, to a man of status or power. In the patriarchal context, donkeys were valuable possessions and a sign of wealth; naming a prince of Shechem may highlight his importance or role as a leader.
H2544.emploi: Hamor appears twelve times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of Genesis 34, which recounts the incident involving Dinah. He is first seen selling a field to Jacob (Genesis 33:19), then intervening to arrange the marriage between his son Shechem and Dinah: he speaks to Jacob and his sons, circumcises all the men of his city, and ultimately is killed along with his son by Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:4-26). The context portrays Hamor as a political leader respected by his people, willing to negotiate, but whose efforts lead to catastrophe. He is mentioned a final time in Joshua 24:32, where Jacob reaffirms that the field purchased from Hamor has become the inheritance of Joseph.
H2544.portee: The story of Hamor highlights the difficulty of God's people coexisting with the Canaanite peoples without spiritual compromise. It shows how alliances and marriages with unbelievers, even under the guise of honorable negotiations, can lead to tragedies. The land purchased from Hamor becomes the place where Joseph's bones are buried (Joshua 24:32), symbolizing God's faithfulness to His promises and the continuity of His heritage with those who remain faithful to Him.

sens: The mother of a woman's husband
The mother of a man's wife
H2545.detail:
1. Mother-in-law is the mother of the husband. It is a relationship of alliance created by marriage. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law (Ruth 1:14), while Ruth clung to hers with remarkable loyalty.
2. The term also refers, by extension, to the mother of a man's wife. In the book of Ruth, Naomi is Ruth's mother-in-law — she is the mother of Ruth's deceased husband, and this bond persists even after widowhood.
H2545.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "heat" or "ardor," and it originally evokes the mother. In Israel's family culture, this alliance was considered important: the mother-in-law remained a figure of authority and counsel in the household. The Segond translates this word as "mother-in-law" in ten occurrences, all in the Old Testament.
H2545.emploi: The term appears mainly in the story of Ruth and Naomi, where their relationship becomes the heart of the narrative. Naomi guides her daughter-in-law Ruth toward marriage and security (Ruth 3:1 and 3:11). Ruth, in turn, submits to her mother-in-law's counsel and fulfills her task with respect. The term also denotes a potential source of conflict: Micah 7:6 speaks of the mother-in-law as an enemy, reminding us that this bond, while significant, is not always harmonious. These usages illustrate how the extended family functioned in ancient Israel.
H2545.portee: The relationship between Ruth and Naomi illustrates how loyalty to one's in-laws transcends ethnic boundaries and life's misfortunes. Ruth honors her mother-in-law through her work, obedience, and love, which becomes the foundation of her blessing. For the Christian reader, this bond invites reflection on how to treat in-laws with respect and generosity, even when circumstances are difficult.

sens: Land or aquatic animal considered unclean in Mosaic law
H2546.detail: 1. The snail is an animal mentioned only once in the Bible, within the list of creatures declared unclean according to the law of Moses. The Segond 1910 translates the Hebrew word this way, although its exact identification remains uncertain: it could refer to a snail, a slug, or a creature that has become extinct that the ancient Hebrews knew but which we have lost track of (Leviticus 11:30).
H2546.origine: The Hebrew word chomet appears only once in Leviticus. Its exact etymology is not definitively established. Unlike other animals in the same list (the hedgehog, the tortoise, the chameleon), this term has no clear equivalents in neighboring Semitic languages, suggesting that it likely refers to a creature that is either extinct or very little known. Ancient Greek translators and rabbinic tradition themselves hesitated over its identification.
H2546.emploi: This word appears only in Leviticus 11:30, at the heart of the list of land animals that the Israelites are not to eat, according to the purity rules established by God. It is listed among other creeping creatures: the hedgehog, the frog, the tortoise, and the chameleon. The absence of other occurrences makes it difficult to specify the context or nuance of its use, but its role is clearly legislative and ceremonial.
H2546.portee: This word reminds us that the Mosaic law governed all details of the ordinary life of the Israelites, including diet and relations with animals. For the Christian, who is no longer bound by these dietary prescriptions (see Mark 7:19 and Romans 14:14), this term invites reflection on the difference between the law of Israel and freedom in Christ, and on how God guided His people through concrete symbols.

sens: Village in Judah located near Hebron
H2547.detail: Humta is a small mountain village located in Judah, near Hebron. The name means in Hebrew "place of lizards" (chum = lizard). It is a village of little importance that appears only once in the Bible, during the enumeration of cities in the territory of Judah (Joshua 15:54).
H2547.origine: The Hebrew name חֻמְטָה (chumtah) derives from חם (cham), which designates the lizard. The suffix -tah indicates a place. It is a geographical name that likely describes the natural environment of the site: an area where lizards were numerous.
H2547.emploi: Humta appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:54, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest. It is mentioned among nine cities in the mountainous region near Hebron. It is a locality from the time of the land distribution, with no particular story or event reported about it.

sens: food seasoned with salt
having the taste of salt
H2548.detail:
1. Food to which salt has been added for preservation or seasoning. The text of Isaiah 30:24 speaks of salted fodder given to oxen and donkeys: it is a prepared and enriched food, better than simple hay.
2. Having the flavor of salt. The word describes the result of this preparation: food whose taste has been altered by the addition of salt.
H2548.origine: The Hebrew word חָמִיץ (cha.mits) comes from a root related to the idea of brining or preserving with salt. In Hebrew, this use of salt was common for preserving food and enhancing flavor. The agricultural and pastoral context of the text shows that ancient Near Eastern peoples also enriched livestock food with salt.
H2548.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:24. It describes superior food given to working animals: the salted fodder that farmers prepare by winnowing grain. This unique occurrence suggests a technical usage, specific to agricultural vocabulary and livestock feeding.
H2548.portee: This detail reveals generosity toward working animals: even the laboring animal receives careful and pleasant food. It invites the believer to see the divine providence that cares for every creature and reminds us that service, whether human or animal, deserves respect and care.

sens: Which occupies the numerical rank 5 in a sequence or enumeration
Which corresponds to the 5th month of the civil or Hebrew religious year
Which designates the 5th day of the week or of creation
In restitution ordinances, the additional share of one-fifth to be added to the price or value
H2549.detail:
1. The word designates the ordinal number 5, which comes after the fourth in a sequence: thus in Genesis 1:23, the fifth day is the day when God created the aquatic creatures and the birds. It is also found to enumerate the sons (1 Chronicles 26:3: "Elam the fifth, Johanan the sixth"), the portions of the Temple (1 Kings 6:31), or the divisions of the priestly service (1 Chronicles 24:9).
2. It designates the fifth month of the Hebrew calendar, later called "Ab." This month is mentioned notably during the destruction of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:8: "On the seventh day of the fifth month") and in the captivity narratives (Jeremiah 1:3).
3. In the restitution laws given to Moses, the word "fifth" designates a penalty added to the compensation: if someone has stolen or misappropriated a consecrated thing, he must return its value plus one-fifth (Leviticus 5:16; 27:13). This surcharge was a judgment from the Lord against the sin of fraud.
H2549.origine: The Hebrew word חֲמִישִׁי (chamishi) derives from חָמֵשׁ (chamesh), which means "five." It is a regular ordinal adjective, formed according to Hebrew conventions to express numerical ranks. The root חמש itself is very ancient and common to all Semitic languages to designate this number.
H2549.emploi: The word appears 44 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly for three uses: first, to enumerate elements in a series (days, people, positions), then to designate the fifth month of the year (very frequently in historical and prophetic books to date events), and finally to express the legal penalties of restitutions imposed by the Law (especially in Leviticus). It is found in all the major historical books and also among the prophets.
H2549.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that everything that exists—the time, the numbers, the order of creation—depends on the word of God. The ordinances of the fifth (restitution with penalty) also teach that sin has a cost: it is not enough to return what one has taken; one must add compensation, a figure of divine justice that never leaves evil without reparation.

sens: To hold back one's hand, not to strike or destroy
To have pity, compassion towards someone
To refuse to do harm, to show mercy
Not to spare: to abandon to destruction, to strike mercilessly
H2550.detail:
1. To spare means to hold back one's raised arm, not to strike. The daughter of Pharaoh sees the crying baby Moses and "she had pity on him" (Exodus 2:6): she does not kill him, she takes him in. It is the gesture of one who stops their hand before destroying.
2. This word expresses compassion, the inner feeling that drives one not to cause suffering. When God speaks of His love for Israel, He says: "I will spare him" (Malachi 3:17), like a father who spares his favored son.
3. To spare means to choose mercy instead of strict justice. It is to deliberately refuse to do the evil one has the right or power to do. This implies a certain tenderness, a voluntary restraint.
4. Conversely, "not to spare" means to strike without mercy, without regard for the cries of the victim. God says: "I will not spare" (Jeremiah 13:14), announcing punishment without compassion. It is the complete absence of pity in the execution of judgment (Lamentations 2:17).
H2550.origine: The Hebrew verb חָמַל comes from a root that evokes the idea of "holding back" or "sparing." It expresses a movement of the heart before a movement of the arm: one feels pity, and this feeling holds back our hand. It is a very concrete word, linked to the action of preserving someone from the blow intended for them. In biblical Hebrew, this verb forms a rich family: there are also derivatives that express this nuance of compassion tempered by a certain reserve.
H2550.emploi: This verb appears about forty times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Lamentations) and historical narratives. Positively, it describes the attitude of one who saves or spares: the daughter of Pharaoh spares Moses, David spares Saul (2 Samuel 21:7), God spares His people. Negatively, very frequent in prophetic judgments, it paints a God who "does not spare," who executes punishment mercilessly— a terrible image of judgment that strikes without restraint. This duality shows that the word does not designate a fleeting feeling, but a decision of the will: to spare or not to spare engages the whole being.
H2550.portee: This word teaches the believer two major truths. First, divine sparing: God has spared us when He could have destroyed us, and this compassion prevails in His heart. Secondly, a responsibility: to call to spare others is to call to cultivate mercy towards those who are in our power. Between vengeance and forgiveness, to spare is the path of justice united with compassion.

sens: Active compassion of a person towards one who suffers
Benevolent love that drives one to spare and to help
Tender pity of the heart in the face of distress
H2551.detail:
1. Mercy is the feeling of compassion that arises when one sees the suffering of another. It is this emotion of the heart that drives one to help those in pain. In Isaiah 63:9, God is described as the one who, in His love and mercy, saved the people through all their distresses—this is the image of a protector moved by the misery of those He loves.
2. Mercy is also a concrete action: it is not limited to a feeling, but is expressed through help, salvation, support. God does not abandon His people; He redeems them and constantly carries them—this is mercy in action. It is the tender pity of the heart that manifests in acts of deliverance.
H2551.origine: The Hebrew word chemlah comes from a root that expresses the idea of tenderness and care towards one who is in difficulty. It is very close in meaning to other Hebrew words for mercy (hésèd, rahamim), but chemlah particularly emphasizes this emotion of the heart moved by distress. This word is rare in the Bible, which makes its uses all the more poignant.
H2551.emploi: Chemlah appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first mention is in Genesis 19:16, in the context of Lot's deliverance. The second, more developed, is in Isaiah 63:9, where the prophet celebrates God's mercy towards His people throughout history: God has saved, redeemed, and supported them out of love and mercy. In both cases, the word describes the benevolent intervention of a protector towards one who is in danger or distress.
H2551.portee: For the believer, God's mercy is not a distant emotion: it is a reality that saves and supports. This word reminds us that God sees our distress and acts with tenderness and strength to deliver us. It is a call to place our trust in the one whose heart is moved for us, and a model for our own compassion towards those who suffer.

sens: To become hot or warm, to warm up
To feel physical warmth, to be hot
To be ardent, burning with passion or anger
To ignite, to become emotionally excited
H2552.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of becoming hot or moving to a higher temperature. The image is concrete: when the sun rises, the heat of the day melts the manna (Exodus 16:21), or the waters melt when the heat of summer returns (Job 6:17). It is the transition from a cold or lukewarm state to a hot state.
2. The word also expresses the fact of feeling hot physically, especially in the context of personal warming: when two people lie together, they "warm" each other (Ecclesiastes 4:11), or a young girl must "warm" the sick king by sleeping near him (1 Kings 1:2).
3. In its more figurative uses, it means to ignite with intense emotion, particularly anger or passion. The hearts of drunkards "burn" like fire (Hosea 7:7), an image of destructive and uncontrollable fervor.
4. The verb can also express the idea of becoming intense or ardent figuratively: a situation that ignites, a passion that rekindles, an anger that rises to incandescence.
H2552.origine: The verb חָמַם (chamar) comes from a root that evokes the fundamental idea of heat and fire. This root is close to the word חֹם (khom, heat), and it expresses the active transition from a cold state to a hot state. In Hebrew, it is used for both physical heat and intense emotional states, as the Ancients saw heat as a natural metaphor for the ardor of the heart.
H2552.emploi: The verb חָמַם appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Ecclesiastes) and in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel). It is first used for the heat of the sun or fire: the manna melts when the heat of the day comes (Exodus 16:21), or one warms oneself by a fire (Isaiah 44:15-16). It also describes physical warming: the sick king must be warmed by a young girl lying near him (1 Kings 1:2), or two people who "are hot" together to stay alive (Ecclesiastes 4:11). Figuratively, it expresses emotional inflammation: the heart of those who drink burns like fire (Hosea 7:7). The verb can also be transitive (to heat, to warm) or reflexive (to heat oneself, to ignite oneself).
H2552.portee: This word reminds the reader that heat, in all its forms, is a vital power — it invigorates the body, but it can also consume and destroy. Spiritually, it warns against the passions that inflame us: anger, lust, drunkenness can ravage us like fire. But it also suggests the idea of a warming closeness, a communion that gives us life. It is a call to discern between the heat that invigorates and that which consumes.

sens: stone or metal object erected in honor of the sun
idol pillar or monument raised in high places
symbol of sun worship in Canaanite religion
image made by human hands, object of veneration
H2553.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a physical object: a statue or pillar erected to honor the sun, a pagan god worshiped by the Canaanite nations. In Isaiah 17:8, the Lord reproaches Israel for contemplating "what their fingers have made, the idols of Astarte and the sun statues," showing that these objects were crafted by humans and became the object of their worship.
2. These sun idols were an integral part of high places, idolatrous sanctuaries built on hills. In 2 Chronicles 14:4, King Asa destroys "the sun idols" that stood in the cities of Judah, showing that they were associated with a religiosity contrary to true faith.
3. These objects symbolize the worship of false deities and Israel's infidelity. Leviticus 26:30 threatens that if Israel turns away, the Lord "will destroy your sun idols"; this is an act of divine abolition of idolatrous worship, a judgment on the people who have gone astray.
H2553.origine: The Hebrew word חַמָּן (chamman) is related to the idea of heat and solar radiation (from the root חַם, "hot"). It literally designates columns or statues dedicated to sun worship among the Canaanites. This type of religious object was common in the ancient Near East, where the sun was revered as a divine power. The form of the word suggests a monument erected, often in stone.
H2553.emploi: This word appears eight times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the books of Chronicles, Isaiah, and Ezekiel, always in a context of denouncing idolatrous worship. It is regularly associated with the altars of Baals, the idols of Astarte, and the high places. The pious kings of Judah — notably Asa (2 Chronicles 14:4) and Josiah (2 Chronicles 34:4, 34:7) — destroy these idols as an act of religious reform. Isaiah and Ezekiel present them as signs of Israel's sin: objects made by humans to which the people offer worship that belongs only to the Lord.
H2553.portee: This word reminds us that worshiping objects made by human hands is a perversion of true adoration. It invites the believer to reflect on what they truly honor: wealth, prestige, or human creations that present themselves as divine? The constant condemnation of these idols underscores that true faith rejects anything that diverts the heart from God alone.

sens: To physically harm someone, to treat them brutally
To commit injustice, dishonesty
To transgress, profane, violate (a law, a commandment)
To cause harm or damage to someone
H2554.detail:
1. The word primarily means to treat someone with physical violence: to strike, to mistreat, to harm their body. It is to act brutally towards a defenseless person, as in Jeremiah 22:3 where the Lord forbids to "mistreat" the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow — vulnerable people.
2. It also extends to moral injustice and intentional harm: to commit iniquity, dishonesty. In Job 21:27, the "wicked" thoughts are false and disloyal judgments.
3. It can mean to transgress or profane something sacred, particularly a divine law. In Ezekiel 22:26, the priests "violate" the law of the Lord in contempt of His commandments.
4. The word also encompasses the harm, the damage one causes to a soul or a life. In Proverbs 8:36, one who sins "harms" their own soul by refusing wisdom.
H2554.origine: The verb חָמַס (chamass) comes from a root that expresses the idea of forcing, using power to do harm. Its basic meaning is thus the violent and abusive use of force. The word belongs to a small group of Hebrew verbs that speak of intentional violence and malice, distinct from words for simple accidental harm. Its etymological link with the word חָמָס (khamas, "violence") shows the unity of meaning around this theme of intentional harm.
H2554.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic books (Job, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel). It describes concrete acts of malice: treating someone violently (Jeremiah 22:3), but also abstract or spiritual harms (violating the law in Ezekiel 22:26). The context is almost always that of sin, injustice, or punishment. The law forbids this violence; wisdom condemns it; the prophets accuse Israel and the nations of having committed it. The word is also used to describe God's destructive action upon His own people (Lamentations 2:6), showing that even divine judgment is presented under the seal of force used against what resists.
H2554.portee: This word calls the believer to respect justice, dignity, and the rights of others. It reminds us that intentionally causing harm — through force, deceit, or transgression — is a serious sin in the eyes of God. It is a call to protect the vulnerable (the orphan, the widow, the foreigner) and to obey divine commandments without violating them. The contrast with justice and equity in Jeremiah 22:3 shows that God desires a people who refuse violence and seek the good of others.

sens: Act of brute force that injures or kills
Unjust act committed against someone, theft or oppression
Lying words or false testimony
Character that is violent, brutal, or cruel
Abrupt breaking of a relationship or promise
H2555.detail:
1. Violence is primarily the act of striking, killing, or destroying by physical force. It describes a brutal aggression committed against a person or thing. Genesis 6:11 speaks of the earth as "full of violence," meaning ravaged by acts of destruction and aggression.
2. It also denotes deliberate injustice: stealing, oppressing, extorting, stripping someone of their goods or rights. Ezekiel 45:9 commands the princes to "cease violence and robbery," linking theft to systematic oppression.
3. Violence can also be verbal: false testimony, slanderous accusation, words that hurt. Exodus 23:1 forbids making a "false report" (literally violence by words).
4. It is also the violent temperament itself, habitual cruelty. Proverbs 4:17 speaks of those who drink "the wine of violence," meaning they live in brutality and impiety.
5. It includes betrayal or renunciation of a covenant. In 1 Chronicles 12:17, David asks his allies if they come to help him or to "deceive" him (committing violence against him by delivering him to his enemies).
H2555.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "treating roughly" or "devastating." This root is found in other Hebrew words that describe force, oppression, and violation. The Hebrew term chamac is used 59 times in the Bible for all acts that violate justice, life, and peace: it is a key concept in the biblical mentality of what offends God and destroys community.
H2555.emploi: The word violence (chamac) appears 59 times in the Old Testament. In the beginning, in Genesis 6:11-13, the earth is full of violence in the time before the Flood. The Psalms constantly denounce the violence of the wicked against the righteous (Psalms 55:10, 140:2). Proverbs contrasts it with wisdom and justice: the violent is a fool, while the wise avoids the path of the violent (Proverbs 3:31). The prophets Ezekiel, Jeremiah, and Habakkuk condemn it as the major sin of Israel and the nations, a sign of a people who have turned away from God and His Law. The word thus covers any serious violation of order, justice, and covenant.
H2555.portee: Violence, in the Old Testament, is presented as a serious transgression that cries out for vengeance from God and distances one from Him. It reveals the absence of fear of the Lord and contempt for His justice. For the Christian, this word reminds that God sees and hates injustice, oppression, and cruelty in all their forms, and calls His faithful to righteousness, to protect the weak, and to refuse anything that hurts or oppresses.

sens: To increase the volume of dough by the fermentation of leaven
To become sour, to become bitter or irritated in one's heart
H2556A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of leaven which makes the dough of bread rise. When leaven (a portion of fermented dough) is mixed with fresh dough, it "rises": it increases in volume under the action of the microbes that cause fermentation. This is why, during Passover, the Israelites were to eat unleavened bread — dough that had not risen (Exodus 12:34: "The people took their dough before it was leavened"). This haste symbolized their flight from Egypt, without the time to wait for the dough to ferment.
2. By extension, the word takes on a figurative meaning: to become sour, to become bitter, or to be irritated in one's heart. It is the bitterness of leaven that ferments, applied to feelings. In Psalm 73:21, the psalmist confesses: "When my heart was embittered, And I was pierced in my innermost being" — the image of leaven transforming the dough describes how envy or doubt can ferment in the soul and poison it.
H2556A.origine: The Hebrew word חָמֵץ (chamets) comes from a root that evokes fermentation, acidity, bitterness. Its basic image is that of leaven working the dough by swelling and acidifying it. From the same root comes the word חָמֵץ (chamets) which designates the "leaven" itself, and חָמוּץ (chamouts), "acid" or "sour." The central idea is that of the chemical change produced by fermentation: the dough transforms, becomes something else, rises and sours at the same time. This is why the word can describe both physical swelling and emotional bitterness.
H2556A.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in two different contexts. First, it is very present in the ordinances of Passover (Exodus 12): it describes four times the leavened bread that is forbidden to eat or possess during the feast (Exodus 12:19, 12:20, 12:34, 12:39). These uses are concrete and cultic: they speak of the dough that had time to ferment, which must therefore be avoided. Then, the word shifts to an emotional sense in the Psalms and Hosea (Psalms 73:21; Hosea 7:4): here, it describes the heart that becomes bitter or the people that ferments with unfaithfulness. The passage in Hosea even compares the adulterers of Israel to an oven where the dough rises — the image of leaven becomes that of corruption that silently spreads.
H2556A.portee: This word teaches believers that the unleavened dough of Passover was a sign of swift judgment, sudden deliverance, and separation from evil. But it also reveals how a small thing — a pinch of leaven — can transform an entire mass, which helps to understand Paul's warning against "a little leaven" that "leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). On the heart level, the word reminds that bitterness and resentment, like fermentation, work silently and swell the soul until they poison it.

sens: To have the color red
To be stained or marked with red (notably with blood)
H2556B.detail:
1. The verb literally means to have the color red, that of blood, reddish earth, or wine. In Isaiah 63:1, the prophet describes one coming from Edom with "red" garments: the image is that of a warrior whose clothes are stained red, probably by the blood of battle.

2. By extension, the word can evoke anything that is marked or stained red, recalling violence, judgment, or sacrifice. Edom, a mountainous and rocky country, was known for its reddish lands, which reinforces the image of a warrior covered in red, a symbol of his warrior power and victory.
H2556B.origine: The root חמץ (cha.mats) is related to the idea of tint or coloring. It expresses the state of being red or reddish. The word is rooted in the Semitic context where the color red was often associated with earth, spilled blood, or divine judgment. It is a simple descriptive verb that translates a visual reality: the manifest presence of a reddish hue.
H2556B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 63:1. It describes the bright red garments of one who returns from Edom with pride, after an act of judgment or victory. The prophetic context suggests an image of divine warrior power, where the red color of the garments symbolizes both the violence of battle and the certainty of triumph. This unique occurrence makes it a rare but highly vivid word in prophetic poetry.
H2556B.portee: This word helps us grasp the vividness of prophetic imagery: the Bible does not speak abstractly of God's judgment; it paints it in intense colors. Seeing a warrior in red blood-stained garments forces the reader to imagine the reality of divine judgment, not as a distant idea but as a concrete and formidable power. It is a reminder that God's victory over evil is never merely theoretical.

sens: To mistreat someone brutally and mercilessly
To act in a cruel and oppressive manner
To exercise tyrannical domination
H2556C.detail:
1. The word describes a brutal and malevolent action: someone who harms another person without regard for their suffering. In Psalms 71:4, the psalmist asks God to deliver him from the hand of the violent wicked, one who acts without compassion.
2. It also designates systematic oppression: an act or attitude that crushes, unjustly stripping away. It is the image of a force that falls upon the weak.
3. The word carries the idea of deliberate cruelty, of intentional harshness, as if reducing something by brute force without respect.
H2556C.origine: The Hebrew root חמץ (chamats) originally evokes the idea of pressing, of squeezing tightly. It resembles the physical image of a hand that grips or crushes. The word suggests a brutal force applied without restraint or pity, hence its meaning of cruelty and oppression.
H2556C.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 71:4. It designates the conduct of the wicked who exercises cruel authority. Even though rare, this word illustrates the category of the "violent" or the "oppressor" that the Bible constantly opposes to the just and the merciful. The context of the psalm places it in a cry of prayer: the faithful calls upon God to protect him precisely from one who acts with this unrestrained violence.
H2556C.portee: This word reminds the believer that God knows and sees the cruelty of the powerful who oppress the weak. It affirms that violence and tyranny do not go unpunished. Calling upon God against the violent is to place one's trust in Him who alone can stop injustice and protect the oppressed.

sens: To move about here and there, without a fixed direction
To turn back, to go around in circles
To hesitate, to waver in one's choices
To stray, to turn away from a person or a path
H2559.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the physical movement of someone walking aimlessly, turning and returning upon themselves. In Song of Solomon 5:6, the "wandering" young woman seeks her beloved while moving about without finding her way — she is lost, desperately searching.
2. This wandering implies an oscillation, like someone turning around a point, hesitating between two directions. The word evokes the indecision of a body that does not know where to go.
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, it means to hesitate or waver in one's convictions, to turn away from someone or from God. Jeremiah 31:22 uses it for Israel: the people "wander" in their unfaithfulness, deviating from the path that God has laid out for them.
4. Finally, the word can simply mean to distance oneself or to turn away — to withdraw from the presence or kindness of someone.
H2559.origine: The Hebrew word חָמַק (chamaq) comes from a root that expresses the idea of circumventing, evading, or turning away. The movement is that of a body that turns, wavers, and dodges. The intensive form (Hithpael) reinforces the idea: to turn in all directions, hesitating while spinning. This root paints the image of a person who cannot settle, who constantly changes direction.
H2559.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Song of Solomon 5:6, it literally describes the young woman wandering in the night searching for her beloved — unrequited love makes her wander, losing herself in the quest. In Jeremiah 31:22, the prophet uses it metaphorically: Israel is a "wandering daughter," oscillating between idolatry and faithfulness, turning away from God. These two uses unite the image of aimless movement and that of infidelity or spiritual wandering.
H2559.portee: For the believing reader, this word reminds us of the danger of moral and spiritual instability — of turning away from God to chase after nothingness. It also invites trust: in the midst of wandering and unfaithfulness (like that of Israel), God promises a new restoration. Wandering is never the final divine word.

sens: To enter into a state of boiling, to foam at the surface
To ferment, speaking of a liquid that transforms
To be in inner agitation, troubled, disturbed in one's feelings
H2560A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: a liquid that boils and foams at the surface, like the sea when its waves rise and foam. The clearest example is found in Psalms 46:4, where the waves of the sea foam and rise to shake the mountains. It is the image of unleashed, visible, and turbulent force.
2. The word is also used for fermentation, the chemical process where a drink transforms into bubbles and internal movements. In Psalms 75:9, the wine ferments in the cup of God's judgment: it is no longer a simple visible boiling, but an invisible change that prepares the punishment of the wicked.
3. By extension, the verb describes the inner agitation of the soul: a heart boiling with fear, pain, or revolt. In Lamentations 1:20 and 2:11, it is the prophet's innards that boil with distress in the face of Jerusalem's calamities. The image shifts from the physical world to the world of emotions: what boils inside is not visible, but just as real and violent.
H2560A.origine: The Hebrew verb חָמַר (chamar) fundamentally expresses the idea of tumultuous movement up and down. It is related to the notion of fermentation and disturbance. The root suggests a substance that cannot remain still, that rises and falls, that transforms. Words from the same family are found to denote leaven or yeast, which causes fermentation. The word captures the very essence of physical and emotional disorder: something from below rising up with force.
H2560A.emploi: The verb חָמַר appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in an atmosphere of turbulence or suffering. Two uses describe natural or liquid phenomena: in Psalms 46:4, it is the sea foaming under catastrophes, and in Psalms 75:9, it is the fermented wine of judgment. The other two uses are found in the book of Lamentations (1:20 and 2:11), where the same verb qualifies the inner agitation of the prophet in the face of Jerusalem's destruction. In each case, the verb emphasizes a force in motion: either visible and external, or invisible and internal. The context is always one of disturbance, crisis, judgment, or mourning.
H2560A.portee: This word teaches us that the Bible does not shy away from describing human emotions in physical and violent terms. When our innards boil with distress or revolt, it is not a spiritual defect: it is a reality that God acknowledges and takes note of. The verb also helps us understand the image of God's judgment: just as fermenting wine increases its strength and changes its nature, God's judgment transforms and fulfills His anger. Finally, boiling reminds us that we are living beings: our emotions are not a corruption of the soul, but a part of the heart that God sees and listens to.

sens: To cover a surface with a sticky or waterproof substance
To seal or protect by applying a material
To impregnate or immerse in a viscous material
H2560B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to cover a surface with a sticky or waterproof substance, like tar or pitch. In Exodus 2:3, Moses' mother coated a basket made of bulrushes with tar and pitch to make it waterproof and to place her baby in it without getting him wet.
2. The word also refers to the action of sealing or protecting something by applying a material. The coating forms a barrier between the contents and the outside, making the object waterproof and durable.
3. By extension, it means to impregnate or immerse in a viscous or sticky material, which transforms the object and prepares it for a new function.
H2560B.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of covering or coating. The starting image is manual: that of someone applying a paste or liquid substance to a surface with their hands or a tool. It is a simple and concrete verb, common in the vocabulary of practical work and construction.
H2560B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 2:3. It describes the action of Moses' mother who waterproofs a basket made of bulrushes with tar and pitch to transform this fragile object into a floating cradle capable of protecting her newborn from the waters of the Nile. It is a very concrete verb, rooted in a specific and dramatic situation in the story of Moses' infancy.
H2560B.portee: This word reminds us of the ingenuity and dedication of parents in the face of adversity: a mother finding practical means to protect her child, even in seemingly desperate circumstances. It also illustrates how God uses simple and ordinary gestures to accomplish His purposes, in this case saving the future liberator of Israel.

sens: to be turned red or dark
to lose its natural color or luster
to have a spoiled or damaged appearance
to be changed in an unfavorable way
H2560C.detail:
1. The verb specifically denotes the act of becoming red or taking on a dark hue. In Job 16:16, the tears have "altered" Job's face: his constant tears have reddened and inflamed his skin, transforming his appearance.
2. More broadly, "to be altered" means to be damaged, degraded, or changed for the worse. The idea is one of a negative transformation that affects the outward appearance of a person or thing, making it unrecognizable or weakened.
H2560C.origine: The Hebrew root חמר (chamár) evokes the idea of redness or fermentation. It is related to other Hebrew words that denote what ferments, bubbles, or takes on a dark hue. The context of Job suggests that the verb describes the visible physical effect of tears and suffering on the body: the skin becomes red, inflamed, and its complexion is altered.
H2560C.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 16:16. Job describes his state of extreme distress: overwhelmed by illness and grief, his constant tears have literally transformed his face. The tears have reddened and altered his skin, while death seems to approach him. The use of the verb emphasizes not only physical suffering but also the visibility of inner desolation: the body becomes a mirror of the torment of the soul.
H2560C.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is never purely internal: it manifests in the body and is visible on the face. For the Christian reader, it invites us to take seriously the reality of human pain and to recognize that those who weep bear visible traces of their distress.

sens: fermented drink made from grapes
product of the vine, symbol of abundance and blessing
poetic expression of the blood of the grape
H2561.detail:
1. The word refers to the drink obtained by fermenting grapes, a common product in the Holy Land. In Deuteronomy 32:14, Moses sings that the people have drunk "the blood of the grape, the wine," a poetic expression that describes the red liquid of ripe grapes as a form of life.
2. Wine represents wealth and divine blessing: it is one of the fruits of the promised land, a sign that God has blessed His people. Its abundance manifests prosperity.
3. The expression "blood of the grape" shows how closely this drink was associated with the idea of life and vitality in Hebrew thought.
H2561.origine: The Hebrew word חֶמֶר (chémer) comes from a root that denotes fermentation and bubbling. It is a concrete term, derived from the observation of the natural process: crushed grapes "bubble" as they transform. Aramaic uses a very similar form, חֲמַר (chamar), indicating that this word was widespread throughout the Levant. It is not a borrowed term but belongs to the ancient core of the Semitic language.
H2561.emploi: The word appears only once in this particular usage in Deuteronomy 32:14, at the heart of a poetic blessing where Moses enumerates the goods that God has bestowed upon Israel. Wine is among the luxury products and signs of prosperity: milk, cream, the fat of the animals, wheat, and wine. It is an element of the enumeration that emphasizes how the Lord has abundantly provided for all the needs of His people.
H2561.portee: Wine in this passage reminds us that God does not merely provide the bare necessities: He offers abundance and joy. It is a call to gratitude and recognition toward the One who generously provides. For the reader, it is a reminder to see in every daily gift a mark of divine kindness.

sens: fermented drink made from grapes
valuable food provision
element of worship and sacrifices
symbol of debauchery and sin
H2562.detail:
1. Wine is the fermented drink obtained from grapes. It is a common product on the table, especially in the ancient Near East. Belshazzar drinks it during his feast with his nobles (Daniel 5:1-2): it is a moment of conviviality and abundance.

2. Wine constitutes a valuable provision, often stored and accounted for as a good. When the king's decree allows for the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem, wine is among the resources to be provided for the priests, alongside wheat and oil (Ezra 6:9 and 7:22). It is an element of an organized economy.

3. Wine has its place in offerings and religious worship. It is regularly delivered to the priests for the burnt offerings to the God of heaven (Ezra 6:9), integrated into the temple service as an offering or libation.

4. In the context of Belshazzar's impious feast, wine becomes a symbol of drunkenness, disorder, and impiety. As Belshazzar drinks wine and abuses the sacred vessels of the temple, he praises mute gods and forgets the living God who holds his life in His hands (Daniel 5:23). Drunkenness marks here moral and spiritual waywardness.
H2562.origine: This is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word חֶמֶר (chémer), which also means "wine." The word belongs to an ancient and stable vocabulary in both Semitic languages. It denotes the product of the fermentation of grape juice, well known throughout the ancient Levant. Aramaic and Hebrew share this fundamental word of daily and cultic life.
H2562.emploi: The word appears six times in the Aramaic corpus of the Bible: five occurrences in Daniel and one in Ezra. Three passages are in the administrative context of the return from exile (Ezra 6:9 and 7:22), where wine is a resource legally provided for the temple. Three others, in Daniel 5, depict the sacrilegious feast of King Belshazzar, where wine facilitates the forgetting of the true God. The word retains its concrete meaning everywhere: a drink consumed or distributed, but the context imbues this consumption with moral or cultic significance.
H2562.portee: Wine appears in Scripture as a gift from God and an element of His liturgy, but also as a potential trap for those who abuse it and turn away toward impiety. For the believer, this reminds us that material goods and pleasures are legitimate only when they remain connected to the knowledge and obedience of the living God. Belshazzar illustrates the path of one who forgets God amid abundance: his end is all the more dark (Daniel 5:30).

sens: Malleable, soft, and sticky earthy material that can be shaped
Mortar or cement used to bind construction materials
Mud, soaked and dirty earth
Metaphorically, fragility and dependence of the human creature
H2563A.detail:
1. Clay is the raw material that humans work to create objects. In Genesis 11:3, during the construction of the Tower of Babel, the people use fired bricks, which are shaped and hardened clay. It is a substance that can be kneaded and molded by hand.

2. Clay mixed with other substances serves as a binder: it is the mortar or cement that joins stones or bricks together. In Babel, bitumen plays this role for the constructions of men.

3. When clay is soaked and dirty, it becomes mud, thick and degrading. Job 30:19 describes humiliation: "God has cast me into the mud, and I look like dust and ashes." This is the image of degradation and filth.

4. The Bible often uses clay to represent fragility and dependence: humans are clay vessels, created and shaped by God. In Isaiah 45:9, the clay "speaks" to the potter, symbolizing the folly of the creature that contests its Creator. Job 4:19 teaches that man dwells in clay houses and can be crushed like a worm.
H2563A.origine: The word חֹמֶר comes from a root that evokes the idea of heat or fermentation, but in Hebrew, it simply refers to earthy material, particularly that which is baked or bound. It is related to other Hebrew words for vessels and things made of clay. It is a very ancient word, rooted in the daily life of the peoples of the Near East: clay was everywhere, in constructions, pottery, and bricks of houses.
H2563A.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books (Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah). In Genesis 11:3, it is the material of bricks. In Job, especially, clay becomes a theological image: Job reminds God that he was "shaped from clay" (Job 10:9, 33:6), affirming his fragility before the divine. In Isaiah, the potter and the clay embody the relationship between God the creator and humanity created. The image of mud (Isaiah 10:6, Job 13:12) symbolizes oppression, profanation, and humiliation.
H2563A.portee: This word reminds us of a fundamental spiritual truth: we are created, fragile, dependent on God. Clay evokes both dignity (we are shaped, therefore thought of, desired) and humility (we are matter, destructible, not autonomous). For the Christian reader, this invites trust: our Potter knows our constitution and our limits, and it is by recognizing this reality that we find our true place.

sens: Pile, accumulation of things stacked together
Mass of water raised, foam or mud of the waves
H2563B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a heap, a pile of things stacked on top of each other. In Exodus 8:10, the dead frogs are gathered in heaps, literally in piles — the image is that of a disorderly accumulation that needs to be cleaned up.
2. By extension, it describes the movement of waters: the tumultuous mass, the foam or mud that the agitated water raises. In Habakkuk 3:15, when the prophet speaks of the Lord who treads the sea with his horses, it is the mud of the great waters — the mixture of sand and water that the hooves stir up as they advance.
H2563B.origine: The Hebrew word חֹמֶר comes from a root that evokes the idea of piling up, accumulating. It describes the action of gathering, putting together. The primary image is that of a heap, a material accumulation, which naturally also applies to the muddy or tumultuous movement of waters.
H2563B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first occurrence, in Exodus 8:10, places it in the context of the plagues of Egypt: the dead frogs are piled in heaps. The second, in Habakkuk 3:15, uses it for the mud or mass of waters whipped by the hooves. In both cases, the emphasis is on accumulation, agitation, a compact or troubled mass.
H2563B.portee: This word reminds us that even the smallest things — dead frogs, troubled water — testify to the power of God. The notion of "heap" also speaks of judgment: the creatures that rebel against God accumulate, piling up under His sentence. For the believer, it is an invitation to see the hand of the Lord in all things, great or small.

sens: Unit of measurement for capacity for grains and liquids
Quantity of material (clay, mud) shaped or malleable
H2563C.detail:
1. The homer is an ancient unit of measurement used in Israel to quantify harvests: one speaks of a "homer of barley seed" (Leviticus 27:16) or a "homer of seed" that produces only an ephah (Isaiah 5:10).
