It is an important measure — the quails gathered in the desert amounted to ten "homers" (Numbers 11:32). It corresponds to about 300 liters, or the load of a camel or donkey.
2. The word also refers, by extension, to a mass of malleable and amorphous material. The earth transforms "like the clay that receives an imprint" (Job 38:14), and the powerful are trampled "like mud, like clay that a potter treads" (Isaiah 41:25). This image evokes a formless, passive material, subject to the will of the one who works it.
H2563C.origine: The Hebrew word חֹמֶר (homer) comes from a root that suggests the idea of heap, accumulation. It is related to חֹמֶר (hemer, clay, material) — indeed, "clay" and "mud" share the same root as "homer" as a measure. This reveals a concrete origin: at a time when measurements were calculated by heaps or bundles, the homer designated a load of a donkey. The image of clay or shapeless mud reinforces this link: it is raw material, a heap to be shaped.
H2563C.emploi: The homer appears nine times in the Bible, mainly for measuring grains and harvests. In Leviticus 27:16 and Isaiah 5:10, it evaluates agricultural lands and their yield. Numbers 11:32 also testifies to this: the Israelites gather the quails "ten homers" each — a huge quantity showing miraculous abundance. Ezekiel 45:11, 45:13, and 45:14 use it to fix proportions between measures (the bath and the ephah). Hosea 3:2 also uses it for grains. The word shifts from the meaning of "measure" to that of "amorphous material" (clay, mud) in Job 38:14 and Isaiah 41:25, revealing a deep semantic kinship: both refer to something raw, formless, and moldable.
H2563C.portee: The homer reminds the believer that God knows and controls abundance — He measures our harvests and our sustenance. When the Word speaks of mud and clay, it invites a healthy humility: we are of the "homer", a material that God shapes according to His will. The image of the potter who treads the clay (Isaiah 41:25) shows that divine power reduces empires to nothing; our moldability in the hands of the Creator is a fundamental truth.

sens: Black, viscous substance that flows from the earth, used for sealing and binding
Material that makes waterproof and protects against water
Sticky substance used as a binder or cement in construction
H2564.detail:
1. Bitumen is a black, thick, and sticky material that naturally emerges from the ground. In the Tower of Babel, the builders use it as cement to bind together the bricks they have fired (Genesis 11:3), somewhat like mortar in modern construction.
2. This substance has the valuable property of being waterproof and impervious. When Moses is placed in a basket of bulrushes, his mother coated it with bitumen and pitch (Exodus 2:3) so that the waters of the Nile would not enter and drown the child.
3. The Valley of Siddim was naturally covered with it, making it slippery and dangerous: the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell there while fleeing (Genesis 14:10), with the bitumen acting as a sticky trap.
H2564.origine: The Hebrew word חֵמָר (ḥēmar) literally refers to a substance that flows and thickens. Its basic image is that of a viscous and adhesive material. Bitumen was well known in Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt, where it was naturally exploited for construction and waterproofing. It is a product of nature that the ancients used without refinement.
H2564.emploi: The word appears only 3 times in the Bible, always to refer to natural bitumen. In Genesis 11:3, it is among the building materials of the Tower of Babel, showing that it was a known binder used by ancient builders of the Near East. In Exodus 2:3, Jochebed uses it to protect Moses from the waters. In Genesis 14:10, it is present in the earth itself, forming pits or deposits that become a danger for those who fall into them. These three uses reveal both its practical application and the natural risks it poses.
H2564.portee: Bitumen in the Bible symbolizes both human capacity to master materials and the limits of that power. At Babel, it represents the audacity of men who build using the resources of the earth, but it is also a sign of an enterprise doomed to failure. In Exodus, it becomes a means of maternal protection, linking Moses' story to the divine providence that saves him. These images remind us that everything we build and use ultimately depends on God's will.

sens: Accumulation of piled material
Large quantity of stacked or heaped items
Mass, heap, accumulated weight
H2565.detail: 1. A mound is a heap, an accumulation of things piled on top of each other. It is a concrete image of piling up: grain, stones, debris stacked form a mound. In Judges 15:16, Samson exults after his victory by saying that with a simple jawbone of a donkey he killed a thousand men — the biblical poet plays on the word by saying "a mound, two mounds" of enemies struck down, like bodies piled on the battlefield. 2. By extension, the word also evokes a weight or burden accumulated, something that gathers and becomes heavy. For Samson, it is the imposing mass of carnage — a thousand warriors reduced to a heap.
H2565.origine: The Hebrew word חֲמוֹר comes from the root חמר which expresses the idea of piling up, accumulating. It is a simple noun that describes the action of things that naturally or voluntarily accumulate. The underlying image is that of a movement of accumulation, of things multiplying and heaping up until they form a visible mass.
H2565.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 15:16. It is Samson who pronounces it immediately after killing a thousand Philistines with a jawbone of a donkey. The usage is poetic and emphasized — Samson repeats "mound, two mounds" to highlight the extent of the carnage, the accumulation of corpses. It is a moment of warrior pride and divine glorification, where the mound becomes an image of brilliant and supernatural victory.
H2565.portee: For the believer, this passage illustrates how God can grant extraordinary and disproportionate victory to those who trust Him. Samson, a simple judge of Israel, defeats an entire army with a rudimentary weapon — the image of the mound of enemies speaks of the irresistible power of God acting through those who rely on Him. The word also reminds us that the conflict with evil leaves traces, an accumulation of consequences that should not be forgotten.

sens: Man living in the time of the patriarchs, descendant of Esau
H2566.detail: Hamran is a man from the lineage of Esau, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Dishon and the brother of Eshban, Jithran, and Keran (1 Chronicles 1:41). His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Esau, who populated the region of Edom.
H2566.origine: The name Hamran (חַמְרָן) is a spelling variant of Hemdan (חֶמְדָּן). The exact meaning of the name is not clearly known, but it could evoke the idea of hardness or firmness. This name belongs to the family of Edomite names predating the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
H2566.emploi: Hamran appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 1:41. He is listed in the genealogical record of the peoples descending from Esau who inhabited the region of Edom before the formation of Israel. This mention fits within the context of patriarchal genealogies that establish the links between the neighboring peoples of Israel and the lineage of Abraham.

sens: collect a tax equal to one-fifth of the harvest
demand a share of one-fourth of the production
establish a taxation system based on the number five
H2567.detail:
1. The word describes the action of levying a fifth, that is, taking a share equal to one-fifth of a harvest or production. In Genesis 41:34, Pharaoh considers "taking a fifth of the harvests" during the years of abundance, meaning that for every five measures of grain harvested, the state takes one for its reserves. It is a fixed and predictable tax.
2. By extension, the term expresses the idea of establishing a tax regime based on a well-defined portion that the people can anticipate. This method of taxation is fair because it applies uniformly, without arbitrariness.
H2567.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root חמש (ḥā.mash), which fundamentally means "five." The verb derived from it expresses the action of dividing or counting by five, then taking a share from it. This root reflects the importance of the number five in Hebrew systems of counting and sharing goods.
H2567.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 41:34. It is part of the story of Joseph in Egypt, when the young man proposes to Pharaoh a strategy to face the announced famine: to build reserves during seven years of abundance. The levy of the fifth of the harvests is presented as a reasonable and justified taxation system that allows the state to store grain without ruining the producers.
H2567.portee: This narrative shows how fair and transparent taxation — neither arbitrary nor burdensome — can serve the common good and prepare the people for future trials. It reminds the reader that justice in the management of goods comes through clear and proportionate rules.

sens: the cardinal number 5
a measure or quantity of five units
a multiple of five (combined with another number)
the ordinal rank: fifth
H2568.detail:
1. The number 5: it is simply the digit we call five, used for counting. Seth lived one hundred five years (Genesis 5:6), that is, 105 years.
2. A concrete measure: the word refers to a length, width, height, or any physical quantity expressed in units of five. The lower story of Solomon's Temple was five cubits wide (1 Kings 6:6).
3. A multiple of five associated with another number: expressions like fifteen (ten plus five) or enumerations in groups of five can yield totals like five hundred fifty (Exodus 38:26).
4. The ordinal rank: the word can mean "fifth" when it designates order or position. Ezekiel had a vision on the fifth day of the fourth month (Ezekiel 1:1).
H2568.origine: The Hebrew word חָמֵשׁ (chamesh) comes from an ancient root that refers to the idea of the five fingers of the hand, hence the primary meaning of the number 5. This root also gives rise to words that designate structures with five elements or pentagrams. It is a fundamental number in the Bible for the measurements of the Tabernacle and the Temple.
H2568.emploi: The word appears more than 270 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and the books of Kings and Chronicles. It is used for ages (Seth is one hundred five years old), military or tribal counts (forty-five thousand warriors, 2 Chronicles 13:17), architectural dimensions of the Tabernacle and the Temple (five cubits in width, Exodus 26:3), and liturgical quantities (five shekels, Exodus 22:1). Rarely, it takes on the ordinal value of "fifth."
H2568.portee: This simple number reminds us that the Bible does not disregard concrete and quantified details: it speaks of the real, of measurements, of constructions, of generations that succeed one another. This shows that God cares about order, precision, and the organization of worship and the life of His people. Knowing these numbers helps the reader visualize the Tabernacle and appreciate the grandeur of Israel's counts.

sens: part of a whole divided into five equal parts
tax or levy representing this fraction
sovereign's right over a portion of the revenues
H2569.detail:
1. The fifth is a part obtained by dividing something into five equal parts. It is a simple mathematical fraction: if you divide an asset into five parts, the fifth is one of them.
2. In the biblical context, this term refers to a tax or levy imposed on lands and their harvests. During the famine in Egypt, Joseph established a law: one fifth of every harvest goes to Pharaoh, the other four fifths remaining with the people and the farmers (Genesis 47:26).
3. The fifth also represents the sovereign's royal right: it is the share that the king can demand from his subjects or their goods, a legitimate tax that finances the state and the protection it offers.
H2569.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "five." In Hebrew, fractions are formed from numbers: just as "sixth" comes from "six," "fifth" naturally comes from "five." It is a simple and transparent system for naming parts of a whole.
H2569.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 47:26, at the heart of the story of Joseph in Egypt. Joseph, having become Pharaoh's vizier during the great famine, organizes the grain storage system and establishes a tax law: one fifth of each harvest must be paid to Pharaoh. This law becomes permanent in Egypt, applied to all lands except those of the priests, who enjoy an exemption. The fifth is not an arbitrary confiscation, but a regular and fair tax, established by Joseph's wisdom to ensure the stability of the kingdom.
H2569.portee: This passage shows how a fair and pre-announced tax allows a state to function without oppression. Joseph's fifth does not impoverish the people: it saves their lives during the famine. It is a lesson on the balance between the public authority's right to take a share of wealth and the citizens' right to keep the fruits of their labor. For the Christian, it is also a reminder that fair taxes are legitimate and that wise management of common resources benefits everyone.

sens: The part of the body between the chest and the hips, containing the digestive organs and other viscera
The seat of emotions, deep feelings, or inner life
The region of the belly, particularly the weak or vital point of a person
H2570.detail:
1. The belly refers to the abdomen, that region of the body between the chest and the hips where the stomach, intestines, and other organs are located. In passages from 2 Samuel, this word designates the exact place to strike someone to wound them mortally: Joab strikes Asahel in the belly with his spear (2 Samuel 2:23), then Abner in the belly to kill him (2 Samuel 3:27), and likewise for Amasa (2 Samuel 20:10).
2. The belly can also symbolize the seat of intimate emotions and inner life — what stirs us deeply. It is from there that strong feelings and hidden motivations spring forth.
3. By extension, the belly represents a person's vulnerable part, the place where striking them touches their heart, destroying their life. This is why ancient warriors aimed for the belly to kill the enemy: it is the vital seat.
H2570.origine: The Hebrew word חֹמֶשׁ (chomesh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of what is "hollow" or "emptied," like a cavity. This word can also designate the fifth, and indeed the belly with its five important organs (the liver, stomach, intestines, kidneys, spleen) is among the vital parts of the body. The same root is found in other Hebrew words describing body parts or cavities.
H2570.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible, only in the war narratives of 2 Samuel. Each time, it describes the precise location of a mortal wound: Asahel struck in the belly by Abner (2 Samuel 2:23), Abner himself struck in the belly by Joab (2 Samuel 3:27), the king killed in the belly by his murderers (2 Samuel 4:6), and Amasa struck in the belly by Joab (2 Samuel 20:10). In all these cases, striking in the belly results in immediate death. The word is thus used in a very concrete and military manner, to designate the vital attack point in a fight or murder.
H2570.portee: This word reminds us that the belly is both the seat of our physical life and the home of our deepest emotions. For a biblical reader, it evokes the fragility of human life and the importance of protecting what is most dear to us. These murder accounts also show how vengeance destroys the strongest men and how sin takes root in the heart before producing destructive acts.

sens: Equipped with weapons for battle
Arranged in battle order
Prepared for attack or defense
H2571.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to combatants equipped with their weapons, ready for battle. When Israel leaves Egypt, the men go "armed" (Exodus 13:18), meaning they have their swords, spears, and shields with them.
2. It also evokes a precise military order: the troops do not advance randomly, but "armed," meaning arranged by combat units. At the crossing of the Jordan, the warriors from the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh pass "armed" (Joshua 4:12): they form an organized and protected column.
3. The word can refer to an advance guard or a lookout post, as in "at the outposts of the camp" (Judges 7:11), where armed sentinels are stationed to watch over the enemy camp.
H2571.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "five" or "to count by five." The initial image is that of a military formation in groups of five men — a classic tactical organization in ancient armies. This basic structure reflects how the Israelites organized their troops into columns and compact units for marching and combat.
H2571.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in military and conquest contexts. It is used to describe Israel leaving Egypt in good order (Exodus 13:18), the warriors crossing the Jordan to take the land (Joshua 1:14 and 4:12), and the sentinels posted to watch over an enemy camp (Judges 7:11). In all these cases, the word emphasizes the organization, preparation, and solidarity of the combatants: it is not a disordered crowd, but a structured and disciplined force.
H2571.portee: This word reminds us that God does not ask His people to fight in disorder or without preparation. Order, discipline, and equipment are signs of the seriousness with which Israel faces the challenges ahead. For the Christian reader, this evokes the importance of spiritual and moral preparation: being "armed" with the Word of God and faith.

sens: The cardinal number 50
A measure of length, width, or height in cubits
A number of years or age
A number of people
An ordinal or fraction ("fiftieth")
A multiple in a series of numbers
H2572.detail: 1. The number fifty is used simply as a cardinal number for counting or enumerating, for example, to count the men of Levi from thirty to fifty years old (Numbers 4:30). 2. In architectural descriptions, fifty cubits refers to a measure of length — for example, the width of Noah's ark which was to be "fifty cubits wide" (Genesis 6:15), or the dimensions of the courtyard of the tabernacle (Exodus 38:13). 3. The number also marks stages of life: the age "fifty years" is often the age limit for certain services or responsibilities, such as the service of the Levites which ceased at fifty years (Numbers 4:30 and 8:25). 4. Fifty can count people — thus Abraham asks God if fifty righteous will save Sodom (Genesis 18:24, 26, 28), or David acquires fifty horsemen (1 Kings 1:5). 5. The number also appears in ordinal form or as a fraction ("fiftieth"), notably for the year of Jubilee which comes after forty-nine years (Leviticus 25:10, 11). 6. In the censuses (Numbers 1 to 4), fifty often appears in multiples or as part of a larger count, serving to evaluate the strength or numbers of the people.
H2572.origine: The Hebrew word חֲמִשִּׁים (chamishshim) comes from the root חמש (chamesh), which means "five." Fifty is thus literally "five times ten" — it arises from the combination of two fundamental counting units. The word follows a regular formation of tens in Hebrew (like "ten" = עֲשֶׂרֶת, "twenty" = עֶשְׂרִים). It is a simple and common number in the Hebrew text.
H2572.emploi: The word appears 141 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Torah. It is frequent in Exodus and Numbers, where it measures the dimensions of the tabernacle and its courts. It counts the military and priestly censuses of the people of Israel — the numbers of the tribes, the age of the Levites. It also counts years (Abraham with the number of righteous, or advanced ages) and people: David with his horsemen, the Levites protecting the prophets. In the narratives of Genesis, the number appears for the patriarchs (Noah, Abraham) and in dialogues about the judgment of Sodom. The meaning is always that of the cardinal or ordinal number without ambiguity.
H2572.portee: The number fifty reminds us of the importance of order and counting in the life of God's people — each tribe, each service, each person has their exact place. It is also a key number of the Jubilee, the seventh year of the seventh year, which recalls the rest and liberation that God granted. For the Christian, this evokes how God knows each one by name and number — nothing escapes His precision and order.

sens: A container made from animal skin used to carry liquids, especially water
The contents of this container; the quantity of liquid it holds
H2573.detail:
1. A skin flask is a container made from animal skin, sewn and watertight, that is carried on the shoulder or by hand to transport water or other liquids. It is a common object in the arid regions of the ancient Near East. Abraham gives one to Hagar when he sends her into the desert, along with bread and her child (Genesis 21:14): it is the water supply for survival on the journey.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the water or liquid contained in the flask. When the water in the flask is exhausted, Hagar and Ishmael are in danger of dying of thirst (Genesis 21:15) — the critical moment when God intervenes. Hagar then fills the flask at the well and gives the child something to drink (Genesis 21:19).
H2573.origine: The Hebrew word חֵמֶת (chemet) designates this traditional flask or wineskin. The root evokes the idea of something closed and filled. It is a characteristic utilitarian object of nomadic life and travel in the desert, very present in the patriarchal narratives.
H2573.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the same narrative: that of Genesis 21, where Abraham sends Hagar and Ishmael into the desert with a skin flask of water. The three occurrences follow the logic of the narrative: first, the flask is given as provision (v. 14), then it empties and creates a situation of distress (v. 15), finally it is filled again at the miraculous well, a symbol of divine intervention (v. 19). The word embodies here the fragility of human life in the face of the desert and the necessity of water for survival.
H2573.portee: This concrete detail immerses us in the harshness of desert life and the urgency of survival. The empty flask reveals how Hagar and Ishmael are reduced to helplessness — a moment of crisis where God calls to Abraham (v. 17) and shows His compassion. For the reader, it is a reminder that the most basic provision (water) can run out, and that it is in this critical moment that divine grace is manifested.

sens: main city of Upper Syria, in the Orontes valley
region or territory around this city
northern boundary of the territory of Israel or its conquests
H2574G.detail: 1. Hamath is a large city in Syria, located in the Orontes valley (a major river in the Levant). It is an important urban center, home to powerful kings like Toi (1 Chronicles 18:9), and it maintains a formidable fortress. 2. The name also refers to the region surrounding the city, its lands and peoples, as when Jeremiah speaks of the king of Babylon striking the leaders of Judah "at Riblah, in the land of Hamath" (Jeremiah 52:27). 3. Hamath often marks a boundary: it defines the northern limit of Israel's conquests or the promised territory, during the time of David and Solomon (1 Kings 8:65), and it becomes a landmark for delineating the restored borders in Ezekiel's visions (Ezekiel 47:16-17).
H2574G.origine: The Hebrew name חֲמָת (hamat) literally means "fortress" or "citadel," reflecting its strategic role as a stronghold and defended urban center. It is a historically attested city, well-known in Egypt and Mesopotamia as a regional power hub. Its geographical importance makes it a constant reference point in the Bible for delineating the territory of promises and Israelite conquests.
H2574G.emploi: Hamath appears 32 times in the Bible. It is first mentioned during the exploration of Canaan (Numbers 13:21), then becomes a marker of the northern borders: David conquers the region and establishes relations with Toi, king of Hamath (1 Chronicles 18:9); Solomon extends control over it (1 Kings 8:65). The prophets cite it to show the extent of divine judgment on Syrian powers (Isaiah 36:19). It appears in Ezekiel's visions regarding the restored borders of the land. Several times, Hamath is mentioned alongside cities like Arpad or Sepharvaim, all three being centers of Syrian power.
H2574G.portee: Hamath reminds the reader that God has boundaries for His people. It symbolizes ancient Levant, far from Jerusalem but present in divine plans. The fact that kings reign there and their gods are worshiped shows that, beyond Israel, there are other powers; but the Bible asserts that the God of Israel alone is true and acts over all nations.

sens: fortified city in Northern Syria
H2574H.detail: Hamath is a fortified city located in Upper Syria, in the Orontes valley. It controlled a strategic region on the route between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean coast. In 1 Chronicles 18:3, it is mentioned as a territory that King David sought to dominate by defeating Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and extending his control to the Euphrates.
H2574H.origine: The name Hamath literally means "fortress." The city was one of the main cities of Northern Syria and served as a military and commercial stronghold for the kingdoms of this region. Its geopolitical importance explains why it appears in the accounts of the kings of Israel and Judah who sought to assert their power in the Levant.
H2574H.emploi: Hamath appears in 1 Chronicles 18:3 in the context of King David's military victory. It symbolizes the territorial limits that David intended to reach: by subduing the region between Zobah and Hamath up to the Euphrates, he marked the peak of his geopolitical dominance. This mention situates Hamath as a strategic geographical marker in the consolidation of the Davidic empire.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Naphtali
Location known for its hot springs
H2575A.detail:
1. Hammath is a fortified city located in the territory that the tribe of Naphtali received as an inheritance during the division of the promised land (Joshua 19:35). It appears in the list of the main cities of this tribe, alongside Ziddim, Zer, Rakkath, and Kinnereth.
2. Its name means "hot spring" in Hebrew, indicating that the city was likely established near thermal springs, a remarkable natural resource. These hot waters could have been used or revered by the inhabitants.
H2575A.origine: The word חַמַּת (chammat) derives from the root חַם (cham), which means "hot" or "heat." This geographical name directly describes a physical characteristic of the place: the presence of hot springs. It is a common example in the ancient East, where city names often reflect a remarkable geographical or natural feature.
H2575A.emploi: Hammath appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:35, during the enumeration of fortified cities assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of Canaan after the conquest. It is mentioned among the five main strong cities of this tribe. Its unique appearance and inclusion in the official list of tribal possessions show its strategic or administrative importance in the northern territory of Canaan.

sens: Ancestor of the Rechabites clan
H2575B.detail: Hamath is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:55. He is presented as the father of the house of Rechab, that is, as the ancestor of the Rechabites clan, a group of Kenites (members of a Middle Eastern tribe) who integrated into Israel. His name literally means "hot spring," but it is his spiritual lineage that matters in the biblical text: he founded a family known for its adherence to strict religious principles, notably the refusal to drink wine and cultivate the land.
H2575B.origine: The name Hamath means "hot spring" in Hebrew (from the Hebrew חַם, "hot"). This name evokes the geography of the Middle East, where hot springs spring from the ground. Hamath himself is a distant ancestor whose name has persisted in the identity of the Rechabites clan, who marked Israel's history with their zeal for divine laws.
H2575B.emploi: Hamath appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 2:55. He is mentioned as the father of Rechab and as the ancestor of the house of Rechab (the Rechabites). This genealogical text situates him in the time of the divided monarchy and designates him as one of the founding figures of a clan that would become famous for its strict observance of particular religious and moral practices. His importance lies mainly in the descendants he fathered rather than in his own actions described.

sens: Levitical city of the tribe of Naphtali
Place known for its hot springs
H2576.detail:
1. Hammoth-Dor is a city given to the Levites in the tribe of Naphtali, in the Promised Land. It appears in the list of cities of refuge and Levitical cities (Joshua 21:32), alongside Kedesh in Galilee and Kartan, which constitute the same territorial allocation.
2. The name literally means "hot springs of Dor": "Hammath" refers to the thermal and mineral springs, while Dor refers to the coastal region known for these geological phenomena. It is a city with particular characteristics, linked to the distinctive geography of Naphtali.
H2576.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew elements: חַמַּת (Hammath, "hot spring") and דֹּאר (Dor, a region). Hammath comes from the Hebrew root meaning "heat" or "hot spring," evoking the hot waters that naturally spring from the ground. Dor is the name of an important coastal region of Canaan. Hammoth-Dor is another name for Hammath, designating the same place under its complete compound form.
H2576.emploi: Hammoth-Dor appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 21:32. It is listed among the forty-eight cities given to the Levites, taken from the territories of the twelve tribes of Israel. This verse classifies it among the three cities allocated to Naphtali, with its respective suburbs, forming a coherent group of territorial allocation for Levitical service. This unique mention makes it a well-identified city, linked to the administrative and religious organization of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
H2576.portee: The mention of Hammoth-Dor reminds the reader how God provided for the needs of the Levites by assigning them cities scattered throughout all the tribal territories. This distribution ensured that the ministers of worship could serve the Lord while living among the people, ensuring the teaching of the Law and access to priestly service throughout Israel. It is a sign of divine order and foresight in the organization of the chosen people.

sens: Members of the people originating from Hamath, an ancient city of the Levant
Descendants of Canaan, one of the Canaanite peoples listed in the post-flood genealogy
H2577.detail: 1. The Hamathites are a people whose origin traces back to Hamath, a region or city of ancient Levant. They are among the Canaanite peoples that Genesis 10:18 lists as descendants of Canaan, alongside the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and other groups. 2. This term designates a specific Canaanite population, integrated into the genealogical list of pre-flood peoples and their descendants. This enumeration in 1 Chronicles 1:16 repeats the same catalog, highlighting the administrative or geographical significance of this people in the historical geography of the Levant.
H2577.origine: The name comes from Hamath (חָמָת), an important city-state in northern Levant, also mentioned in other biblical contexts. The Hebrew suffix -ī indicates belonging or derivation, transforming the name of a city or region into an ethnic designation: "those who are from Hamath." This type of nominal formation is common in Hebrew to designate peoples according to their place of origin.
H2577.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, only in two parallel genealogical passages: Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16. These two verses list the Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan according to the Table of Nations. The Hamathites are mentioned there as a distinct and recognized people, appearing in an administrative list of Levant peoples. This presence in two genealogical texts underscores that this people was well-known and established enough to deserve a place in the register of Canaan's descendants.

sens: region and city in northern Syria, vassal or rival of the kingdom of Israel
H2578.detail: Zobah (or Hamath-Zobah) is a region and fortified city located in northern Syria, east of the territory of the Phoenicians. The name "Zobah" appears alone or combined with "Hamath" to designate this strategic territory. It was towards this region that King Solomon marched to occupy and assert his authority: "Solomon marched against Hamath, toward Zobah, and took it" (2 Chronicles 8:3). This military expansion shows the importance of Zobah as a coveted possession of the great kings of Israel.
H2578.origine: The name Zobah comes from an ancient Semitic root likely designating a fortress or fortified refuge. The full title "Hamath-Zobah" combines two names: Hamath (the large Syrian region) and Zobah (the stronghold). This compound name emphasizes the defensive and strategic character of the place. Zobah is known in the history of the ancient Near East as an important regional power center.
H2578.emploi: Zobah appears in the Old Testament as a major Syrian region that the kings of Israel sought to dominate or control. According to the passage in 2 Chronicles 8:3, King Solomon led a military expedition against Hamath-Zobah and succeeded in conquering it, thereby expanding the borders of his empire. This mention reflects the geopolitical importance of Zobah in the 10th century BC, when the great Levantine kingdoms vied for control of trade routes and northern strongholds.

sens: important city in northern Syria, mentioned in the prophetic judgment of Amos
H2579.detail: Hamath-Rabba is a city in northern Syria, cited in Amos 6:2 in a list of great cities that the prophet raises as a warning to Israel: even these powerful cities will not escape divine judgment. The name literally means "Hamath the great" or "Hamath the populous," emphasizing the importance and power of this city. It is likely another name for Hamath itself, the capital of the Aramean kingdom of the same name, one of the most significant strongholds of ancient Levant.
H2579.origine: The compound name "Hamath-Rabba" combines Hamath (a city-state and region in northern Syria, whose name means "enclosure" or "wall") with the adjective rabba ("great," "numerous"). Amos uses this qualifier to emphasize the greatness and influence of this city, as if to say that even the giants of the world are nothing in the face of God's judgment.
H2579.emploi: The name appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 6:2. Amos invokes it alongside other great cities (Gath, Calneh) to show Israel that the power and renown of a city do not save it from judgment. It is a prophetic argument: if God can judge the giants, why would Israel believe it would be spared?
H2579.portee: This passage invites the believer not to place their trust in human power, greatness, or wealth, which do not protect against divine justice. It is a call to fear God rather than the empires of the world.

sens: Kindness, favor granted by one who has power
Charm, attractiveness, elegance in appearance or behavior
Welcoming acceptance, favorable reception
Free gift, assistance provided without obligation
Beauty, ornament that beautifies
H2580.detail:
1. Grace is primarily the kindness of a powerful person towards another, often less favored. When Noah "found grace in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 6:8), it means that God looked upon Noah with particular favor at the time of the flood — an unmerited kindness that saved his life. Similarly, Esther asks the king: "If I have found grace in your eyes, grant me my life" (Esther 7:3), seeking his support in a moment of danger.
2. Grace also refers to the attractiveness or charm of a person. Esther "found grace in the eyes of all who saw her" (Esther 2:15) because she was beautiful and had won their favor. Proverbs speaks of grace as a crown on the head of the wise (Proverbs 4:9) — a moral beauty that adorns them.
3. It is also the benevolent acceptance of a request or presence. When Moses says to God, "grant me your grace" (Exodus 33:13), he is asking God to accept his prayer and favor him with His presence.
4. In some contexts, grace is help or a gift offered freely, without the recipient having earned it: it is the tenderness of one who gives without expecting a return.
5. Finally, the word can refer to the ornament or beauty that beautifies something — for example, grace can be an ornament of wisdom.
H2580.origine: The Hebrew word chen comes from a root that evokes the idea of "bending towards," "inclining before." Grace arises when one who has power "bends" benevolently towards one who is humble. This word is very ancient in Hebrew and appears from the creation narrative. In the Greek Bible, chen is often translated by the Greek word charis, which has the same meaning and will become fundamental in Pauline theology of the New Testament to express God's free gift in Christ.
H2580.emploi: This word appears 67 times in the Old Testament, especially in Genesis, Exodus, the historical books, and Proverbs. In the account of Noah (Genesis 6:8), it expresses divine favor that saves from judgment. In the stories of Joseph, Ruth, and David, it designates the favor that these figures receive from their superiors or from God — a favor that is not due to them but changes their destiny. In Proverbs, grace takes on a moral dimension: it becomes the attractiveness or wisdom of one who fears God. In Esther, it is primarily the personal charm and favor of the king. Grace also appears in the context of prayer (Moses, Exodus 33): seeking God's grace is to implore His benevolent presence. The word thus nuances between two poles: the benevolent action of one who has power, and the attractive quality of one who receives it.
H2580.portee: This word opens a fundamental perspective for the Christian faith: grace reveals that God does not treat us according to our merits, but according to His sovereign kindness. Noah "found grace" not because he was perfect, but because God had inclined towards him. For the believer, this means that their relationship with God does not rest on their works or abilities, but on a favor that they can only receive with humility and gratitude. Grace is also an invitation to contemplate the moral beauty that arises when walking with God: it beautifies the one who receives it.

sens: Contemporary man of Zerubbabel, son of Shephatiah, mentioned during the restoration of the temple after the exile
H2581.detail: Hen is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 6:14, at the time of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem. He is presented as the son of Shephatiah. His name, which means "favor" in Hebrew, was given to a man who participated in this crucial period of restoration for the people of God after the deportation to Babylon.
H2581.origine: The name Hen (חֵן) literally means "favor" or "grace" in Hebrew. It is the same word found elsewhere in the Bible to denote divine or human favor. This name reflects one of the realities of the return from exile: the people enjoyed the favor of the Lord and that of the Persian authorities who allowed the reconstruction of the temple.
H2581.emploi: Hen appears only once in the Scriptures, in Zechariah 6:14. He is mentioned alongside other figures from the return from exile (Helam, Tobijah, and Jedaiah) as a recipient of crowns offered at the temple of the Lord. His name is preserved as a "memorial in the temple," suggesting his role in the significant events of the temple's reconstruction and the renewal of worship after the Babylonian exile.

sens: Leader of a Levitical family during the exile and return
Levitical family involved in the reconstruction of the temple
H2582G.detail: Hénadad is a Levite who leads a family bearing his name. During the time of the Babylonian exile and the return to Judea, his family plays an important role in the religious life of Israel. His descendants, his sons and brothers actively participate in the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the return from captivity (Ezra 3:9), working alongside other Levites like Joshua and Kadmiel to oversee the workers. His name reappears in the book of Nehemiah, where Binnui, one of his descendants, is among the Levites who commit to uphold the covenant (Nehemiah 10:9), showing that this Levitical family remained influential in the reconstituted community.
H2582G.origine: The name Hénadad means "favor of Hadad" (Hadad being a deity of rain and storm in the ancient Near East). The name bears the mark of the Canaanite religious context, although Hénadad serves the God of Israel. His role as a leader of a Levitical family places him among those responsible for worship and service in the temple.
H2582G.emploi: Hénadad appears twice in the Bible, both times in the historical books recounting the return from exile. In Ezra 3:9, he is presented as the head of a Levitical family mobilized to oversee the reconstruction of the temple, alongside Joshua and Kadmiel. In Nehemiah 10:9, one of his descendants, Binnui, son of Hénadad, is among the Levites who sign the people's commitment to obey God's law. This repeated presence shows that it is a prestigious Levitical family, playing a leading role in Israel's religious restoration.

sens: Leader of a Levitical family during the Exile and the Return
H2582H.detail: Hénadad is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:18. He is the father of Bavvai and is among the leaders of Levitical families who participate in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. His son Bavvai leads half of the district of Keilah and works on these fortifications alongside other workers. Hénadad thus represents a Levitical family engaged in the restoration of the people and the holy city.
H2582H.origine: The name "Hénadad" means "favor of Hadad" (from Hebrew "hen" = grace, favor, and "Hadad" = ancient deity). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of a deity, common in Hebrew onomastics, even though this ancient Hadad does not pertain to the faith in the God of Israel. The name reflects the onomastic traditions of the Jewish people.
H2582H.emploi: Hénadad appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 3:18, during the reconstruction of the walls under Nehemiah after the return from the Babylonian exile. He is presented there as the father of Bavvai, who leads his Levitical brothers to work on a section of the wall. This unique mention places Hénadad among the figures of restoration of the temple and the Jewish community returned to the land of Israel.

sens: father of Binnui, leader of a Levitical family during the reconstruction of the temple
H2582I.detail: Hénadad is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah reports on the reconstruction work of the walls of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. His son Binnui is specifically cited as having participated in these repairs, working on a section of the wall between the house of Azariah and the corner (Nehemiah 3:24). Hénadad thus appears as the leader of a Levitical family engaged in this important community project of restoring the holy city.
H2582I.origine: The name Hénadad means "favor of Hadad" (or "grace of Hadad"), where Hadad is an ancient storm deity of the Levant. This name reflects the onomastic traditions of the Hebrews, who sometimes incorporated the names of pagan or foreign deities into proper names, without necessarily implying adherence to the associated cults. This is a common phenomenon in the ancient Near East.
H2582I.emploi: Hénadad is cited only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 3:24, where his son Binnui is presented as the repairer of a portion of the wall of Jerusalem. This brief mention shows that Hénadad was the father of a Levitical family whose members actively contributed to the reconstruction of the temple and fortifications after the return from the Babylonian exile. His absence from the rest of the biblical texts suggests that he likely lived during this pivotal period in Israel's history.

sens: To stop and establish a camp, to set up a campsite
To occupy a position militarily, to besiege
To stand nearby, to station oneself
H2583.detail:
1. To camp primarily means to set up a temporary campsite: to pitch tents, to settle for a time in a given place. This is what the Israelites do during their journey through the desert, who "camped near the Red Sea" (Numbers 33:10), or Isaac who "camped in the valley of Gerar" (Genesis 26:17). The verb evokes the idea of an organized halt, with a structure (the camp of the tabernacle, the tribes arranged each in their place).
2. To camp can also mean to station in a military position, particularly to besiege a city or place. The kings "came to camp together near the waters of Merom, to fight against Israel" (Joshua 11:5): they settle there to wage war.
3. More broadly, the word denotes the act of standing, remaining in one place: the Levites "camped" around the tabernacle to guard it (Numbers 3:35), assuming a position of protection and service.
H2583.origine: The verb חָנָה comes from a root that suggests the idea of inclining, bending, hence the image of pitching tents and settling by leaning towards the ground. It is a concrete and common word from the pastoral and military life of the ancient world. It stands in contrast to walking: one camps when one stops.
H2583.emploi: The verb appears about 135 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical and travel books: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Joshua, Samuel. It is very frequent in Numbers 33, where the entire itinerary of Israel in the desert is enumerated: at each stage, the people "camped." It is also found in contexts of war (the kings "camp" before battle), and in the daily life of the patriarchs. The meaning always remains attached to the idea of temporarily settling in a place, never of a fixed residence.
H2583.portee: The verb "to camp" reminds the reader that the story of Israel is one of a journey: the people are not rooted, they are moving towards a promise. Each campsite is a step, a halt of trust in God who guides and leads. This also speaks to Christians about the condition of the believer: we are on our way to the heavenly city, we are only "camping" in this world (cf. Hebrews 11:9).

sens: Woman from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
Wife of Elkanah and mother of the prophet Samuel
Barren woman who pleaded with the Lord and received a son
Model of sincere prayer and trust in God
H2584.detail:
1. Hannah is a woman living during the time of the judges and the beginning of the Israelite monarchy, first mentioned in 1 Samuel 1:2. She belongs to the family of Elkanah, a man from the tribe of Ephraim.
2. She is one of Elkanah's two wives; the other, Peninnah, had children while Hannah remained barren. Despite this suffering, Elkanah particularly loved Hannah (1 Samuel 1:5).
3. Hannah deeply suffered from her infertility. She pleaded with the Lord in tears at Shiloh, praying silently with such intensity that the priest Eli initially thought she was drunk (1 Samuel 1:13). She promised God that if she had a son, she would dedicate him to His service.
4. The Lord answered her prayer and gave her Samuel, who became one of the greatest prophets of Israel. Hannah thus became an example of faith, perseverance in suffering, and the offering of what is most precious in service to God.
H2584.origine: The name Hannah means "grace" in Hebrew. It expresses God's kindness and favor toward this woman who endured the trial of barrenness. This name reveals the central theme of her story: divine grace toward one who could not bear children, transforming her shame into joy and her painful silence into praise.
H2584.emploi: Hannah appears in the account of the early chapters of 1 Samuel, where she is at the heart of a story of divine fulfillment. She is mentioned eleven times in the provided references, primarily in 1 Samuel 1 and 2. Her role shifts from the suffering and pleading woman (1 Samuel 1:2-15) to one who receives the promise (1 Samuel 1:19-20) and finally to one who praises God with a song of thanksgiving (1 Samuel 2:1). Her story illustrates how God can transform suffering into victory and barrenness into spiritual fruitfulness, making her the mother of the prophet Samuel who profoundly impacted Israel.
H2584.portee: Hannah's story teaches believers that God hears sincere and humble prayer, even when it seems impossible. It shows how suffering can become a path to deep faith and intimate communion with God. Hannah inspires all those who go through doubt or affliction: she reminds us that God does not abandon those who trust in Him with perseverance, and that His grace can accomplish what seems impossible.

sens: Eldest son of Cain
City built by Cain and named after his son
H2585G.detail:
1. Enoch is the eldest son of Cain, born to Cain's wife. He is first mentioned in Genesis 4:17 as the first child whose birth is recorded after the murder of Abel. He later becomes the father of Irad, thus beginning a lineage that continues with Mehujael, Methushael, and Lamech (Genesis 4:18).
2. Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch (Genesis 4:17). This is the first example of urban construction mentioned in the Bible, and it honors the name of Cain's son.
H2585G.origine: The name Enoch comes from the Hebrew חֲנוֹךְ and means "dedicated" or "consecrated." It evokes the idea of something or someone set apart or dedicated to a particular purpose. It is a name rooted in an ancient time, before the Flood, and carries a meaning of separation or distinction.
H2585G.emploi: Enoch appears in the genealogy of Cain, mentioned twice in the provided references: first as Cain's son and then as the father of Irad. He is a figure from the antediluvian era, part of Cain's line. The Bible tells us that Cain named a city after this son, which shows the importance he held in family memory and in the early history of humanity.

sens: Son of Jared, father of Methuselah, antediluvian man who walked with God and was taken up to heaven without experiencing death
H2585H.detail: Enoch is an antediluvian patriarch (before the Flood) whose life is uniquely recounted in Genesis. Born to Jared at the age of one hundred sixty-two (Genesis 5:18), he was born about a thousand years after Adam. At sixty-five, he became the father of Methuselah, the oldest man in the Bible. But what distinguishes him is his exceptional relationship with God: "Enoch walked with God" (Genesis 5:22, 5:24) — an expression that denotes deep intimacy and constant obedience. After living three hundred sixty-five years, Scripture tells us that "God took him" (Genesis 5:24), meaning he did not experience ordinary death but was taken alive to God. He is thus the only man (along with Elijah) to have escaped physical death in biblical history.
H2585H.origine: The name Enoch means "dedicated one" or "initiated." It evokes the idea of consecration, of being set apart. In the antediluvian context, this name aligns with the spiritual portrait of the character: a man wholly devoted to God, walking in His presence rather than succumbing to the corruptions that would invade the world before the Flood. The same name also appears for other minor figures: a son of Cain who received a city named Enoch (Genesis 4:17), a grandson of Midian, and an eldest son of Reuben.
H2585H.emploi: Enoch appears seven times in the Bible, all in Genesis 5 (verses 18 to 24) and once in 1 Chronicles 1:3 (in the genealogy). Genesis presents him as an essential link in the genealogical chain before the Flood: from Jared to Methuselah, who himself will survive the Flood. Verses 22 and 24 emphasize his walk with God, a unique expression that brings him close to Noah (Genesis 6:9), the only two antediluvian men thus characterized. His being taken without death also prefigures the eschatological hopes of the Old Testament: the idea that an authentic relationship with God can lead beyond natural death.
H2585H.portee: Enoch embodies a model of persevering faith: he "walked with God" not for a few years, but for three hundred sixty-five years, the total duration of his life, demonstrating remarkable constancy. His being taken without experiencing death reveals that God rewards those who sincerely seek Him and faithfully follow Him. This is why, in the New Testament, Hebrews 11:5 cites him among the heroes of faith, and Jude mentions him as a prophet. For today's believer, Enoch reminds us that living faith, intimacy with God, and daily walking with Him are the true riches, beyond material wealth and the temptations of the world.

sens: Son of Midian, brother of Ephah, Epher, Abida, and Eldaa
H2585I.detail: Enoch is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned twice in the Bible. He is presented as one of the sons of Midian, the grandson of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:4). His name also appears in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chronicles (1 Chronicles 1:33), within the same list of descendants of Keturah.
H2585I.origine: The Hebrew name חֲנוֹךְ (Hanokh) literally means "dedicated" or "consecrated," derived from a root evoking the idea of setting up or dedicating. Although several biblical characters bear this name (notably Enoch, the son of Jared during the patriarchs, who was "taken by God" without experiencing death), this Enoch is simply a son of Midian, with no particular narrative attached to his life.
H2585I.emploi: This name appears only twice in Scripture: in Genesis 25:4 and in 1 Chronicles 1:33, both as a son of Midian and brother of the other children of Keturah. These two passages are parallel genealogical lists, enumerating the descendants of Abraham after the death of Sarah. Enoch is the third son named among the five children of Midian, but no additional details are given about him. He remains a purely genealogical figure, with no role or event narrated in biblical history.

sens: Firstborn son of Reuben, ancestor of a family of Israel
H2585J.detail: Enoch is the firstborn son of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob (Israel). He appears in the genealogical lists of Israel at the time of the descent into Egypt and during the stay in the desert. His descendants form the family of the Enochites, mentioned in the census of the people (Numbers 26:5).
H2585J.origine: The name Enoch means "dedicated" or "consecrated." It is a classic Hebrew name in the Bible that refers to this son of Reuben, distinct from the much more famous Enoch — the son of Jared who was taken up to heaven without experiencing death (Genesis 5:24). The descendants of Enoch are referred to by the term "Enochites" (חֲנֹכִי), formed from the paternal name according to Israelite custom.
H2585J.emploi: Enoch is named four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the official genealogical lists of Israel. He is listed among the sons of Reuben during the migration to Egypt (Genesis 46:9), in the account of the family leaders at the time of the Exodus (Exodus 6:14), in the census of the tribes in the desert (Numbers 26:5), and in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles (1 Chronicles 5:3). His importance lies mainly in his descendants: his lineage, the Enochites, is counted among the families of Israel and benefits from the promise and covenant with the people of God.
H2585J.portee: Enoch reminds us that the God of Israel sees and counts every family, every person in His people. Although he is not a prominent figure in biblical history, his genealogy is preserved and honored, showing that God does not overlook any of His own and that each has a place in His plan.

sens: King of Ammon, son of Nahash
Man who participated in the repair of the wall of Jerusalem
H2586G.detail: 1. Hanun is the son and successor of King Nahash of the Ammonites, a neighboring people of Israel. Upon his father's death, David sends ambassadors to express his sympathy, a mark of respect between kings (2 Samuel 10:1-2). However, Hanun's advisors persuade him that David harbors malicious intentions: they suggest that this delegation seeks to spy on the city for conquest. 2. Hanun then makes a decision that provokes war: he severely humiliates David's servants by shaving half of their beards and tearing their clothes (2 Samuel 10:4), a major affront to the honor of the king of Israel. 3. This action leads to a war that Hanun and the Ammonites lose against David's armies (2 Samuel 10:1-14). 4. Another Hanun, "the 6th son of Zalaph," contributes to the repair of the wall of Jerusalem, likely on the eastern side, during a later period in Israel's history (1 Chronicles 19:4, possibly referring to another figure named Hanun).
H2586G.origine: The name Hanun means "gracious" or "full of grace" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing kindness and favor. It is a common Semitic royal name in the Ammonite world. The contrast between the benevolent meaning of the name and the cruel behavior of the king towards David's ambassadors highlights the irony of the biblical narrative.
H2586G.emploi: Hanun primarily appears in the accounts of 2 Samuel 10 and 1 Chronicles 19, which recount the conflict between David and the Ammonites. King Hanun, young and perhaps inexperienced, is manipulated by his advisors who fear David's intentions. His humiliation of the ambassadors triggers a major war involving the Arameans as allies of the Ammonites. This conflict shows how a misinterpretation of a diplomatic gesture can lead to destruction. Another Hanun appears in 1 Chronicles, participating in the reconstruction work of the wall after the exile, possibly representing a different generation.

sens: Man who helped in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile
Inhabitant of Zanoach
Foreman at the gates of Jerusalem
H2586H.detail:
1. Hanun is a man who lived during the time of the reconstruction of Jerusalem, after the return from exile. His name means "gracious" in Hebrew. In Nehemiah 3:13, he is mentioned as the one who, along with the inhabitants of Zanoach, repaired the Valley Gate in the city walls.
2. Zanoach was a locality from which the workers who worked under Hanun's direction came. This detail shows that the inhabitants of nearby towns mobilized to rebuild Jerusalem.
3. The Valley Gate (or Desert Gate) was an important passage in the fortifications. Hanun and his team not only repaired the gate but also built over a thousand cubits of wall up to the Refuse Gate, demonstrating the extent of their contribution.
H2586H.origine: The name Hanun comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be gracious" or "to show favor." It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains a reference to God and His grace. Several biblical characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but this entry concerns only the one mentioned in Nehemiah.
H2586H.emploi: Hanun appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:13. He is listed among the builders who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, after the return from exile in Babylon. The Bible does not present him as a leader or an officer, but as an ordinary man who contributed to this essential collective work for the security and religious identity of the people returning to the land of Israel. His work on the wall, like that of many others cited in this passage, symbolizes the unity of the community in service of the common good.
H2586H.portee: This passage reminds us that the restoration of Jerusalem could only happen thanks to the commitment of many, including less famous figures. Hanun represents the faithful worker who does not seek glory but contributes to the common work of reconstruction. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how God uses ordinary people to accomplish His purposes, and how the entire community is called to participate in the common good.

sens: Man who helped in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile
H2586I.detail: Hanun is the sixth son of Zalaph, mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the account of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, after the return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. Along with other workers, he repaired a section of the wall (Nehemiah 3:30). His name means "gracious" in Hebrew. Although little known, he represents those ordinary men, often unnamed, who participated in the collective work of rebuilding the holy city.
H2586I.origine: The name Hanun (חָנוּן) derives from the root חנן (chanan), which means "to be gracious, to show grace." The suffix -un indicates an adjectival form meaning "one who is gracious" or "one to whom grace has been granted." This same name has been borne by other people in the history of Israel, including a king of Ammon during David's time, but this Hanun is simply a wall repairer at the time of the return from exile.
H2586I.emploi: Hanun is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:30. He is listed among the workers who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile around 445 BC. The Bible does not present him as a leader or an officer, but as an ordinary man who contributed to this essential collective work for the security and religious identity of the people returning to the land of Israel. His work on the wall, like that of many others cited in this passage, symbolizes the unity of the community in service of the common good.

sens: Full of compassion, tenderness towards those who suffer
Who forgives and bends down towards one who has committed a fault
Who kindly leans towards one who is in need or distress
H2587.detail:
1. The word describes someone who feels compassion, who is touched by the suffering of others. It is this disposition of the heart that drives one to help, protect, and support. In Psalms 103:8, the Lord is described as "merciful" — he sees distress and responds with tenderness, not indifference.
2. It is also the quality of one who forgives rather than punishes, who refrains from exercising the severity they have the right to exercise. In Exodus 22:27, God promises to listen to the one who cries out to him, for he is merciful: he does not close his ear to misfortune.
3. For a man, being merciful means giving credit to one who has failed, giving them a chance. In Psalms 112:4, the "merciful" man is praised as one who shines through his active goodness, who does not condemn outright but offers clemency.
H2587.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "bending towards" someone with tenderness. It is found in other words of the same family that speak of grace, pity, and mercy. The image is that of a person who bends down to look at one who is below, who suffers — it is therefore the opposite attitude of pride and hardness.
H2587.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily to describe the Lord. It is a fundamental trait of the divine character: it regularly appears in the Psalms (103:8, 112:4, 145:8) and in historical accounts (Exodus 22:27, 2 Chronicles 30:9). The Lord presents himself this way in Exodus 34:6 and Nehemiah 9:17. The word also applies to righteous men (Psalms 112:4): one who follows God becomes merciful himself. Even in anger — the prophet Jonah testifies to this — God remains merciful (Jonah 4:2), which shows that his mercy is never extinguished.
H2587.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on the true nature of God: not an unyielding judge, but one whose heart always leans towards compassion. It is a source of comfort for those who feel guilty or broken. And it is a call for every believer: to become merciful themselves towards those who suffer or who have failed, in the image of the one who loves unconditionally.

sens: Cell or underground chamber of a prison
Dark and narrow place of detention
H2588.detail:
1. A dungeon is a cell or underground chamber, often vaulted, where prisoners are confined. It is a closed space, generally dark and cramped. In Jeremiah 37:16, the prophet is thrown into the dungeons of the king's house, where he will remain for a long time — it is the harshest place in a prison, reserved for important or dangerous detainees.
2. By extension, the word designates any dark and narrow place of detention that completely isolates the prisoner from the outside world. It is less a simple cell than a true pit, an underground space where darkness, humidity, and total isolation prevail.
H2588.origine: The Hebrew word חָנוּת (chanout) likely comes from a root meaning "vault" or "arch" — it evokes the image of a chamber covered by a vault, closed on all sides. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, specialized for designating the dungeons of royal prisons.
H2588.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Jeremiah 37:16, in the plural ("dungeons"). This occurs during the arrest of the prophet Jeremiah by the officers of King Zedekiah. Jeremiah is first imprisoned, then thrown into the dungeons — which shows that it is a particularly harsh and underground part of the prison. The context emphasizes that Jeremiah will remain there for a long time, highlighting the harshness of the place. It is a technical term for designating the worst conditions of detention in a royal prison.
H2588.portee: This word reminds the reader of the sufferings of the prophet Jeremiah, persecuted for proclaiming the word of God. It invites reflection on Jeremiah's faithfulness despite imprisonment and recognizes that those who testify for God may endure severe persecutions. It is also a call to compassion towards prisoners and to justice.

sens: To treat a corpse with spices and aromatics to preserve it
To perfume, to imbue with a pleasant scent
H2590A.detail:
1. To embalm means to prepare a dead body by coating it with aromatic and spicy substances to preserve it from decomposition. It is an Egyptian practice that the Bible mentions during the deaths of Jacob and Joseph: "The physicians embalmed Israel" (Genesis 50:2), and "He was embalmed, and placed in a coffin in Egypt" (Genesis 50:26). These aromatics protected the body and manifested the respect due to the deceased.
2. By extension, the word designates the action of releasing a pleasant fragrance, like ripe fruits that "embalm" their aromas: "The fig tree embalms its fruits, and the blossoming vines exhale their fragrance" (Song of Solomon 2:13). The same gesture — covering with perfume — applies to the body prepared for eternity and to ripe fruits that give off their scent.
H2590A.origine: The verb חָנַט (chanat) comes from a root that evokes the action of coating, of imbuing with a substance. The word is specific to biblical Egyptology: it well expresses the image of the careful treatment of the deceased with spices and aromatics, a practice well attested in ancient Egypt. This root is found in other Semitic terms related to aromas and perfumes.
H2590A.emploi: The verb חָנַט appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. The first two uses concern the funerary embalming in Egypt, during the deaths of patriarch Jacob and his son Joseph (Genesis 50:2 and 50:26). These two verses document a pagan practice that the Hebrew patriarchs accepted in the land of Egypt, out of respect for the dead and adaptation to the cultural context. The third use (Song of Solomon 2:13) changes the register entirely: it refers to a fruit tree that diffuses its fragrance, showing that the verb can apply to anything that "embalms" or exudes an aroma, not just to corpses. This romantic passage uses an image of fertility and natural beauty.
H2590A.portee: For the believer, these passages remind us that death is not a taboo, but a reality that the patriarchs accepted with dignity. Embalming shows how believers, even in a foreign land, maintain rites that honor the body. The verse from the Song invites us to see the beauty and fragrance of creation as gifts from God that spread their natural blessing.

sens: to treat a corpse with chemicals and processes to preserve it
to prepare a body according to Egyptian funeral rites
H2590B.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of treating a dead body with oils, resins, and other substances to preserve it from decomposition. It is an elaborate funeral practice, especially known in ancient Egypt. In Genesis 50:3, Egypt embalms Jacob's body for forty days, a long and meticulous operation.
2. More broadly, it encompasses the entire process of preparing the deceased according to Egyptian rites: wrapping the body, mummifying it, placing it in a coffin. Embalming was a rite of honor and respect for the dead, particularly practiced for important figures like Jacob.
H2590B.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root חנט (chanaṭ), which literally means "to embalm, to anoint." This root evokes the action of putting balm or oil on something. The word belongs to the realm of Egyptian practices: it is a term that the Hebrews borrowed or adapted to describe this specific funeral ritual in Egypt, which is very different from the customs of Israel.
H2590B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 50:3. It is precisely in this context: Jacob, the father of Joseph, dies in Egypt, and the Egyptians proceed to embalm him according to their custom. This unique usage shows that the Bible acknowledges and names this Egyptian practice of body preservation, without incorporating it into the funeral customs of Israel. It is a historical detail that situates the action in Egypt and reveals the respect that Joseph had for his father by allowing him this Egyptian honor.
H2590B.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is situated in a real world, with foreign customs. It also shows how believers can honor their parents according to the customs of the land where they live, without denying their own faith. Jacob, although a patriarch of Israel, receives this Egyptian honor, and the Bible does not condemn it: it shows a certain respectful integration into a foreign land.

sens: Cereal cultivated to make bread, with golden grains in ears
H2591.detail: 1. Wheat is a plant cultivated for its grains, which are used to make bread and basic food. In the two occurrences in the book of Ezra, wheat is among the provisions delivered to the priests of Jerusalem for the needs of the temple and offerings: it is a valuable commodity, counted alongside money, wine, and oil (Ezra 6:9 and 7:22). Wheat was in Israel what it was in the West — the main cereal, nourishing and economically important.
H2591.origine: This Aramaic word (chinTah) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word "hitTah" (חִטָּה, H2406). Aramaic and Hebrew are two sister languages spoken in the ancient Near East, and the book of Ezra, partially written in Aramaic, uses this term to refer to the same wheat as the Hebrew Old Testament. The root comes from a verb meaning "to grind" or "to crush," as wheat must be ground to produce flour.
H2591.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Ezra, which is written in Aramaic for certain passages. Ezra 6:9 and 7:22 list the supplies granted to the priests of the Jerusalem temple by the Persian authority: wheat is listed alongside money, wine, oil, and salt. In these two verses, wheat does not have a figurative meaning: it is simply a material good, a concrete provision necessary to feed the temple servants. The repetition of the word in a context of supply shows its economic and practical importance.
H2591.portee: Wheat reminds us that God provides for the material needs of those who serve Him. The priests of the temple could rely on daily wheat, a sign of divine faithfulness and support even from pagan authorities. For the Christian reader, this sheds light on how God cares for those who dedicate their lives to Him.

sens: Prince of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Ephod
H2592G.detail: Hanniel is a chief of the tribe of Manasseh mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Moses organizes the distribution of the territory of Canaan among the twelve tribes of Israel. He is designated as the prince (the official representative) representing his tribe during this solemn allocation of the promised lands (Numbers 34:23).
H2592G.origine: The name Hanniel means "favor of God" or "one whom God has favored": it combines two Hebrew elements, "hen" (favor, grace) and "el" (God). This theophoric name expresses the belief that this man enjoyed divine favor. Hanniel's father, Ephod, also bears a significant name in the Bible.
H2592G.emploi: Hanniel appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 34:23, in the context of the sharing of the promised land. Moses lists the leaders of the twelve tribes who will oversee the allocation of territorial inheritances after the conquest of Canaan. Hanniel represents the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. His unique mention indicates that he was a recognized authority figure at the time of entry into Canaan.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H2592H.detail: Hanniel is a chief of the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Ulla and appears in the genealogy of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7:39, alongside his brothers Arach and Ritsja. His name means "favorite of God" or "one whom God favors."
H2592H.origine: The name Hanniel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Han" (favor, grace) and "El" (God). It expresses the idea that this person is regarded with favor by the Lord. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel to express divine blessing or protection.
H2592H.emploi: Hanniel appears only once in the biblical texts, in 1 Chronicles 7:39. He is mentioned in the genealogical record of the tribe of Asher, among the direct descendants of Ulla. This brief mention situates him in the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. Although not detailed, this passage informs us that he held a position of responsibility (chief) within his tribe.

sens: Servant trained for war, seasoned and capable
Man formed by experience, knowledgeable and reliable
H2593.detail:
1. The word refers to a servant who has received military or practical training and has proven to be trustworthy. Abram has "three hundred eighteen trained servants, born in his house" (Genesis 14:14): these are men he has raised and trained, experienced and loyal enough to follow him into battle. The image is one of progressive learning that shapes the servant.
2. More broadly, the word can apply to any man who has been trained and tested, who possesses know-how and experience. It is someone in whom one can trust because he has proven himself.
H2593.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to train" or "to form." It is related to the vocabulary of education and preparation. The central idea is one of progressive learning: one trains someone by placing him under instruction and testing him until he becomes capable and reliable. It is less a formal education than the transmission of know-how through practice and experience.
H2593.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 14:14. Abram arms servants "born in his house" — men he has raised and trained from their youth, who have grown under his tutelage and received the necessary training. It is a term that emphasizes both loyalty (these men belong to him and are attached to him) and competence (they have been trained and tested). The warrior context shows that they are reliable servants, capable of fighting alongside their master.
H2593.portee: This word reminds us that the training of servants is a work of patience and time: it is not by decree that one creates a trustworthy man, but through teaching and testing. For the reader, it invites consideration of how one can be trained by God Himself, shaped by His instruction and trials, to become a capable and faithful servant.

sens: Benevolent favor granted without being deserved
Compassion, pity shown towards one who suffers or has failed
H2594.detail:
1. Grace is a favor, an act of kindness received without having earned or requested it. It is what God freely grants, out of pure mercy. In Jeremiah 16:13, the Lord says that He will not "grant grace" to Judah: He will refuse to show her this free favor, this compassion that she might have hoped for despite her unfaithfulness.
2. Grace also expresses compassion — a feeling that leads one to take pity on someone who suffers or has committed a fault. It is the tenderness of one who could punish but chooses to show mercy.
H2594.origine: The Hebrew word חֲנִינָה comes from the root חנן ("to be gracious, to have pity"), whose primary meaning is "to bend towards someone with kindness." This same root is found in other words of the family: חֵן ("grace, charm") and חָנוּן ("merciful"). The central idea is that of a favor given freely, not as a right of the one who receives it.
H2594.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 16:13. God declares to Judah that He will not grant her grace — that is, He will refuse to show her this free compassion that she needs. It is a word often synonymous with "mercy" or "goodness," but it particularly emphasizes the aspect of a favor granted despite the unworthiness or guilt of the one who receives it.
H2594.portee: This word reminds us of a central truth of the Christian faith: grace is a free gift from God, not a right that can be claimed. It also shows us that refusing grace — as Judah did by forsaking the Lord — leads to serious consequences. But it especially invites us to receive with gratitude the benevolent favor that God continues to offer us.

sens: Combat weapon with a long shaft and a metal tip
Symbol of warrior power and royal authority
Instrument of protection and defense
Figure of divine power
H2595.detail:
1. The spear is a weapon composed of a long shaft (the wood) and a sharp metal point. It is the characteristic weapon of the warrior and fighter. Thus, Saul carries his spear into battle (1 Samuel 18:11), and Goliath brandishes a huge spear against David (1 Samuel 17:7).

2. The spear symbolizes the power of the king and military leader: it is carried only by those who have the authority and responsibilities of command. The spears of King David kept in the temple represent his past power (2 Kings 11:10).

3. In the hands of the warrior, the spear is also an instrument of personal and collective defense. David protects himself by turning away from the spear that Saul raises against him (1 Samuel 18:11), and the spear fixed in the ground beside Saul becomes a symbol of his military vigilance (1 Samuel 26:7).

4. In prophecies and psalms, the spear represents the strength of God Himself who fights for His people. The psalmist cries: "Rise up and come to my aid" when speaking of the Lord's weapons (Psalms 35:3), and the prophets announce that spears will be turned into instruments of peace (Isaiah 2:4).
H2595.origine: The Hebrew word חֲנִית (hanit) primarily refers to the simple object: a pointed shaft, a projectile weapon. It comes from a family of words expressing point and penetration. In the Greek Old Testament, this word has come to describe this characteristic military equipment. The spear is one of the oldest and most prestigious weapons of the ancient fighter, long before the sword became its rival.
