H2595.emploi: The word appears forty times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the accounts of the kings of Israel and wars (books of Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the psalms and prophecies. In the accounts of David and Saul, the spear is the weapon of choice for the jealous king who threatens David (1 Samuel 18:11; 19:9-10). It also characterizes the most famous warriors: Goliath with his massive spear (1 Samuel 17:7), or David's mighty men who strike with the spear (2 Samuel 23:18). In prophetic context, spears represent war itself: they will be turned into plowshares in the time of messianic peace (Isaiah 2:4; Micah 4:3). The word is thus concrete in military history but symbolic when it comes to describing divine power or the future order established by God.
H2595.portee: The spear in the Bible reminds us that warrior power, even that of a king anointed by God, remains temporary and subject to the will of the Lord. David refuses to kill Saul despite his opportunities because he recognizes that God alone controls weapons and victory. For the believer today, the spear also symbolizes that human conflicts are not the final answer: biblical hope announces a day when spears will be transformed into instruments of life and work.

sens: To take possession of a new house, to settle in for the first time
To solemnly dedicate a building or place to God through a ceremony
To train a child by teaching him the principles and habits he should keep
H2596.detail:
1. To inaugurate a house is to enter it and dwell in it for the first time. The verb evokes this personal taking of possession: a man who has built a new house must first settle in before going to war (Deuteronomy 20:5), otherwise another will enjoy his work.
2. To inaugurate also applies to the solemn dedication of a holy place. When Solomon completes the Temple, he offers enormous sacrifices to dedicate it before the Lord (1 Kings 8:63; 2 Chronicles 7:5): he thus marks the transition of the building to its sacred use and its relationship with God.
3. To instruct a child is to train him from his youth by instilling a direction in life. Proverbs 22:6 speaks of "training a child in the way he should go": it engraves in his heart the principles and habits he will keep throughout his life.
H2596.origine: The Hebrew verb חָנַךְ (hanakh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "beginning" or "setting in motion." Its primary image is that of taking possession: one inaugurates something by putting it to use for the first time, by opening it. This is why the word applies both to the act of dwelling in a house and to that of forming a person — in both cases, one is "putting into operation" something new.
H2596.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible. It first describes the dwelling in a house (Deuteronomy 20:5). It is then used for the festive dedication of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:63; 2 Chronicles 7:5), where the king and the people "dedicate" the house of the Lord through sacrifice. Finally, it applies to the education of children (Proverbs 22:6), where it means to instruct and train them according to the path they should follow. Its meaning thus varies from the concrete (to dwell, to dedicate) to the figurative (to educate), but always with the idea of an initial setup and a lasting orientation.
H2596.portee: This word reminds us that our relationship with God begins with a dedication: we are not merely passive believers, but temples that must be inaugurated, that is, put into service for Him. It also teaches us the importance of spiritual education from childhood: to instruct is to lay solid foundations that will bear fruit throughout life.

sens: Action of solemnly dedicating a building or object to God or for religious use
Public and festive ceremony marking this dedication
Action of inaugurating or officially putting into service a monument or statue
H2597.detail:
1. Dedication is the solemn act by which a place or object is consecrated to God — for example, a temple or an altar. It is a religious action that marks the transition of an unfinished building to its holy purpose. Ezra 6:16 recounts how the children of Israel "joyfully dedicated" the rebuilt temple.

2. This dedication is accompanied by a joyful public ceremony, often rich in sacrifices and gatherings. Ezra 6:17 specifies that for the dedication of the temple, one offered one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve goats — an impressive celebration that engages the entire community.

3. The term also applies to the official inauguration of a statue or monument, even if secular. When King Nebuchadnezzar commands all officials to come and attend the "dedication" of the statue he has erected (Daniel 3:2-3), it is a public and solemn commissioning, accompanied by the convocation of all the notable figures of the kingdom.
H2597.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to consecrate" or "to set apart for sacred use." It evokes the idea of separating something from the profane to dedicate it to God or a particular function. The root is related to the biblical concept of holiness — not merely moral purity, but belonging to God. The word also appears in Aramaic with the same meaning, showing the importance of the concept in Jewish religious life.
H2597.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, always in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount events from the Persian period. Two occurrences concern the dedication of the rebuilt temple in Jerusalem after the exile (Ezra 6:16-17): it is a moment of joy and restoration, where the community regains its place of worship. The other two occurrences (Daniel 3:2-3) describe the dedication of King Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue, a state ceremony intended to impose obedience and worship. The context shows that a dedication is always a major public event, mobilizing authorities and the population, marked by a solemn and official commissioning.
H2597.portee: For the believer, the dedication of the temple reminds us that the places and objects of worship become holy only through consecration to God — they are sacred only if they are devoted to Him. The example of the joyful dedication of the temple found after the exile invites the reader to see the restoration of spiritual life as a cause for celebration and gratitude towards God. Conversely, the dedication of Nebuchadnezzar's statue warns that one can solemnly dedicate things to false deities — it is therefore important to recognize to whom or what we dedicate our lives and efforts.

sens: action of dedicating an object or place to God
solemn ceremony marking this dedication
feast or celebration accompanying this ceremony
H2598.detail:
1. Dedication is the act of dedicating something to God — an altar, a temple, walls — by setting it apart for His service. It is a solemn moment where one acknowledges that this object or place now belongs solely to God.

2. Dedication is expressed through an official ceremony, often marked by anointing (pouring of oil) and prayers. When the princes of Israel presented their offerings for the dedication of the altar, they were performing a public ritual that consecrated this new altar for the worship of the Lord (Numbers 7:10).

3. Dedication frequently includes a celebration, thank offerings, music, and singing. At the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem, not only were sacred words spoken: they celebrated with praises, cymbals, lyres, and harps, as at a great feast (Nehemiah 12:27).
H2598.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to form, instruct, initiate." The basic idea is that of an "inauguration" — when something is inaugurated, it is "launched" or "set in motion" for the first time. Thus, dedication is the official inauguration of an object or place set apart for God.
H2598.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Old Testament, mostly in accounts of consecration. Three-quarters of the occurrences concern the dedication of the altar during its construction in the wilderness (Numbers 7). The princes of Israel presented their gifts over twelve days, performing an act of dedication that marked the beginning of worship at this altar. The dedication is also applied to Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 7:9) and to the walls of Jerusalem after reconstruction (Nehemiah 12:27). In each case, it is about solemnly inaugurating a sacred object or place.
H2598.portee: Dedication reminds us that worship towards God is not a private or invisible act, but a public and solemn affair. It also teaches us that dedicating something to God deserves joy, celebration, and commitment: one does not inaugurate a sacred work in silence, but through sacrifices, prayers, and songs that engage the whole people.

sens: descendant of Henoch, son of Reuben
H2599.detail: 1. The Henokites are the members of the family clan descending from Henoch, son of Reuben. Henoch is the firstborn of Reuben, and during the census of Israel in the wilderness, Moses enumerates the families descended from each of his sons. Henoch thus establishes a lineage that bears his name (Numbers 26:5).
H2599.origine: The word comes from the proper name Henoch (חֲנוֹךְ), which means "dedicated" or "consecrated." The suffix הִי transforms the name into a tribal adjective, following the model of other families of Reuben: one says "Henokites" just as one says "Palluites" or "Hezronites," to designate all those who descend from a common ancestor. This is a common way in Israel to group tribes and clans by genealogy.
H2599.emploi: The Henokites appear only once in the Bible, during the second census of Israel in the wilderness, in the book of Numbers. This group is among the tribes of Reuben that Moses counts when assessing the forces of Israel before entering Canaan. This mention is part of the great genealogy of the sons of Israel, intended to show how God multiplied the people from the twelve patriarchs to the clan leaders in the wilderness.

sens: Portion of a whole that belongs to someone
Land, territory assigned to a tribe or family
Inheritance, possession received
What is reserved or destined for someone by God
Food, sustenance that nourishes
H2506A.detail:
1. The part is primarily a concrete portion: a quantity of something shared among several. Abram tells his companions Aner, Eschol, and Mamre: "they will take their part" of the conquered goods (Genesis 14:24), meaning their share of the spoils.
2. Very often, this word designates a given territory: each tribe of Israel receives its part of the promised land (Joshua 18:5-9), just as the Levitical priests receive their part in tithes and offerings instead of possessing a region (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9).
3. The part can also be a personal inheritance, what one possesses from father to son. Rachel says to Jacob: "Do we not have a part in the inheritance of our father's house?" (Genesis 31:14).
4. In the deepest sense, it is the part that God intends for each person: their destiny, their lot. The righteous confess, "The Lord is my part" (Psalms 119:57); the wicked receive "the part that God reserves" (Job 20:29), meaning their deserved punishment.
5. Rarely, the word means the food itself, the portion that sustains someone, like the portion of a Levite (Deuteronomy 18:8).
H2506A.origine: The Hebrew word חֵלֶק comes from a root meaning "to share, to divide." Its basic image is that of sharing: dividing a property, land, or harvest to give a part to each. Related words express sharing, division, smoothing. In Aramaic, the same word exists in the form חֲלָק with the same meaning.
H2506A.emploi: This word appears 62 times in the Old Testament, very often in the legislative books (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) where it designates the part of the priests and Levites in the offerings, and in conquest narratives (Joshua) where it refers to the division of the promised land among the tribes. It is also frequent in wisdom poems and Psalms, where it takes on a theological meaning: the part that God reserves for the righteous or the wicked, their personal destiny. In a military context (1 Samuel 30:24), it is the portion of spoils. The word thus gains a spiritual dimension: recognizing God as "one's part" means choosing Him as one's most precious possession.
H2506A.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian life is a sharing: God's grace is distributed to each according to His will, and the believer receives their part. To say that the Lord is one's part is to confess that God alone satisfies the heart more than any earthly wealth. It is also an invitation to see one's lot, one's circumstances, as what God has reserved for them—not by chance, but by love.

sens: smooth and attractive words that seduce
sweet and charming flattery
ability to persuade with honeyed words
H2506B.detail: 1. The word designates smooth and attractive words, like honey on the tongue. They flow easily, without roughness, so that they are welcomed without resistance. In Proverbs 7:21, the adulterous woman "entices" the young man with her "smooth lips": it is a deceptive sweetness that seems pleasant but conceals a trap. 2. It is flattery in the most subtle sense: not a grand promise, but a verbal caress, words that glide, that touch the heart before the mind has time to reflect. This apparent sweetness masks a wicked intention.
H2506B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of what glides, what is smooth, without grip. In Hebrew, "smooth" and "deceptive" are often close: what glides easily escapes control. The same root produces nouns and adjectives evoking flattery, seduction through language.
H2506B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in this passage from Proverbs where it characterizes the seduction of the unfaithful woman. The context is that of wisdom, which warns the young man against the traps of covetousness. The sweetness of the words is presented as a weapon of evil, particularly formidable because it acts without apparent violence: it captures before one realizes they are captured.
H2506B.portee: The word warns us of a threat that we often underestimate: that of pleasant words serving evil. They are more dangerous than loud threats because they bypass vigilance. It is a call to listen not only to the words but to the intention behind them, and to cultivate wisdom to discern deception that disguises itself as tenderness.

sens: substance or mass that has fermented, containing leaven
breads or foods that have risen, swollen by fermentation
in sacrifices, what is expressly forbidden because of fermentation
H2557A.detail:
1. Leavened bread is the result of fermentation: the dough has risen because leaven (a fermented old dough) has been added. It is the opposite of unleavened bread, flat and compact. Exodus 12:15 clearly distinguishes "leavened bread" from the unleavened bread that the Israelites must eat during Passover.
2. By extension, the word designates the breads themselves that have risen—the finished, swollen, and fermented food. During the seven days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Israel must eat none of these leavened breads (Exodus 13:3 and 13:7): they are to be removed from the house and the land.
3. In sacrificial worship, leavened bread is forbidden: it cannot be offered as a sacrifice to God with the blood of a victim (Exodus 23:18 and 34:25), nor burned in offerings on the fire (Leviticus 2:11). This prohibition is due to the fact that fermentation, a process of degradation, is incompatible with the purity required in the divine presence.
H2557A.origine: The Hebrew word חָמֵץ (hamets) comes from a root that means "to become sour, to ferment." The leaven, which makes the dough rise, also causes a slight fermentation that makes the bread slightly sour. In biblical Hebrew, the same root produces the name for leaven (שְׂאֹר, sear) and the general idea of fermentation. Leaven traditionally symbolizes corruption or aging in biblical language.
H2557A.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the ritual laws of Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. The usage focuses on two areas: first, the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, where leavened bread is strictly forbidden for seven days (Exodus 12:15, 13:3, 13:7; Deuteronomy 16:3); second, sacrifices, where leavened bread cannot be offered or burned on the altar (Exodus 23:18, 34:25; Leviticus 2:11, 6:10, 7:13, 23:17). There is only one profane occurrence: Amos 4:5 mentions leaven in an ironic context, as an impious luxury. The meaning remains constant: leavened bread is either forbidden or defiantly offered.
H2557A.portee: For the Christian reader, the unleavened bread of the Jewish Passover foreshadows the purity of Christ, the unblemished Lamb. The prohibition of leaven reminds us that the presence of God demands purity and rejects what ferments, ages, or corrupts. The Apostle Paul takes up this image by warning the Church: "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), showing that sin, like leaven, silently spreads and corrupts. Meditating on these laws reveals how God teaches His people, through concrete and ritual actions, the holiness that the heart must imitate.

sens: Sour beverage obtained by the fermentation of wine or other fruits
Acidic liquid used as a condiment or preservative
Inexpensive drink, common among workers and soldiers
Substance that irritates or displeases
Image of what wounds or afflicts
H2558.detail:
1. Vinegar is wine or a beverage made from grapes that has fermented and turned sour. Ruth dips her bread in vinegar (Ruth 2:14), a common drink for harvesters and the poor. The Nazarite under the vow abstains from it, just like from wine (Numbers 6:3).
2. It is a sour liquid that can serve as a condiment to enhance a dish or as a preservative. Its acidic taste makes it useful in cooking, but also unpleasant when consumed pure or in excess.
3. An inexpensive drink, accessible to workers and soldiers, unlike pure wine which was more expensive. It was the daily drink of humble people.
4. Vinegar irritates the teeth as smoke irritates the eyes: it is the image of the lazy person who is unpleasant to those who use it (Proverbs 10:26). Its stinging acidity symbolizes what wounds or tires.
5. When poured on nitre (an alkaline substance), it causes a reaction: it is like singing to someone whose heart is saddened (Proverbs 25:20). Vinegar becomes an image of what exacerbates pain instead of relieving it.
H2558.origine: The Hebrew word חֹמֶץ (khomets) comes from a root meaning "to be sour" or "to be acidic." It literally denotes the transformation of wine or grape juice through fermentation. Vinegar was a common product in the ancient Near East, homemade through natural fermentation. It is a simple and concrete word that has retained the same meaning throughout biblical history.
H2558.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs and historical accounts. It first denotes a concrete and ordinary drink: Ruth drinks it with bread (Ruth 2:14), and the Nazarite abstains from it by vow of separation (Numbers 6:3). Then, it becomes an image: in the Psalms, vinegar symbolizes the affront and cruelty inflicted on the righteous (Psalms 69:22), foreshadowing the drink given to the Crucified. Finally, Proverbs uses it as a comparison for what displeases or exacerbates suffering (Proverbs 10:26; 25:20), using its bitterness and acidity to speak of the effects of sin or clumsiness.
H2558.portee: Vinegar reminds us that even the humble details of daily life can become spiritual images. It is a drink of the poor and workers, which speaks to us of Christ's humble condition. Above all, its use in passages of suffering (Psalms 69:22) invites us to contemplate how Jesus accepted humiliation to the end — even this bitter drink offered at the cross. Vinegar also teaches us, through its bitter images, how our clumsy words or actions can exacerbate the pain of others.
